en: [1] Lakṣmīdhara’s *Kṛtyakalpataru* (The Wish-Granting Tree of Duties)
The Auspicious Invocation for the Section on Liberation:
The darkness of māyā, which is difficult to dispel, has been overcome by the power of discernment arising from the declarations of Vedānta.

In the fourteenth chapter, that best of the twice-born, Lakṣmīdhara, speaks of liberation for him whose self is one-pointedly absorbed in the immeasurable, supreme Brahman consisting of consciousness, which unfolds spontaneously, and whom Sananda and others— having attained supreme bliss— desire.
The formal proposition, the introduction to liberation, the determination of the nature of liberation,
the stage of the forest-dweller, and likewise the duties of the forest-dweller— these are presented here in their proper sequence.
The stage of the ascetic (yati), renunciation (saṃnyāsa), the duty of the ascetic, and dispassion—
these have their cause in the complete abandonment of desire and the like, which is accompanied by [the cultivation of] sprouts [of virtue].
The conquest of the senses, the creation of the principles, reflection on the body,
discrimination regarding the body, and likewise the identity of the individual soul with Brahman.
[2] The utility of knowledge and action, the means of self-knowledge,
and the various forms of yoga along with their branches are, in sequence, the characteristics of those who are liberated.
The true nature of the object of meditation, the characteristics of the engagement in yoga,
the obstacles that arise therein in their proper sequence, as well as the supernormal powers of yoga;
The conduct of one whose wisdom is established, the destiny of one who has fallen from yoga,
the portents of death, the process of departure [from the body], and likewise the path beginning with light.
Thus the illustrious Lakṣmīdhara, an expert in the knowledge of the self,
composed the twenty-sixth section here in the Mokṣakāṇḍa concerning the sacred festivals (parvan).
[3] 1 — Therein, the introduction to liberation is found in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
The thought "I" is its sprout; the thought "mine" is its possession of the aggregates;
houses, fields, and so forth are its branches; and sons, wives, and so forth are its foliage.
With wealth and grain as its great leaves, nourished over many periods of time,
with merit and demerit as its flowers, and happiness and suffering as its great fruits;
A great tree has grown within my heart, pervading the path to liberation, watered by contact with the deluded, and thick with swarms of bees in the form of the desire to act.
For those wise ones who, exhausted by the path of saṃsāra, have taken refuge in its shade and possess the bliss of internal knowledge, how could there be anything ultimate for them?
But those by whom that great tree was cut down with the axe of knowledge, sharpened on the stone of the company of the virtuous— they have gone by that path.
Having reached the cool forest of Brahman, which is free from passion and thorns,
the wise attain supreme cessation, devoid of worldly activity.
Pervading the path to liberation, it is an obstruction to the way of release.
‘Vidhitsā’ means the desire to obtain. ‘Śitam’ means sharpened. ‘Vṛttivarjitām’ means devoid of mental activity. From the Mahābhārata:
“Happiness indeed is liberation in this world, yet the world does not perceive it;
it remains attached to sons and wives, and is overwhelmed by wealth and grain.”
Some, having reached heaven through sacrifices, austerities, observances, and vows, fall back down; therefore,
one should resort to that which is supremely purifying.
For they say that liberation is indeed the supreme auspiciousness.
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"Traversing the path of saṃsāra through many thousands of births,
this [being] undergoes the fatigue of delusion, obstructed by the dust of latent impressions (vāsanā)."
When that dust of his is washed away by the water of knowledge,
then the exhaustion of delusion for the traveler on the path of saṃsāra comes to rest.
When the exhaustion of delusion has come to rest, the person whose inner organ is composed attains supreme nirvana,
which is unsurpassed and free from affliction.
[5] 2 — Now, regarding the nature of liberation (*mokṣasvarūpa*), it is stated therein in the *Mārkaṇḍeyapurāṇa*:
That disjunction from ignorance which is preceded by knowledge on the part of the yogi is liberation; it is unity with Brahman and non-unity with the material qualities.

‘Knowledge’ here refers to the final direct realization of Brahman. ‘Separation from ignorance’ is the cessation of nescience (avidyā). ‘Yoga’—the specific movement of the mind that depends upon personal effort; its union with Brahman is designated as yoga.

One who possesses the yoga taught in such sources as the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* understands that liberation is "oneness with Brahman. This means that when there is this separation of the yogin from ignorance (*avidyā*), which is non-knowledge, the manifestation of the individual soul (*jīva*) in its true nature as Brahman—namely, the revelation of unsurpassed bliss—is precisely what is meant by the term "liberation. Furthermore, the absolute separation from the material qualities (*guṇa*), which is the lack of oneness with them, is also that very same thing and nothing else; this is the meaning.
As it is said in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"Liberation is the breaking of the bond of ignorance, and it is absorption into Brahman."

The qualities of nature (*prakṛti-guṇa*) are described in the *Bhagavadgītā*: "Goodness, passion, and darkness—these qualities born of nature bind the imperishable embodied soul within the body, O mighty-armed one. Thus it is said.
In the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"Having attained the state of being absorbed in the nature of that [Supreme Self], he then becomes non-different from the Supreme Self; and his sense of difference would be produced by ignorance."
When the knowledge that produces the sense of duality has undergone absolute destruction,
who will create the unreal distinction between the Self and Brahman?
‘The cultivation of that state’ (*tadbhāvabhāvanā*) is the contemplation of the self as “I am Brahman. Dakṣa [says]:
“If one does not perceive a second thing here apart from the Self, he alone has become Brahman”; thus is the position of Dakṣa illustrated.

And it is heard in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: “Having attained the supreme light, he emerges in his own form. This is the meaning here: when the knowledge of the direct realization of Brahman has arisen, because of the dissolution of ignorance—which is also known by the name *avidyā*—and upon the subsiding of the perception of difference caused by that [ignorance], one attains the supreme light, which is the very nature of Brahman; having become that, one “emerges in one’s own form,” meaning one becomes manifest in one’s innate form consisting of consciousness, bliss, and so forth. And thus:
[7] Vedāntasūtra: "Upon attaining [Brahman], there is manifestation by means of one's own [nature], because of the word [of scripture].
Likewise, after describing the multitude of worldly sufferings in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"[The state of liberation] is characterized solely by the nature of bliss, which is unsurpassed and beyond all increase."
"The attainment of the Blessed One is considered the medicine that is absolute and final. Thus [it is said].
In the *Mahābhārata*: "Nirvāṇa is the supreme bliss; this Dharma is called the highest. Thus [it is said].
Having stated that "one turns away from sufferings through the state of being a living soul," Devala says:

"He who has thus turned away is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), his bonds severed, and liberated from the sufferings of birth, old age, and death; like one asleep, like one intoxicated, or like one who has inhaled poison or smoke, he is free from the [guṇas] such as sattva, remains established in the state of the subtle elements alone (tanmātra), and attains absolute supreme bliss."

Thus ends the Sāṃkhya. "Likewise, having ceased" means that when the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of ignorance (*avidyā*), which brings about the state of being a living soul (*jīvatva*), has dissolved, one becomes Brahman. There is no tautology among terms such as "devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇa*) and so forth, because each refers to specific distinctions such as cause and effect. Furthermore, Devala has already stated previously that liberation (*apavarga*) is the absolute cessation of birth, old age, death, and suffering—that is, the absolute non-existence of birth and death. Devala again demonstrates, by means of the analogy of a dream and other examples, the absence of the experience of suffering inherent within oneself.

The fourfold purpose consists of *sāyujya* (union), *sālokya* (residing in the same world), *prakṛtilaya* (merging into primordial nature), and *mokṣa* (liberation). Among these, *sāyujya* is the state of being of one voice with the deities—such as Hiraṇyagarbha, Nārāyaṇa, Śiva, Mahendra, Soma, Sūrya, Skanda, Jyeṣṭhā, Umā, Devī, and others—by means of attaining their sovereign power (*aiśvarya*).

Residence in the same world (*sālokya*) is not explicitly taught [here] because it is a particular form of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*). Among the elements beginning with earth, there is the state of being a presiding deity (*adhidaivatattva*) and the state of being permeated by that nature (*tadbhāvabhāvitva*), which constitutes absorption into primordial matter (*prakṛtilaya*). Furthermore, for Earth, Fire, Varuṇa, Vāyu, and Sarasvatī, there is the state of being supported within earth, fire, water, air, and ether, as well as the state of being a presiding deity and the state of being permeated by that nature; this occurs through a specific yoga. "Non-return" (*apunarbhava*) is liberation (*mokṣa*). Here, "the eldest" (*jyeṣṭhā*) refers to the power of Maheśvara. As stated in the *Mahābhārata*: "Through sacrifice one attains the gods, and through austerity, the realm of Virāj."
Through renunciation one attains the station of Brahman; through dispassion, dissolution into primordial nature.
Through knowledge one attains liberation; these five are recorded as the destinies.

*Vairāja* refers to the Virāṭ, the nature of the Supreme Self as delimited by the power of the enjoyer of the body composed of the gross elements; its state. *Brahman* is the subtle [state], the Supreme Self itself as delimited by the vital breaths and the senses. *Prakṛti* is that very same [Self] as delimited by the desire to create. As stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"He is joined with the eightfold city, the subtle body (*liṅga*), consisting of the vital breaths and so forth."
For one who is bound by that, there is indeed bondage; but for one who is liberated from it, there is liberation.
When transmigratory existence has ceased, one who is liberated is released from the *liṅga*;
and that liberation is said by the seers of reality to be indeed threefold.
[9] The first disjunction is through ignorance; the second is from the destruction of passion.
But through the absence of the subtle body (liṅga), there is absolute liberation (kaivalya); and through absolute liberation, one is stainless.

The *puryaṣṭaka* is the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*). As it is said in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*: "Just as a statue made of gold, O King, which has been defiled by base metal, attains unity with a second piece [of gold] once its impurities have been burnt away by fire."
Just as one does not attain distinction [in water], so too is the state of one whose self is yoga;
having burnt away all defects, he attains oneness with Brahman.
When fire is cast into fire, it follows after its identity; being designated by that name and consisting of that, its distinctness cannot be perceived.
Likewise, having attained oneness with the Supreme Brahman, the yogi whose impurities have been burnt never again assumes a separate state; he is eternally exalted.
Just as water poured into water attains oneness with it,
so too does the self of the yogi attain identity with the Supreme Self.
"A fragment from gold" means it has become separate; "identity" means oneness. As stated in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Clarified butter extracted from milk does not again become milk;
and the Self, once separated from the qualities, does not again become possessed of qualities."
Just as milk merges with milk, water with water, and wind with wind,
so too does the yogi attain identity with That through the contemplation of Brahman.
Thus, the yogi who has attained absorption through the meditation on Brahman,
having abandoned both sorrow and delusion, perceives everything as Brahman alone.
Just as a pure crystal gem shines by its own radiance,
so too does consciousness alone shine through the light of the Person's (puruṣa’s) intelligence.
In the Mahābhārata: Just as rivers that have entered the ocean abandon their distinct forms and names,
yet do not lose their own nature, so too does the dissolution of the constituent elements (sattvas) come under its control.
This being so, how could there be the notion of "re-existence" after death,
when the living being is thoroughly intermingled and cannot be perceived as distinct?
Having truly united with another, he indeed becomes another’s dharma;
freed from karma, pure, awakened, and possessed of excellent intelligence.
Having united with one whose self is stainless, he himself becomes stainless;
for when he abandons both suffering and pleasure, he attains the state known as liberation, free from all limiting marks.
And by means of the auspiciousness of the authority of scripture and tradition,
he should be known as one who has transcended the fear of old age and death.

"And they do not maintain their own nature" means that they do not abandon their essential form, which is the nature of water. "The dissolution of existence" (*sattvasaṃkṣaya*) means the complete destruction of the individual soul, that is, the severance of bondage. "Post-mortem state" (*pretyabhāva*) means birth. "Without marks" (*aliṅga*) means devoid of the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*). [11] Likewise:
Having disciplined the self through austerity and having cast off delusive envy...
Having abandoned both desire and delusion, one thereafter attains the state of Brahman.
In the Nṛsiṃha Purāṇa: "Indeed, he who dwells in the forest and practices austerity in the woods, endowed with great courage and meditative concentration..."
Freed from evil, steadfast, and tranquil,
he goes to the divine, ancient Person.
Now, regarding the stage of the forest-dweller (*vānaprasthya*),
it is stated therein in the *Mahābhārata*:
"One should go from stage of life to stage of life"—this is the rule that has been proclaimed;
for death, ever-approaching, does not wait for one's turn.
Having procreated sons and freed himself from debt, having provided them with some means of livelihood,
and having established all his daughters in suitable positions—
Having reached the forest, one should desire to become a sage.
Yama says:
Having lived for the second portion of his life at home,
a twice-born man should dwell in the forest as a householder during the third portion of his life.
When a householder perceives his own wrinkles and grey hair,
as well as the loosening of his limbs, then he should take refuge in the forest.
Having procreated sons according to the law of dharma, having performed sacrifices according to his ability,
and having seen the offspring of his offspring, a Brāhmaṇa should take refuge in the forest.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

Having procreated sons, performed their sacraments, taught them the Veda, provided them with a means of livelihood, united them with wives, and entrusted the family responsibilities to a virtuous son, one who has manifested the signs of departure should set out for the sake of a specific mode of life. Gradually, having practiced the way of life of the *yāyāvara* [wandering ascetics], he should resort to the forest during the northern course of the sun and in the bright fortnight. Manu says:
Having abandoned village food and all personal belongings,
and having entrusted his wife to his sons, he should go to the forest, either alone or together with her.
Having taken up the Agnihotra and the domestic implements for the sacred fires,
he should depart from the village to the forest and dwell there with his senses restrained.

"Every household article" means domestic items. "The domestic fire" refers to the fire maintained according to the Smṛti rules. "Fire-appurtenances" include the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and so forth. Yama says:
"Taking the implements of sacrifice, the *agnihotra*, cows, and the equipment for his chariot, a twice-born man may go to the forest together with his wife."
Having settled that family with his virtuous eldest son,
or having entrusted his wife to him, he should depart, free from possessiveness and with his senses conquered.
Yājñavalkya: Having entrusted his wife to his son, or accompanied by her, the forest-dweller (vānaprastha),
observing celibacy, shall depart for the forest taking with him the sacred fires and the domestic fire (aupāsana).

[14] A "brahmacārī" is one whose vital energy is drawn upward (an ascetic). One who is "with the sacred fires" (sāgni) is accompanied by the three Vaitāna fires. One who is "with the domestic fire" (saupāsana) is accompanied by the Gṛhya fire.
Chāgaleya says: Having established his wife with his sons, he should go to the forest according to the prescribed rule.
A Brahmin who is without a wife may, having consigned his sacred fires, renounce the life of a householder for the life of a wandering mendicant.
Āpastamba.

Now, regarding the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*): for this very reason, one who has observed the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) enters the wandering life (*pravrajati*). For him, they prescribe: he should maintain a single fire, have no fixed dwelling, be without shelter or clothing, and be a silent sage (*muni*), relinquishing all speech except for his private Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*). Forest attire is ordained for him. Thenceforth, he should live subsisting on roots, fruits, leaves, and grasses; eventually, even these may cease. Then he should resort to water, air, and space. Among these, each subsequent practice is superior in its fruit. Alternatively, some teach the following sequence specifically for the forest-dweller: having completed his studies, taken a wife, and established the sacred fires, he begins the ritual acts, including those beginning with the *Soma* sacrifices that are prescribed in the scriptures. Having built a house, he should dwell outside the village together with his wife, his offspring, and his fires. Or, he may live alone, subsisting by gleaning ears of grain or picking up individual grains. From that point forward, he should not accept gifts. When performing the consecrated oblation (*abhiṣikta*), he should offer sacrifice. He should approach the water slowly, striking it [with his hand], and touch the water while facing the sun; this is the rule for touching water in all cases.

He should avoid alkaline substances, salt, honey, and meat. Regarding the pairs of implements for cooking or eating—such as the sword, axe, and sickle—they prescribe that he take one from each pair, give away the others, and dwell in the forest. From that point forward, his fire-offering, livelihood, waiting for alms, and shelter are ordained to be provided solely by the forest. In those rites where there are *puroḍāśa* cakes or *caru* oblations, these should be prepared [from forest produce]. Everything, including the private recitation of the Veda (*svādhyāya*), should be performed silently; he should not cause the forest to resound with the sacrificial call. He may build a shelter for the sake of the fires, but he himself should live in the open air. His place of rest should be on the bare ground. When new grain arrives, he may permit the use of old grain. Or, seeking a more rigorous discipline, he should fetch food every day, morning and evening, in a vessel. Then, subsisting on roots, fruits, leaves, and grasses, he should practice until finally he resorts to the "set-in-motion" stages: water, air, and space. Among these, each subsequent stage is superior to the preceding one in its fruit.

‘From this very *brahmacarya*’: from that state of celibate studentship. ‘Having a single fire (*ekāgniḥ*)’: when the student becomes a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), then a single worldly fire is to be brought forth. ‘Without a dwelling (*aniketaḥ*’): devoid of a house. ‘Without comfort (*aśarmā*)’: devoid of pleasure. ‘Without refuge (*aśaraṇaḥ*)’: lacking a protector. ‘A sage (*muniḥ*)’: one who observes silence. ‘Engaged finally (*antataḥ pravṛttāni*)’: having spent some time on wild grains such as *nīvāra* and the like, he should thereafter pass his time with roots and so forth, down to grass. ‘Finally (*antataḥ*)’: subsisting by taking only those very roots and so forth that have fallen through wind and the like, without causing injury, he should live. ‘He should resort to (*abhiniḥśrayet*)’: he should become [thus]. ‘Those rites inferior to the Soma sacrifice (*somāvarārdhyāni*)’: the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other rites prior to the Soma sacrifice. ‘Anointed (*abhiṣiktaḥ*)’: bathed. ‘Striking (*abhighnan*)’: striking the water with his hand to drive away aquatic creatures. ‘For him, a pair of implements (*tasya dvandvaṃ dravyāṇām*)’: they teach that for that forest-dweller, a pair of each prescribed implement, such as a sickle and so forth, is to be taken up. ‘With forest [produce] (*āraṇyena*)’: the remainder is that it should be with forest produce such as fruits and the like. ‘Hospitality (*pratīkṣā*)’: the reception of guests. ‘And the entire section of silent rites (*sarvaṃ copāṃśukarmakāṇḍam*)’: every rite must be performed silently. ‘He should not announce the forest [produce] (*nāraṇyam abhyāśrāvayet*)’: he should not announce the sacrificial offering (*havir*) excessively with mantras and the like, nor with loud tones. Even the mantra should be recited only in the middle pitch. ‘A shelter for the sake of the fire (*agnyarthaṃ śaraṇam*)’: he should build a hut; the remainder is that he should not make beds or seats for his own sake. ‘He should permit old [food] (*purāṇam anujānīyāt*)’: the remainder is that he should give old food to the Brahmins. ‘Every day with a vessel (*anvaham eva pātreṇa*)’: by this, the practice of not storing for the morrow (*aśvastanavṛtti*) is expressed.
[17] 4 — Now, the duties of the forest-dweller; regarding this, Manu says:
With various kinds of pure food fit for sages, or with vegetables, roots, and fruits,
he should perform these very great sacrifices according to the prescribed rule.
He should wear either a skin or a garment of bark; he should bathe in the evening as well as in the morning;
and he should always bear matted hair, as well as a beard, body hair, and nails.
From whatever he may eat, he should offer a portion as a bali-oblation and give alms according to his ability;
he should honor a guest who has arrived at his hermitage with water, roots, fruits, or alms-food.
One should be constantly devoted to the private recitation of the scriptures, self-controlled, friendly, and composed;
one should always be a giver, never a taker, and compassionate toward all living beings.
He should perform the Vaitānika Agnihotra according to the rules,
not omitting the Darśa and Paurṇamāsa sacrifices at their proper times through yoga.
One should perform the Ṛkṣeṣṭi, the Āgrayaṇa, and the Cāturmāsya sacrifices,
as well as the Uttarāyaṇa and Dakṣāyaṇa rites in their proper sequence.
With pure forest foods fit for sages, gathered by himself during the spring and autumn seasons,
he should separately prepare the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) and the cooked oblations (caru).
[18] Having offered that most pure forest-grown oblation to the deities,
he should consume the remainder, as well as salt prepared by himself.
Vegetables growing on land or in water, flowers, roots, and fruits,
as well as other oils produced from fruits, provided they originate from pure trees.
One should avoid honey, meat, mushrooms growing from the ground,
bhūstṛṇa grass, siddhaka, and the fruits of the śleṣmātaka tree.
One should not eat what has been ploughed by a plowshare, even if it has been discarded by someone; nor, even when distressed, should one eat flowers or fruits that have become stale.

The *ṛkṣeṣṭis* (star-sacrifices) are those mentioned in the *Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa*, beginning with the words, "Agni, indeed, desired... The *uttarāyaṇa* (northern course) is that described in the *Āpastamba Sūtra*: "Having performed the sacrifices for a year... The *dakṣasyāyana* is the Dākṣāyaṇa sacrifice. The *bhauma* (earth-born) is here well known among forest-dwellers as *gojihvikā* (a type of plant). Regarding *kavakas* (mushrooms), although their consumption is already prohibited by the rule against eating things of "twice-born" origin, this specific prohibition is reiterated so that the same expiatory rite applies to the eating of *bhūstṛṇa* (a grass) and similar substances as well. Yama says: "Roots and fruits grown without cultivation, and other grains gathered [wild]..."
One should offer food fit for sacrifice at the five great sacrifices.
For whichever [deity], one should likewise properly prepare the sacrificial oblation separately according to the Śrāvaṇa rite;
one should perform the ritual ablutions morning and evening.
[The grains are] bamboo-seeds, śyāmāka, nīvāra, tantuya, yodha, and gavedhuka.
One should consume fruits and avoid cooked meat;
one may eat roots, flowers, fruits, and leaves, whether grown on land or in water, during the daytime.
One should eat [the leaves] having gathered them oneself, and one should avoid what has been plucked;
for while one may take the leaf, one should not take the flower.
From where one might take a flower, from there one should not take the fruit;
and from where one might take the fruit, from there one should not take the wood.
One should dwell in the shade of that tree from which one should not take anything;
one should not harm gadflies or mosquitoes, and one should endure cold and heat.
Drying up his own body through austerity, he shall attain perfection;
he should not eat anything at night, but when thirsty, he may drink water.
A twice-born man should always dwell constantly among all living beings with self-restraint.
Chāgaleya says:
One's food should consist of vegetables, roots, and fruits, as well as wild sesame flowers; or else, it should be wild rice, meat, or indeed forest produce alone.
During the rainy season, having set aside the fruits and grains for the new harvest,
he should prepare his own salt, while abstaining from honey and meat.
Contented with the supreme within, having conquered anger and subdued the senses,
one should always be devoted to meditation at night and avoid sleep and laziness.
In this context, it is stated that only meat obtained from the killing of tigers and other such animals is fit for consumption, and no other. Yājñavalkya says:
"Self-controlled, bathing at the three periods of the day, abstaining from accepting gifts, devoted to Vedic study, disposed toward giving, and intent on the welfare of all beings."
[20] Bṛhaspati says: He should wear either a skin or a bark garment, being devoid of an umbrella and shoes.
Sumantu said: The fire-ritual, ritual bathing, sleeping on the ground, matted hair and deerskin,
forest food, and dwelling in the forest are proclaimed as the duties of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha).

Vasiṣṭha: Having established the sacred fire according to the Śrāvaṇaka rite, he shall be one who maintains the consecrated fires. After six months, he may dwell at the foot of trees, remaining without fire and without a fixed dwelling. He should make offerings to the gods, the ancestors, and men; such a person shall go to eternal heaven.
Bhartṛyajña states that the *Vaikhānasa* scripture is called *śrāvaṇaka* because it is to be recited (*śrāvaṇa*). The meaning is: "according to the procedure prescribed therein."

He should be a refuge for all beings, delighting in sharing, free from envy, and avoiding slander, calumny, and falsehood. Being pure, he should not enter a village. Dwelling in the forest, he should offer a portion of fodder or a sacrificial pap (caru) for the sake of the animals. During the festival periods, he should honor the gods with their respective shares. Devoted solely to the single fire, he should not consume food discarded by others or obtained from those living in other stages of life (āśramas). He should step upon ground that has been thoroughly cleansed and sprinkled. He should place the sacrificial vessels on the fire after they have been consecrated with mantras.
[21] Bodhāyana says: Established in the forest, contented, fond of skins, rags, and deerskins,
devoted to the service of the gods, the Brahmins, and the sacred fire, he is an ascetic engaged in austerity.
On that day, she adopted a difficult and irremediable mode of life, one shared with beasts and birds,
sustained by a diet of astringent and bitter herbs, and maintained by the resources available at the moment of her birth.
Having embraced this auspicious way of life, which is avoided by the wicked,
and having taken refuge in dwelling in the forest, a Brahmin does not come to grief.
Moving about together with the deer and dwelling together with them—
such a way of life is the manifest characteristic of heaven.
Gautama states: "One should not stand upon ploughed land, nor should one enter a village. Devala says:

"Compassion toward all living beings, contentment of heart, concern for the avoidance of sin, and the renunciation of all enjoyments; sleeping always on one of these—earth, stone, grass, sand, or gravel; constant awareness of sentient beings, righteousness, uprightness, and lack of arrogance.
Here, "anukrośa" means compassion (*dayā*). Paiṭhīnasi [says]:

The forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), having gone to the wilderness and performed the *brāhmī* sacrifice, having paid homage to the fire with the words "O fire, O smoke," should live on forest produce—subsisting on wild rice (*nīvāra*), *iṅguda*, jujube (*badara*), and leafy vegetables—while performing libations for guests, ancestors, and deities. By eating at night, during the day, or at midnight, or by observing fasts for two, three, four, or more nights, becoming coarse, greyish, emaciated, hairy, and covered with veins, or practicing the way of the deer, he should subdue the collection of his senses. Or, he may follow the mode of life of the wandering ascetics (*yāyāvara*).

‘Brāhmī’ means having Brahman as its deity. Regarding the passage beginning with “by night and by day,” Bodhāyana states that there is an option concerning eating at these times, which is prescribed in consideration of one’s capacity.

Now, there are two types of forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*): those who cook their food and those who do not cook. Among them, the cooks are of five kinds: those who subsist on all forest produce, those who eat grain that has been dehusked, those who eat tubers and roots, those who eat fruits, and those who eat vegetables. Among these, those who subsist on all forest produce are of two kinds: those who resort to various forest areas, namely the *indrāvasikta* (those watered by Indra) and the *retovasikta* (those watered by seed). Therein, the *indrāvasikta* are those who, having gathered [grain] from creepers, shrubs, and trees, perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice morning and evening, give to ascetics, guests, and others, and then eat the remainder. For those who subsist on tubers, roots, fruits, and vegetables, there are likewise five [non-cooking types]: the non-cookers, the surface-divers (*unmajjaka*), the opportunistic eaters (*pravṛttāśin*), the mouth-gatherers (*mukhenādāyin*), and those who subsist on water or air. Among these, the "surface-divers" are those who gather with their hands, excluding the use of metal or stone tools; the "opportunistic eaters" [eat what comes to them]; the "mouth-gatherers" take [food] with their mouths; the "water-subsisters" subsist solely on water; and the "air-eaters" are those who abstain from food entirely. These ten initiations are prescribed for the *vaikhānasas*. Having undertaken the rules of their own scripture—staff-bearing, silence, benevolence, and vigilance—the *vaikhānasas* attain perfection through fasting; such is the scriptural injunction for all Brahman-forest-dwellers.

Hārīta: Having established the *tretā* or *śrāvaṇaka* fire, and wearing garments of bark, hemp, skin, rags, *kuśa*, *muñja*, or wooden planks, one follows the rule prescribed for the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*). The forest-dweller is of two kinds: the one who lives by his own permission (*svānujñāyika*) and the one who follows the path of the forest (*anuprasthāyika*). The one who lives by his own permission is of four types: the one who subsists on a single practice (*ekavṛtti*), the one who washes everything away (*saṃprakṣālaka*), the one who subsists by himself (*ātmavṛtti*), and the non-violent one (*ahiṃsaka*).

Living a solitary life, permitted by his teacher, he should go forth in a particular direction and sustain himself for six months on whatever he first sees among bitter, sour, salty, sweet, pungent, or astringent roots and fruits. Upon completion, he undergoes initiation again. Having gathered enough tubers, roots, fruits, bamboo seeds, *śyāmāka*, and *nīvāra* grains for one month, he consumes them on that very day; such are the modes of subsistence for those who live like the *saṃprakṣālins*, the *dantolūkhalikas*, the *mṛgopacāriṇas*, and others. One who is non-violent and does not store provisions may collect four kinds of food—withered leaves, moss, cow dung, and so forth—for half a month, four months, six months, or a year; this is one [mode]. Having brought these provisions through such modes of subsistence, he should perform the rites for the gods, ancestors, and men, and eat the remainder. Regarding the phrase "or the *śrāvaṇaka* fire," it should be understood that because he is without a wife, the *tretā* fires are absent. The construction is: "having established the *śrāvaṇaka* fire according to the rules proclaimed by the *Vaikhānasas*."
Manu says:
In the month of Āśvayuja, one should discard the food of sages previously stored,
as well as worn-out garments, vegetables, roots, and fruits.

Gautama: "One should not eat food stored for more than a year. Viṣṇu: "One who has accumulated a year's supply should discard his previous stores on the full moon day of Āśvayuja. Manu: "He may either subsist on food cooked by fire, or indeed eat only what is ripened by time."
He may be one who grinds with stones, or even one who uses his teeth as a mortar.
One should eat food at night or during the day, having procured it according to one's ability; or one may eat only at every fourth mealtime, or at every sixth or eighth mealtime.
Or he should conduct himself according to the rules of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance during both the bright and dark fortnights;
or else, at the end of each fortnight, he should eat boiled barley gruel only once.
Or he should always subsist solely on flowers, roots, and fruits;
he may either wash his food immediately after eating or store enough for a month.
He may have a store for six months, or he may have an equal amount [for each month];
abiding by the doctrine of Vaikhānasa, he uses naturally occurring fruits that have fallen of their own accord.
He should roll about on the ground or stand on his tiptoes for a day; he should pass his time by alternating between standing and sitting, approaching the waters at the times of the three libations.
In summer he should practice the penance of the five fires; during the rains, he should live under the open sky;
and in winter, he should wear wet clothes, gradually increasing his austerity.
He should perform ablutions at the three periods of the day and offer libations to the ancestors and the gods;
practicing even more rigorous austerity, he should wither his own body.
"In the bright and dark fortnights"—this is the ellipsis. "With the foreparts of the feet" means with the tips of the feet. Yama says: "Some drinkers of the sun’s rays stand on one foot;
some drink the smoke of the five fires; and some stand balanced on their big toes."
Some were devoted to the six times of the day, some to twelve times;
some observed fasts for a fortnight, and some observed fasts for a month.
[25] Some drink warm vapors, some drink soma, and others likewise subsist on air;
some drink boiled barley-gruel once during the bright fortnight.
In the dark fortnight, some drink [the milk] while others eat it as it comes;
in the bright fortnight, some drink the milk, and in the dark fortnight, they drink cow dung.
These and various other initiations belong to those great-souled ones;
and the fourth, the dharma based on the Upaniṣads, is recorded as common to all.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"Even in the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) stage of life, these four modes of subsistence are prescribed:
some are those who wash [their bowls] immediately after eating, while others accumulate for a month."
Some store up provisions for a year, while others store for twelve years;
they do so for the sake of honoring guests and for the performance of sacrificial rituals.
In the Śrī Rāmāyaṇa: "The Vaikhānasas, the Vālakhilyas, the Pṛśnis, and the Marīcipas—
these sages subsist on water and likewise feed upon air."
There were ascetics who used stones as mortars, those who used their teeth as mortars, those who subsisted on leaves,
and those who dwelt in the Daṇḍaka forest.
For the highly fortunate rishis possess a radiance equal to fire and the sun;
they dwell in the sky and likewise sleep upon the bare ground.

Likewise, there were high-souled twice-born ones with bellies and loins restrained, as well as those who went naked; they were engaged in silent recitation and likewise practiced the austerity of the five fires.
Those who eat only once every four months, as well as those who remain without food at all,
and those who perform great austerities by walking with their feet fixed to the tops of trees;
Those who practice the Dharma through non-perception, firm in their vows,
and those who stand on a single big toe, being non-violent toward living beings;
Some subsisted on grain, some on milk, and some ate only the fruits prescribed for them;
others were devoted to eating fruit alone, while still others subsisted on air.
These and other sages, knowers of dharma and lovers of righteousness,
having assembled together, came to the hermitage of Śarabhaṅga.
Yājñavalkya: One should perform rites and ritual actions pertaining to the Śruti and Smṛti with fruits and oils, and likewise [other substances]. And so it is said:
He who pricks with thorns and anoints with sandalwood paste,
remaining neither angry nor pleased, is equal toward both that person and this one.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "He should have a black antelope skin as his upper garment. In the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"He should make his lower garment and upper garment out of skins, kāśa grass, or kuśa grass; and anointing his limbs with forest-produced oil is recommended for him."

Hārīta says: One should emaciate oneself by standing on one foot, on one side, facing upward, facing downward, or by enduring the heat of the summer sun, rain, exposure to the open air, cold, water, sleeping on a bed of *kuśa* grass, on a heap of gravel, on a bare ground, on a stone, on a pestle, on a wedge, or on a bed of thorns, and so forth.
Regarding this, they cite the following:
This body, composed of blood and flesh, originating from semen and the womb,
is indeed not capable by itself of attaining the higher worlds in any way whatsoever.
Through the renunciation of wealth and enjoyments, by abandoning passion and greed,
and through dispassion, knowledge, and higher realization, one shall attain perfection by means of austerity.
Through the renunciation of desire and anger, by avoiding attachment and affection,
and through the restraint of the senses, one shall attain perfection by means of austerity.
Through ritual purity, bathing, and other rites, as well as through the recitation of mantras, burnt offerings, and the like,
and by means of austerity, one attains everything, including a divine and unsurpassed body.
Austerity is charity, austerity is sacrifice, austerity is accomplishment, and austerity is exaltation;
there is nothing impossible for austerity, therefore austerity is the most excellent.
In forests abounding with various flowers, fragrant with honey,
and in the meritorious groves of the gods, the forest-dweller should practice austerity.
The world is attained through austerity; the unwholesome is purified by austerity;
through austerity one obtains everything whatsoever that one desires in the mind.
One who knows the rules of the Vaikhānasa, established in the self of reality,
attains the supreme, imperishable Brahman, which is subtler than the subtle.

The modes of standing posture are described by the passage beginning with “sthāṇv-ādi” and ending with “ūrdhvabāhuḥ. “Grīṣmatapanaṃ” means the practice of fire-worship during the summer season. [One should] spend time through various ascetic penances (kṛcchras) and observe celibacy (brahmacarya).
Having thus spent his time in the forest, the twice-born man shall become one who dwells in the stage of the Veda (brahmāśramī).
[28] A forest-dweller does not go to heaven by means of tending the sacred fire, by self-restraint, or by various kinds of ritual bathing; he goes there by abstaining from food.
Manu says: Having duly internalized the sacrificial fires within himself,
he should be without fire and without a fixed dwelling, a sage subsisting on roots and fruits.
Exerting no effort for the sake of pleasures, practicing celibacy, sleeping on the ground, having no sense of "mine" regarding shelters, and making his dwelling at the foot of trees.
He should obtain alms for his sustenance only from Brahmins who are ascetics,
or from other twice-born householders living in the forest.
Living in the forest, he should eat eight mouthfuls after bringing them from the village,
receiving them either in the hollow of his hands, in a leaf-cup, or in a potsherd.
A Brahmin living in the forest should practice these and other initiations,
as well as various Upanishadic scriptures, for the sake of self-perfection.
These modes of livelihood were indeed practiced by the sages and by householders alike,
for the sake of increasing knowledge and austerity and for the purification of the body.
And having taken recourse to Aparājitā, he should proceed straight toward that direction,
subsisting on water and air, until his body falls, being liberated.
Having cast off his body by means of any one of these practices of the great seers,
the Brahmin, freed from sorrow and fear, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
‘Aparājitā’ is the north-eastern direction. ‘Ajihamagaḥ’ means one who moves straight forward;
[this refers to] Yama. [He is the lord] of the great-souled maharṣis who are devoted to austerity in the forest.
In the northern direction, the celestial palaces of the ascetics are seen.
And likewise, other kṣatriyas dwelling in the forest have gone to heaven,
subsisting on leaves, vegetables, water, roots, tubers, fruits, wind, and flowers.
And by employing these [practices] while remaining in the forest, a twice-born man shall go from here to heaven.
Thus ends the section on the forest-dweller’s stage of life in the Kṛtyakalpataru.
regarding the stage of life of the ascetic,
Manu says:
Having thus spent the third part of his life in the forests,
he should renounce all attachments and wander as a mendicant during the fourth part of his life.
Having gone from stage to stage of life, having offered oblations, having conquered his senses,
and being exhausted by begging and making offerings, one who goes forth as a renunciant prospers after death.
Having discharged the three debts, one should direct the mind toward liberation;
but by pursuing liberation without having discharged them, one goes downward.
Having studied the Vedas according to the rules, having procreated sons in accordance with dharma,
and having performed sacrifices to the best of one's ability, one should direct the mind toward liberation.
A twice-born man who, without having studied the Veda, without having procreated sons,
and without having performed sacrifices, desires liberation, falls from his vow and sinks downward.

‘Having dwelt’ (vihṛtya) means having wandered about; that is to say, having performed the prescribed rites. ‘He should wander forth’ (parivrajet) means he should spend his time according to the rules for renunciation (saṃnyāsa). ‘Exhausted by begging and offerings’ (bhikṣābalipariśrāntaḥ) means one who has been fatigued by the giving of alms and offerings. ‘He should establish himself in liberation’ (mokṣe niveśayet): by the word ‘liberation,’ the stage of wandering asceticism (pravrajyā-āśrama) is indicated because of its predominance. [31] Śaṅkha and Likhita.

After dwelling in the forest, when he is peaceful and his age is ripe, having renounced out of desire and having internalized that very fire within himself, he—free from fear, greed, delusion, anger, grief, malice, pride, and envy—should not worry about the future. Because the mind is unstable, faith indeed becomes uncertain; therefore, one should not wait for tomorrow. On that very day, one should renounce, casting off all undertakings and possessions. As stated in the *Mahābhārata*: "Having worn the saffron robe through the three stages of life..."
One should go forth into the supreme state, the unsurpassed life of a wandering mendicant.
"And in the three stages of life," namely the stages of life beginning with studentship (*brahmacarya*). Yājñavalkya says:

"Having performed from the forest or from the house the *Prājāpatya* sacrifice, in which all one's possessions are given as the sacrificial fee (*sarvavedasadakṣiṇā*), and at its conclusion having internalized those sacred fires within oneself..."

Having studied the Vedas, performed recitations, fathered sons, given food, maintained the sacred fires, and offered sacrifices according to his ability, one should then direct the mind toward liberation; it should not be otherwise.

Vasiṣṭha says: “A wandering mendicant should depart after having given the gift of fearlessness to all beings. Furthermore, they cite this: “For that sage who wanders about having granted fearlessness to all beings, no fear from any being shall ever arise.”
[32] But he who, having granted safety to all beings, turns back from his purpose,
kills both those born and those unborn, and he receives [the sin] of that person.
‘Nivartate’ means he falls away from the state of wandering mendicancy; this is the sense. Manu says:
“Having departed from the household, the sage, purified by sacred observances, should wander as a mendicant, indifferent toward all objects of desire even when they are present.”
‘Purified by purifiers’ means endowed with the recitation of purifying mantras. ‘When [obstacles] have been brought near’ means when they have been withdrawn.
Chāgaleya says:
attachment to the objects of passion and so forth, as well as children, wife, and [the fruits of] good and evil deeds.
The abandonment of both worldly affairs and fear is called renunciation (saṃnyāsa).
In the Narasiṃha Purāṇa:
"He by whom the house, wife, children, and field— which cause suffering— have been renounced,
preceded by dispassion and knowledge, is indeed equal to none in this world."
That Brahmin who keeps these well-guarded— the tongue, the genitals, the stomach, and speech— should renounce the world while remaining celibate and unmarried.
In the Mahābhārata: "There are four kinds of mendicants: the *kuṭīcaka*, the *bahūdaka*, the *haṃsa*, and the *paramahaṃsa*; each subsequent one among these is superior."
[33] 6 — Now follows the procedure for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*);
on this point, Baudhāyana says:

Now, therefore, we shall explain the rule for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*). According to some, one who has already completed his period of studentship (*brahmacarya*) may go forth [into renunciation] from that very state. Alternatively, it is for those of the *śālīna* and *yāyāvara* classes who are childless, or for one who is incapacitated. Or else, having established their offspring in their own duty, they prescribe renunciation after the age of seventy. Or it may be at the cessation of ritual duties for a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*). This is the eternal greatness of a Brahmin: he does not increase by action, nor does he become less. Having known the path of the Self of that very [Brahman], he is not stained by evil action.

It is called *nitya* because it leads to the state of non-rebirth; it is called *mahimā* because it causes one to attain greatness. Having shaved his hair, beard, body hair, and nails, he prepares [the following]: a staff, a sling, a water-strainer, a water-pot, and a bowl. Having taken these, at the edge of the village or at the boundary of the village, in a fire-hut, he should consume the threefold mixture of clarified butter, milk, and curds, or he may fast on water.

[34] *Oṃ bhūḥ, I enter the Sāvitrī: "That excellent splendor of Savitṛ. Oṃ bhuvaḥ, I enter the Sāvitrī: "We meditate upon the glory of the god. Oṃ svaḥ, I enter the Sāvitrī: "Who may impel our thoughts"*—thus, [reciting] by quarters and by half-verses, and then with the whole verse both separately and collectively, having led himself from one stage of life (*āśrama*) to the next, he becomes purified by Brahman; so it is known. Moreover, they cite this:
"Having gone from stage to stage, having performed the fire-oblation, and having conquered his senses..."
"Only after being exhausted by begging and alms does one become a mendicant.

That very mendicant [acts] for the sake of infinity. Before the setting of the sun, having kindled the *gārhapatya* fire, having brought the *ānvāhāryapacana* fire, and having drawn out the flaming *āhavanīya* fire—[having otherwise kindled it]—he melts clarified butter over the *gārhapatya*, purifies it, takes four portions into the *sruva* ladle, and offers a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) into the *āhavanīya* while it contains a fuel-stick, saying "Oṃ Svāhā! It is known that this is the Brahman’s *anvādhāna*.

Then, when the evening *agnihotra* has been offered, having spread grass to the north of the *gārhapatya* fire and placed the vessels upon them in pairs with their openings facing downwards, and having spread *darbha* grass in the *brahmāyatana* to the south of the *āhavanīya* fire and laid a black antelope skin over it, he remains awake for that night. A Brahmin who, knowing this, fasts through the "night of Brahmā" (*brahmarātri*), ascends his fires, and dies, crosses over all evil; he crosses over even the murder of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*).

[35] Then, having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, he performs the morning *agnihotra* at the proper time. Then, having strewn the *pṛṣṭhyā* line and having brought forward the water, he offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara. That well-known sacrifice is thus completed.

Having cast the *āhavanīya* fire and the materials for the *agnihotra*—provided they are not made of clay or iron—into the *gārhapatya* fire with the verse, "May the two kindling-sticks (*araṇī*) be of one mind for us," he then deposits the fires within himself. With the verse, "That body of yours, O Agni, which is worthy of sacrifice," he smells each of the fires three times. Then, standing within the sacrificial altar (*antarvedi*), having recited three times in a whisper and three times aloud, "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ; renounced by me, renounced by me, renounced by me"—for it is known that "the gods are indeed true to their triple word"—he pours out a handful of water, saying, "Fearlessness to all beings from me. Furthermore, they cite this:
"The sage who wanders having granted fearlessness to all beings, for him no fear arises from any beings even in this world. Thus,
he proceeds while restraining his speech.

Having taken up a staff, a sling, a water-strainer, a water-pot, and a bowl, he goes to where there is water; having bathed, sipped water, and purified himself with the *surabhimatī*, *ābliṅga*, *vāruṇī*, *hiraṇyavarṇā*, and *pāvamānī* verses, he enters the water and performs sixteen breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) while reciting the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn. Having emerged from the water and wrung out his garment, he puts on another clean garment, sips water, and taking the purifier (*pavitra*) with the words "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," he offers libations.

*Oṃ bhūḥ, I satiate.* *Oṃ bhuvaḥ, I satiate.* *Oṃ svaḥ, I satiate.* Having offered a handful of water to the ancestors with the words, *Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, mahas, namaḥ*, as one does for the gods, he satiates them. Then: *Oṃ bhūḥ svadhā; Oṃ bhuvaḥ svadhā; Oṃ svaḥ svadhā; Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svadhā; Oṃ mahaḥ svadhā.* Then he worships the sun with the two verses, "Upwards that [light]" (*ud u tyam*) and "The bright [face]" (*citram*). "Om! This is Brahman; this light which shines is indeed Brahman. This is the Veda; this light which shines is the Veda. This very thing is what is to be known. This [sun] satiates this very thing. In this very way, he satiates himself; he pays homage to himself. The self is Brahman; the self is the light."

One should repeat the Sāvitrī one thousand times, or a hundred times, or an unlimited number of times. Having taken up the vessel with "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," he takes water. From this point forward, he shall not sip water that has not been drawn out, nor that which is unstrained, nor that which is unpurified. And from this point forward, he shall not wear white clothing, or he may carry a triple staff. Now, these are the observances:

Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, abstinence from sexual intercourse, and renunciation—these indeed are the five minor vows (upavratas): freedom from anger, service to the teacher, vigilance, purity, and the proper qualities of diet.

[37] “The rule for renunciation” (*saṃnyāsavidhim*) refers to the duties pertaining to the fourth stage of life (*caturthāśrama*). It includes all the sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*), beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*). For this very reason, he is one who has lived the life of a student (*brahmacaryavān*), meaning one whose celibacy is unbroken. The phrase “of some” (*ekeṣām*) implies that this is the view of certain authorities. The grammatical connection is: they teach renunciation for a man who is “bereft” (*vidhure*), i.e., one whose wife has died. “Upon the cessation of ritual action” (*karmavirāme*) means when his capacity for performing rituals has come to an end. The word “this” (*eṣa*) is a designation for the Self (*ātman*) as described in the Vedic scripture: “by whom the sun shines. The phrase “belonging to the Brāhmaṇa” is to be supplied; by this, he shows that the Brāhmaṇa alone has the qualification (*adhikāra*) for renunciation. “And that eternal Self” does not increase through merit (*puṇyena*), nor does it become less through sin (*pāpena*); the word “sin” is to be supplied. “Of that very one,” i.e., of the Supreme Brahman, the Self is its own nature. “One who knows the path” (*padavit*): here, “path” (*padam*) is that by which one goes, namely the Veda. “He prepares” (*upakalpayate*) means it becomes possible for him. “Staves” (*yaṣṭayaḥ*) are three bamboo rods. “Vessel” (*pātram*) is the alms-bowl. “Threefold” (*trivṛt*) refers to the mixture of the three substances, clarified butter and so forth. “He should fast” (*upavaset*) means he should not eat again. “Or water” (*apo vā*) is an alternative in the absence of clarified butter and the other substances. “By quarter” (*pacchaḥ*) means by foot; “by half-verse” (*ardharcaśaḥ*) means by half-verse. [He recites] either in its entirety (*samastayā*), or in full (*kṛtsnayā*), or separately (*vyastayā*), devoid of the *vyāhṛtis*. “The Self by the Self,” etc. By the word “Brahman,” the *Sāvitrī* is meant here. “Purified” (*pūtaḥ*) means he indeed becomes cleansed of sin; such is the meaning.

Furthermore, by the mention of the *āśrama* (stage of life), it is stated that after entering the *Sāvitrī*, there is no returning again; the remainder of the sentence is: "This very mendicant (*bhikṣu*) is fit for infinity. "Having kindled" means having set fire to it. Having brought [the fuel], even in the case of [wood] from a different source, he places it in the sacrificial ground (*āyatana*) and adds fuel (*samidh*). Having placed a fuel-stick of *Palāśa* wood the size of a span, and having stirred [the fire], he places grass and *Darbha* blades in the *Āhavanīya* fire. Having spread out the vessels, the sacrificial implements, and the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*)—having laid them upon the *Darbha* grass—even at an improper time, i.e., before sunrise, having strewn the *Pṛṣṭhyā* line, and having made a row of reeds (*ulaparāji*) between the *Gārhapatya* and *Āhavanīya* fires, he throws into the *Gārhapatya* fire those [implements] which are not made of clay or stone—that is, those other than clay or stone, such as those made of bamboo; this is the sense. With the verse beginning "O Dadhikrāvan," which is "possessing fragrance" (*surabhimatī*). The "verse containing the word water" (*abliṅgā*) is the hymn beginning with "O Waters, you are most healing" (*āpo hi ṣṭhā*). The "verse addressed to Varuṇa" (*vāruṇī*) is the one beginning with "Hear this my cry, O Varuṇa" (*imaṃ me varuṇa*). The four verses beginning with "Golden-colored, pure" (*hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ*) are the "Pāvamānī" verses, namely the section beginning with "The purifying, light-winning" (*pāvamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ*). The "Aghamarṣaṇa" is the hymn beginning with "Righteousness and Truth" (*ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ ca*). The "purifier" (*pavitra*) is the water-strainer. The phrase "like a god" (*devavat*) is for the purpose of prohibiting the wearing of the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*). "Om, Brahman," etc.
The hymn ending with "the Self is light" is the syllable Om.

After the worship of the Sun, one should repeat the Sāvitrī mantra one thousand times, beginning with "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. Whenever one takes [water], then—having taken it thus with the Vyāhṛtis accompanied by the Praṇava—one should take water; this is the remainder of the sense. "With *parisrut* waters" means mixed with a water-strainer (*jalapavitra*). "Not purified" means not having had impurities removed by inspection and other such means. Some read, "either a single-staffed or a triple-staffed [ascetic]," but the commentator Bodhāyana states: "That is a faulty reading, because the preparation of the three staffs was prescribed previously. "Renunciation" refers to attachment; this is the remainder of the sense.
[39] In the *Narasiṃhapurāṇa*: "Thus, while dwelling in the forest hermitage, having burnt away his sins through austerity,
the twice-born man should proceed to the fourth stage of life according to the rules for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*)."
Having diligently performed the *śrāddha* for the divine ancestors, the gods, his own ancestors, the sages, human beings, and likewise for himself.
Having performed either the Vaiśvānara sacrifice or the Prājāpatya sacrifice,
and having established the fire within his own self according to the mantras, he may then go forth again as a wandering mendicant.
From that time forward, one should abandon affection, greed, and the like toward sons and others;
and one should offer water upon the ground as a means of salutation to all beings.
The triple staff (tridaṇḍa) should be made of bamboo, pleasing to the sight, possessed of strength, with its joints even,
four finger-breadths in thickness, and wrapped with a cord of black cow-hair.
Or, provided it is equipped with three knots and purified with water above,
the knower of mantras should take hold of it in his right hand with the mantra itself.
A carrying-net made of those very materials— whether linen, kusha grass thread, or cotton thread— should be fashioned in the shape of a lotus.
[40] A wise person, by means of the mantra, should take up a water-pot characterized by a carrying-net, or even an alms-bowl, joined with either six or five fist-measures.
A seat made of wood is prescribed—level-tipped, circular, and even;
it was practiced by those sages for the sake of purification and as a seat.
One may accept a garment to cover one's private parts, a patched cloak to ward off the cold, and also sandals; one should not make a collection of anything else.
These are declared to be the signs of that ascetic according to dharma;
having embraced them and performed renunciation, he went to an unsurpassed sacred ford (tīrtha).
Having bathed and sipped water according to the rule,
and having indeed gratified [the ancestors] with water while wearing a cloth purified by water, one should bow to the Sun according to the rule.
Seated, facing east, and observing silence, one should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) or recite the Gāyatrī according to one's ability, meditating upon the supreme state.
The capable one: whatever he may say, even when his life-breaths have reached his throat,
that [act] liberates thirty ancestors, thirty descendants, and thirty more beyond them.
By the very act of renunciation, he immediately delivers his ancestors from hell.
In the *Mahābhārata*:
"For this alone is sufficient for a mendicant who dwells in solitude:
that no one dies because of him, nor does he die because of anyone."
Lamenting piteously, afflicted and overwhelmed by old age, he dies in the midst of weeping kinsmen; such a man is no true man at all.
Having attained with great effort this human body, which is so difficult to obtain, he who does not withdraw from the cycle of existence is a destroyer of the self and the lowest of men.
[41] Dakṣa said: Even those gods, who are preeminent in strength, have been brought under control by sense objects;
what then can be said of humans, who are of little strength and prone to negligence?
Therefore, the wielding of the staff must be performed by one whose passions are matured;
otherwise, this matter cannot be accomplished, for he is surely led astray by sense objects.
Many people live by the pretext of the triple staff;
for indeed, O Brahmin, he who truly knows [the truth] is not one who merely deserves the triple staff.
[42] 7— Now, regarding the duties of an ascetic (yati): after the statement concerning the mendicant’s desire for absorption into Brahman through Sāṃkhya and Yoga, Hārīta says:

Desiring that very liberation, he should offer oblations into the fires abiding within himself, renounce the staffs of mind, speech, and action, grant fearlessness to all beings, and go to the forest from which he should not return. Without fire, without a fixed dwelling, providing for no more than the morrow, shaven-headed, clad in ochre robes, carrying the triple staff, water-pot, water-strainer, and a fine cloth to ward off minute creatures; having abandoned that state of the mind, speech, and action which constitutes a "staff" due to its nature of causing pain to others—for this very reason, there is the granting of fearlessness to all beings—the departure to the forest is for the purpose of complete renunciation.

This means: "Having done this, one should not return. Having entered the fourth stage of life (*caturthāśrama*), one must not again resort to a lower stage or to independence. The phrase "without fire" prohibits the fire used for cooking; the absence of the *śrauta* and *smārta* fires is already established. A "water-pot" (*kuṇḍikā*) is a water-jar (*kamaṇḍalu*). A "purifier" (*pavitra*) is a piece of cloth for straining water. Manu says:
"Control of speech, control of mind, and likewise control of action—he whose intellect has these fixed is called a 'triple-staffed' one (*tridaṇḍin*)."
Having laid down this triple staff among all living beings, that man who has desire and anger under control attains perfection.
Dakṣa says: One must never study, dwell, or listen [to these things].
Perfected through all of these, one becomes a *yati*, and no other.
Manu says: "One should always wander alone for the sake of purity, without a companion;
perceiving the perfection of solitude, he neither abandons [the path] nor is he abandoned."
He should be without fire and without a dwelling, resorting to a village only for the sake of food;
indifferent, free from accumulation, a sage endowed with true being.
An alms bowl, the roots of trees, wild rice, and solitude;
equanimity toward all things—this is the characteristic of one who is liberated.
One should not rejoice in death, nor should one rejoice in life;
one should simply await the time, just as a servant awaits his master's command.
One should place one's foot down purified by sight; one should drink water purified by a cloth;
one should speak words purified by truth; and one should act with a mind that is purified.
One should endure harsh words and should not despise anyone;
nor, depending upon this body, should one harbor enmity toward anyone.
One should not respond with anger to one who is angry; when reviled, one should speak kindly;
and one should not utter false speech scattered through the seven gates.
Delighting in the inner self, seated, indifferent to external things, and free from worldly desire,
one who seeks happiness should wander here with only oneself as a companion.
With his hair, nails, and beard trimmed, carrying a staff, a bowl, and a water-strainer,
he should wander constantly, self-restrained, without causing pain to any living beings.
For the sake of protecting living beings, whether by night or by day,
he should always walk upon the earth with careful observation, even when his body is exhausted.
He should generally wander during the eight months of summer and winter;
for the sake of compassion toward all living beings, he should dwell in one place during the rainy season.

By the phrase “all alone,” the abandonment of those previously familiar is expressed; by “without companion,” the abandonment of even those not previously known is stated. Seeing that success belongs to one who is solitary, free from all attachments, and devoid of the sense of "mine," he should wander alone. Otherwise, having formed an attachment to sons and others, he neither abandons them nor is he liberated from them—this is the meaning. Regarding the phrase “scattered through the seven gates”: the six [external] senses and the intellect (*buddhi*) as the seventh are meant. Since speech proceeds toward objects grasped by these, they are called "gates. Therefore, one should not utter speech regarding objects grasped by these; rather, one should speak only that which has liberation as its basis. *Kuśumbha* refers to a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*).
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "For ascetics of restrained mind, there should be wandering for eight months;
they should, however, dwell in one place for the four months of the rainy season."
For those who have entered Avimukta, no dwelling [in a physical body] exists;
there, the body shall not remain—this has been seen in the ancient scripture.
[45] Manu:
By consuming little food and by staying and sitting in solitude,
one should turn back the senses when they are being carried away by sense-objects.
Through the restraint of the senses, through the destruction of passion and hatred,
and through non-violence toward living beings, one becomes fit for immortality.
Yama said:
Free from the sense of "mine," free from egoism, free from expectations, and free from worldly desires—
he who wanders with the self alone as his companion becomes happy.
Carrying a clean wooden staff, a water-pot from the triple-heavened world, a patched garment, and a sacred, meritorious strainer, he should wander as a mendicant with light possessions.
When the path has been pointed out by the sun, he should wander the earth like an insect;
wearing a single garment or no garment at all, with a single-pointed vision and free from greed.
A righteous man, non-violent, wise, and well-composed, should wander alone for alms,
providing only for the day without storing for the morrow.
Dwelling in an empty house, in caves, on mountains, and by rivers;
or at the edge of a village, at the foot of a tree, or even in a pure temple.
Seated there with a tranquil mind, he should practice the threefold concentrations; he should assume the cross-legged posture (paryaṅka) at the corners of the staff according to the prescribed rule.
He should always sleep on the bare ground, dwell in an uncertain residence,
be a permanent resident of the forest, keep his head shaved, and practice for knowledge with his mind.
Likewise: "In the evening and in the morning, one should not eat to satiety, nor should one be addicted to eating;
one should never, out of desire, become attached to the objects of the senses."
Whether one should anoint his right arm with sandalwood paste,
or another should carve his left arm— these two persons are considered equal.

In this way, his disposition toward both the pleasant and the unpleasant would always be such that he should conduct himself with equanimity toward everything, whether it be toward what is desired or toward what is disliked.
One should be equal toward the virtuous and the sinful, and equal toward enemy and friend;
one should be equal in cold and heat, in pleasure and pain, and free from attachment.
He does not rejoice in honor nor does he become angry in dishonor;
he for whom passion and hatred are equal is a sage, free from all longing.
That man who, having heard, touched, seen, tasted, or smelled something,
neither rejoices nor desponds, should be known as one who has conquered his senses.
Free from anger and delight, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with grief abandoned and both alliance and conflict gone,
he is beyond blame and praise, and indifferent to the unpleasant—
The beloved monk wanders about just like one who is indifferent.

‘Pippalaka’ is a sewing thread; ‘tripiṣṭya’ is a tripod; ‘laghumātraḥ’ means having few belongings. ‘The road is indicated by the sun’—the remainder of the sense is that it should be so; that is to say, he should travel by day. ‘Ekavāsā’ means wearing a single lower garment. ‘But avāsās’ (without clothing) means devoid of a garment, according to the statement of Vasiṣṭha: “clad in a single (ra)śāṭī or with an antelope skin. Regarding ‘paryaṅkadaṇḍakoṇeṣu’: ‘paryaṅka’ is a cross-legged posture; ‘daṇḍa’ refers to a pillar and the like; ‘koṇa’ refers to the corners of houses and so forth. The remainder of the sense is that he should take his support upon these. Some, however, explain that when there are various types of seats denoted by the words ‘paryaṅka,’ ‘daṇḍa,’ and ‘koṇa,’ he should apply himself [to yoga]. ‘Yuñjīta’ means he should practice yoga. ‘He should dwell in an impermanent residence’ means he should not dwell long in one place. Or rather, the reason for this is given in the phrase ‘he should not be satiated in the evening or in the morning. ‘He should not be attached to eating’ is a restriction established by the scripture.
In the Mahābhārata:
One should move through the middle of the village keeping it to the right and remaining pure;
one who has not yet entered upon the practice of begging for alms should not go there having been previously invited.
He should never associate with forest-dwellers or householders; he should eat whatever is obtained by any means and sit wherever he finds himself.
And wherever he may sleep, the gods know him as a Brahmin.

The three modes beginning with "pradakṣiṇam" (clockwise) are for the purpose of avoiding erratic wandering for alms. "Anāpannaḥ" means free from calamity. "Ketitaḥ" means invited. Thus say Śaṅkha and Likhita.

He should carry the triple staff and the water-pot; he should attend to the requirements of the *pakṣma* and *pavitra*; he should be shaven-headed, wear ochre-colored garments, and subsist on alms. He should have no desire for sharing [his food], and he should avoid those who are accused, outcasts, or censured, as well as those who have done him harm. He should wear only a loincloth, be content with merely anointing his wounds, and have his passions fully matured (*pakvakaṣāya*). Expecting [the end] in due time, he should always be disciplined, delighting in the Self, and habitually free from worldly preparation. He should be devoid of hypocrisy, deceit, and pretension. He should never dwell in a single village, but be habituated to wandering because of the fault of attachment. Always skilled in the purpose of self-knowledge and discernment, he should not take pleasure in staying in one place after the rainy season has passed. He should not void urine or excrement in the same spot; he should perform his necessary duties with water that has been drawn up and purified. His purifying staffs consist of two girdles, *kuśa* grass, bark, or a wooden plank; his clothing is a single garment for protection against the cold.

‘Tridaṇḍakuṇḍī’: one who is equipped with a triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*) and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*). ‘*Pakṣmapavitraprayojanāpekṣī*’: here the word *pakṣma* refers to cow-hair (*govāla*). The purpose (*prayojana*) or utility of the cow-hair strainer (*pakṣmapavitra*) consists of purifying the vessel and purifying the water, and so forth. ‘*Kaupīnamātravāsāḥ*’: one whose clothing covers only the region of the anus; the word *mātra* here serves to exclude any greater quantity. ‘*Vraṇamātralepanaparituṣṭaḥ*’: here the word *vraṇa* refers to the body. *Lepana* means food; he should be content with that food which is merely sufficient for the maintenance of the body. The meaning is that he should not be greedy for flavors. ‘*Kālākāṅkṣī*’: he should await the time of his life’s end; the meaning is that he should not take his own life through detachment or other unscripted means. ‘*Asaṃvidhānaḥ*’: one who possesses no accumulation. ‘*Kalkaḥ*’: evil. ‘*Ātmajñānavivekārthakuśalaḥ*’: *ātmajñāna* is knowledge concerning the Self; therein, ‘*viveka*’ is the realization of the true nature of the Self as distinct from the body and other such things. He is skilled in that very purpose. ‘*Dviparidhānī*’: one who has two coverings, namely the loincloth and the cloth wrapped around the waist. ‘*Phalakam*’: a wooden board. ‘*Śītaprāvaraṇam*’: he should wear an upper garment for the purpose of warding off the cold.
Furthermore, Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"One should not excessively avoid cold, heat, wind, or rain; one should not provide remedies for oneself, nor cause them to be provided, nor approve of their being done.
The word "remedies" (pratīkāram) implies when an affliction or disease has arisen—this is the understood sense. Gautama says:

A monk is one who has no accumulation. With his vital energy drawn upward (*ūrdhvaretas*), firm in his conduct, he may enter a village for alms during the rainy season. He should wander at the last hour when people have retired. He should eat what is offered. He should restrain his speech, eyes, and actions. He should wear a garment only for the purpose of covering his private parts; having washed it once, it should be cast aside. He should not take any part of herbs or trees that has not been detached from them. He should not stay in a village for a second night except during the rainy season. He may be shaven-headed or wear a top-knot. He should avoid taking life. He should be impartial toward all beings. He should refrain from both harming and favoring.

‘Firm in his conduct during the rains’ means that he should not go from one village to another. Here, the word *jaghanya* is used in the sense of ‘after’ in relation to the act of eating as a householder. *Anivṛttam* is an adverb; its meaning is that having gone for alms and being refused, he should not return on that very same day to beg again. *Nivṛttāśī* means one who is devoid of wishing for the welfare of himself or others. *Prahīṇam* means abandoned. *Nirṇijya* means having washed. *Apartuḥ* means except during the rainy season. *Muṇḍaḥ śikhī vā* means either completely shaven or shaven except for the top-knot (*śikhā*). This undertaking is for the purpose of precluding the wearing of matted hair (*jaṭila*). Thus say Bhartṛyajña, Asahāya, and Maskarin.
Viṣṇu: "He should be free from desire; he should be free from ritual salutation. Devala:

A wandering mendicant (parivrājaka) should renounce all undertakings from the time of his initiation (dīkṣā) onwards. He should have his hair and beard shaved at the end of every four months. He should not let the hair on his face or body grow without having washed them. He should not speak of others' learning, conduct, lineage, age, or behavior.

‘Sarvārambhān’—the word ‘of houses and so forth’ is to be supplied as the remainder. ‘Where there is an interval of four months’—this is an adverbial phrase. ‘Adhautaḥ’ means one who has not bathed. [50] Devala says again:

That monk, preeminent in freedom from passion and compassion, though wearing ochre robes and shaven-headed, was intent on the triple staff, water-pot, strainer, alms-bowl, and sandals; clad only in a patched garment, he delighted in knowledge and rejoiced in the Self. Unassociated with kinsmen, he was indifferent to them. Transcending others, his sins were exhausted and gone; he regarded clay and gold as equal, was unattached even to his own mother, and remained impartial. He was the same toward friend and foe, free from possessions, a proclaimer of Brahman, living by means of auspicious conduct and refined observances. And these are the duties of an ascetic: [freedom from] the crest-jewel, wealth, grain, enjoyment of sense-objects, social contact, envy, pride, delusion, deceit, joy, hostility, wonder, dispute, fear, speculation, and drowsiness.

Vasiṣṭha says: Shaven-headed, free from the sense of "mine," and without possessions, he should go for alms to seven houses that have not been previously designated, while the smoke has ceased and the pestle is at rest. Clad in a single garment, or wearing an antelope skin, with his body covered by grass cropped by cows; sleeping on the bare ground, he should dwell in a transient lodging—at the edge of a village, in a temple, in an empty house, or at the foot of a tree. Studying knowledge with the mind alone, he should not wander about when domestic animals are visible. Moreover, they cite this: "For one who dwells constantly in the forest and has conquered his senses..."
For one who turns away from the gratification of all the senses,
whose mind has entered into internal reflection,
and who is equanimous, there is indeed certain non-returning.
With unmanifest signs, manifest conduct, and the appearance of a madman though not mad; as they also say:
"There is no liberation for one who delights in the science of grammar, nor for one who delights in gaining worldly fame."
Not for one who is proud of food and clothing, nor for one who is fond of pleasant dwellings.
"He who has no attachment to a hut, nor to water, nor to clothing, nor to the three hearths;
nor to a house, nor to a seat, nor to food—he indeed is a knower of liberation. Thus it is said.

He should eat only what he obtains from a Brāhmaṇa household. He should avoid honey and meat at both morning and evening meals, yet he should not be overly fastidious about his food.
