He may live either in a village or in the forest. He should be straightforward, free from deceit, not seeking refuge in falsehood, and not fickle. He should not form attachments to anything through the senses. Being indifferent toward all beings by avoiding both injury and undue favor, he should abandon slander, envy, pride, egoism, lack of faith, dishonesty, self-praise, disparagement of others, hypocrisy, greed, delusion, anger, and jealousy. Among all stages of life (*āśrama*), he who is most righteous—wearing the sacred thread, carrying a water-pot in hand, pure, and avoiding the food of Śūdras—is never fallen from the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*).

‘With his body covered by grass cropped by cows’: his body is covered with grass cut by cows. ‘He should not wander about where domestic animals are seen’: wherever he sees domestic animals, he should not remain there constantly; rather, the meaning is that he should be intent upon solitude. ‘Of unmanifested marks’: he should not be solely devoted to the effort of wearing specific external signs; rather, he should be one whose conduct is manifest. The meaning is that he should not be negligent regarding purity and other such duties. This has been stated in the Mahābhārata:

“Even though adorned, one should practice the Dharma, devoted to whichever stage of life (āśrama) one finds pleasure in; being equal toward all beings, the external mark is not the cause of Dharma. [52] The grammatical connection is: “One who is not insane should wander about in the guise of an insane person. This is for the purpose of avoiding honor in the world; some say this refers to the "Tripuṣkara" rite or the "Tridaṇḍin" ascetic. Regarding the carrying of the alms-bowl and the three wooden staffs, it is permitted that even in times of distress such as illness, one may eat food from a single source. "Most virtuous" (dharmiṣṭhaḥ) means the most preeminent among those who follow the Dharma. Thus says Hārīta.

One should perform one's duties with water that has been drawn and purified while the sun is visible; by day, one may travel from one *krośa* up to a *yojana*. One may travel from one *krośa* up to a *yojana*, excluding desolate places or fortresses.

The meaning is that speech [or movement] should not extend beyond a *yojana* from a distance of one *krośa* or more, provided there is no "desolate place" (*śūnya*), such as a wilderness (*prāntara*). Again, Hārīta says:
One should avoid making appointments, socializing, bestowing blessings, and showing anger; one should give equally and maintain an even disposition toward everyone in every respect.
And when these [mantras] are employed for the instigation of violence, the resulting karma arises from that injunction;
it causes the loss of blessings, the wasting away of merit, and the destruction of the accomplishment of one's wrath.
The water for rinsing the mouth, the strainer, and so forth, as well as straightforwardness and the hospitable treatment of monks, lead to heaven;
whereas their neglect leads both [the giver and the receiver] to hell.
When engaged in worldly activity, one who is honored increases through the power of Brahman;
but when withdrawn from activity, he may be extinguished, like a kindled fire doused by water.

Just as there is a fruit when an oblation is poured into the fire, so is there for one who takes [wealth] through active engagement; just as there is none when it is poured into ashes, so is there for one who takes [wealth] through cessation.
Therefore, a monk may accept [food] when [invitations] have been made, provided it is done without causing harm.

[53] Here, ‘ketana’ means an invitation; ‘niyoga’ means the performance of a command. ‘Bhikṣodakapavitrādyā’ (consisting of alms, water, purifiers, etc. is an adverbial compound meaning ‘ārjavam’ (with sincerity). Thus, alms and so forth are excellent when offered with sincerity; the meaning is that this constitutes the proper honoring of the monk. As for the phrase ‘for hell,’ the improper honoring resulting from commands and the like leads to hell; thus, both cases are connected to the result of hell. Again, Hārīta says:

Non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) consists of non-malice toward all living beings; it is the renunciation of actions of the eyes, mind, speech, and body; it is the restraint of the organs of action and the organs of perception; it is the turning away from egoism, desire, anger, and greed. It is the absence of longing for rewards, lack of attachment to status, and the relinquishing of possessiveness; it is the cessation of quarreling, idle talk, and curiosity; it is discipline, constant alertness, devotion to the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and a mind fixed on Brahman. It is the practice of mindfulness during the first and last watches of the night; the cultivation of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*); wandering by day and not at night, nor during the rains; not walking on uneven ground, nor descending with haste; neither agitating nor lifting [living beings]; receiving alms from the virtuous; eating only well-examined food; equanimity toward honor and dishonor, and the equal experiencing of pleasure and pain; and regarding clods of earth, stones, and gold as the same. When creatures mounted upon their bodies are being led away by means of a staff, a chowrie, a fan, or the hem of a garment, one does not move aside to avoid them.
Therefore, a monk should conduct himself with a steady gait and a composed posture, viewing all things with equanimity; as it is said:
"The sage who wanders having granted fearlessness to all beings has no fear from any being anywhere."
He who dwells in the midst of the immortal has no fear;
he is friendly toward all beings, devoted to non-violence, and pure.
Baudhāyana says:

Now, regarding that which the teachers teach concerning the *upaniṣad*—as they illustrate there: for one who is engaged in the observances (*vrata*) at the fourth, sixth, and eighth times of the day, consisting of standing, silence, the hero’s posture (*vīrāsana*), bathing, and sipping water; and who observes a diet of grain-particles, oil-cakes, barley-gruel, flour-meal, curd, milk, or fasting. In this regard, one who is engaged in silence should, having joined his teeth together, contemplate with an inward-turned face as much as necessary, according to the elders learned in the three Vedas, the teachers, the sages, or other highly learned members of the various stages of life (*āśrama*). It is understood that where there would otherwise be a lapse, one should not let it occur. One should be engaged in any one of bathing, silence, or the hero’s posture, but should not combine all three together. If one is constrained by necessity, one should follow only as much as is required; it is understood that in times of distress, there is no lapse of the constraint. This applies to one who is engaged in the practices of bathing, silence, the hero’s posture, the *rasanā* (tongue-restraint), sipping water, and the observances at the fourth, sixth, and eighth times of the day.
"These eight do not destroy a vow: water, roots, fruits, milk, sacrificial oblation (*havis*), the desire of a Brahmin, the word of a teacher, and medicine.
One should mutter the *agnihotra* mantras at dawn and dusk; one should worship the evening twilight with the *vāruṇī* verses and the morning twilight with the *maitrī* verses.

"Let him be without fire, without a fixed dwelling, without shelter, and without refuge; let the sage seek a village only for the sake of alms, and let him abandon speech during his private recitation."

[55] And it is known: "The *ṛc*s are limited, the *sāmans* are limited, and the *yajus* formulas are limited. But there is no end to this which is Brahman; one should explain that to the one who responds (*pratigara*). This is the response. In this very way, until the dissolution of the body, he is a tree-root-dweller, a renunciant of the Veda. The Veda is a tree; its root is the *praṇava*. Meditating on that which consists of the *praṇava*, Prajāpati said: "The *praṇava* is Brahman; it leads to becoming Brahman. One should wash the vessel of Brahman with the seven *vyāhṛtis*, so says Chāgaleya.
Henceforth, I shall proclaim that which rests upon the practice of yoga:
abandon both dharma and adharma; abandon both truth and falsehood.
Non-violent toward all beings in action, thought, and speech—[as stated] in the Mahābhārata:
"Abandon both dharma and adharma; abandon both truth and falsehood."
Having abandoned both truth and falsehood, abandon that by which you abandon them.
Abandon dharma through the absence of volition, and adharma through non-violence;
abandon both truth and falsehood through the intellect, and the intellect itself through supreme certainty.
Dakṣa says: One monk is as described; two are considered a pair;
three are declared to be a village, but beyond that, it becomes like a city.
[56] Indeed, a city should not be built, nor a village, nor likewise a household;
for by doing these three things, an ascetic falls away from his own duty.
For them, talk of kings and the like, or talk of alms, occurs among one another;
affection, backbiting, and envy arise from close proximity—of this there is no doubt.
For the sake of gain and honor, there is exposition and the gathering of disciples;
these and many other such elaborations belong to those ascetics who are merely impostors.
Bathing, purification, begging for alms, and constant practice of solitude—these are the four duties of a monk; a fifth does not exist.
Those emaciated by austerities and recitations, those deserving of infirmaries due to illness, the elderly, those possessed by spirits, those seeking wealth, and others whose faculties are impaired;
And a monk who is free from passion is not worthy of a dwelling by his own word alone.

The phrase "the fifth is not appropriate" means that such [a number] is superior. Saṃvarta says: "Having taken eight alms-meals, that sage—whether seven or five—the best of the twice-born should purify them all and then eat from them."
In a lonely forest, the wise man should dwell again with devotion,
alone and ever self-controlled, while others are accompanied by speech and physical forms.
Vasiṣṭha says: "Shaven-headed, free from the sense of 'mine,' and without possessions, he should wander for alms among seven houses without prior intention. Yama says:
"He should follow the practice of gathering honey, which is like a mound of an anthill."
With a mind free from anger and full of joy, for that indeed is eternal austerity.
A thousand *prājāpatya* penances and alms-gathering were once weighed in a balance;
indeed, alms-gathering alone outweighed the thousand *prājāpatya* penances.
Manu says:
He should go for alms only once a day and should not be attached to an abundance;
for a renunciant who is attached to alms becomes attached to sense-objects.

When the smoke has ceased, when the pestle lies still, when the embers are extinguished, when people have finished their meals, and when the removal of the dishes has occurred— then the ascetic should always go for alms.

One should not be despondent in the absence of gain, nor should gain cause one to rejoice. One should be content with only what is necessary for the maintenance of life, having emerged from attachment to material requisites.
One should utterly despise gains obtained through honor;
for even an ascetic who is already liberated becomes bound by gains obtained through honor.
Likewise:
"He should never seek alms by means of portents or omens, nor by the science of astrology and bodily marks, nor by instructions or discourses."
One should not approach a house that is crowded with ascetics, Brahmins, birds, dogs, or other mendicants.
Śaṅkha says: A mendicant should wander for alms at seven houses and should not beg from one who is already begging.
He should not relish [the food] with his tongue, nor should he eat in anyone's house.
[58] Yājñavalkya says: One should wander for alms with vigilance in the evening, unobserved,
in a village secluded from other mendicants, seeking only as much as is necessary for sustenance and free from greed.
Baudhāyana.

Now follows the practice of begging for alms (*bhikṣācaryā*). When the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice has not yet been performed by Brāhmaṇas of the *śālīna* and *yāyāvara* classes, he should seek alms. He should request them with the word "bhavat" (Sir) at the beginning. He should wait for as long as it takes to milk a cow. Then, having returned from the practice of begging, having set down his belongings in a clean place, having washed his hands and feet, and having sipped water (*ācamana*), he should offer the first portion to the Sun. He offers it to the Brahman with the verses "ud u tyam" and "citram. It is known from scripture: "Brahma jajñānam"—from the time of the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) onwards, the fires belong to the sacrificer himself. His out-breath (*prāṇa*) is the *gārhapatya* fire; his in-breath (*apāna*) is the *anvāhāryapacana*; his diffused breath (*vyāna*) is the *āhavanīya*; and his upward and equalizing breaths (*udāna* and *samāna*) are the *sabhya* and *āvasathya*. Or rather, these five fires reside within the self; he offers the oblation into the self alone. It is known from scripture: "That is the sacrifice of the self, established in the self, resting in the self; it leads the self to security (*kṣema*). Having first distributed [the food] to all beings with compassion, he should mix the remainder with water and eat it like medicine. After eating, having sipped water, he should worship the radiant Sun with the verse "ud vayaṃ tamasas pari," and mutter the mantra: "May speech be in my mouth; may breath be in my nostrils."
"One should eat only as much food as is required for the maintenance of life— food that is unasked for, not prepared in anticipation, and obtained by chance. Moreover,
they also cite this:
An ascetic may eat eight morsels, a forest-dweller sixteen,
a householder thirty-two, and a student an unlimited amount.
One may beg alms from members of all castes, or one may accept food from twice-born men alone; however, one may accept food from all castes, but never food from a single source among the twice-born.
Devala said:

Every day, when the sun has set, when the striking of pestles has ceased, and at a time when the smoke has subsided, he should enter the village for the sake of alms. Wandering everywhere, looking only a yoke’s length ahead, he should enter houses whose doors are open and which have been mentally designated, remaining unattached to the speech of others. Once inside, he should avoid making mental resolves, requests, deceit, hesitation, mockery, begging, or looking about. Having stood there for only as long as it takes to milk a cow, he should depart. Having obtained alms, he should not rejoice; having failed to obtain them, he should not be angry. He should not accept alms from outcasts, enemies, kinsmen, lords, the deceased, spirits, or ghosts, nor should he accept what is unobtainable or rejected. He should avoid food that is specially prepared for himself or that causes harm to others. Having taken alms free from honey, meat, and raw grain, he should eat that food in solitude—either with his bowl or otherwise—with silence and in moderation.

[60] Hārīta says: A monk should enter a village for the sake of alms using a bowl made of clay, wood, split bamboo, gourd, leaf, or his own hand. He should neither give away what remains from his meal nor discard it. [He should not revile it. He should not eat to excess.
Śaṅkha and Likhita say:

One should have a single alms-bowl made of wood, gourd, split bamboo, or clay. It should not be scrubbed with a cow-hair rope or water; rather, purification is to be performed individually [within oneself]. One should not rinse one's mouth over it, nor cast anything upon the ground. While impure, one should not touch it. Having eaten and rinsed, and having rinsed again, one should sprinkle the utensils with water, as well as whatever else may be appropriate and not contradictory. Yama says: "Vessels made of gold and those made of wood..."
A mendicant should avoid the alms-bowls belonging to other ascetics.
Whether one gives alms from vessels of gold or silver, copper, bell-metal, or iron, if one does so while pure, there is merit; but by taking [the food] oneself, one goes to hell.
Manu says:
His vessels should be non-metallic and free from cracks;
their purification with water is prescribed, as in the case of the *camasa* cups during a sacrifice.
In the Narasiṃha Purāṇa:
For the sake of his own subsistence, he should constantly practice the wandering for alms;
at the time of evening, the sage should wander among the houses of the Brahmins.
One should open the amulet with the right hand;
having placed the vessel in the left hand, one should pour out the remainder with the right.
He should go for alms only as long as there is food available from a worthy person;
then, having finished that task, the self-restrained one should set aside his bowl and practice breath-control.
Having covered [the mouth] with four fingers, being composed,
one should offer a mouthful of food together with all its condiments separately into the vessel.
Having offered food to the deities beginning with the Sun and having sprinkled it with water, the ascetic,
restrained in speech, should eat from a vessel made of leaves or a bowl.
One should never eat from the leaves of the *vaṭa*, *aśvattha*, or *arka* trees, nor from those of the *kumbhī*, *tinduka*, *kovidāra*, or *karañja*.
All ascetics who eat from bell-metal vessels are said to be defiled;
the sin incurred by one who uses bell-metal is exactly the same for a householder as well.
A renunciant who eats from bell-metal incurs all the sin of those two;
therefore, a renunciant should always wash his eating vessel with the accompaniment of mantras.
His vessel shall not be defiled, like the chalices in sacrifices;
then, having sipped water and restrained his breath, he should worship the Sun.
The wise man should spend the remainder of the day in recitation, meditation, and the study of the Itihāsas;
having performed the twilight rites (saṃdhyā), he should then spend the night in temples and similar places.
Having meditated upon the stainless Self dwelling in the lotus of the heart,
the self-controlled ascetic, devoted to the duties of a mendicant, peaceful, and equal toward all beings,
attains the supreme state, reaching which he does not return.
Yājñavalkya says:
Or else, by practicing the Veda while residing in the forest, having laid aside ritual actions,
eating only what is unasked for and being moderate in diet, one shall attain supreme perfection.
[62] Likewise:
"The *Āraṇyaka* which I received from the Sun should be known,
as well as the *Yogaśāstra* that has been proclaimed, by one who desires to attain Yoga."
Manu says: One should constantly recite the Brahman pertaining to sacrifice, as well as that pertaining to the deities, that pertaining to the self, and that which is declared in the Vedāntas.
This is the refuge for those who are ignorant; this is for those who understand thus;
this is for those seeking heaven; this is for those seeking the infinite.

The *adhiyajña* is the Brāhmaṇa portion that prescribes the performance of sacrifice. The *ādhidaivika* is that which reveals the deities. The *ādhyātmika* refers to specific mantras such as "I became Manu, I became Rudra," and so forth, as declared in the Vedānta.
[Also mentioned are] Yama, and those known as the ten, twelve, twenty, or indeed twenty-four [syllables].
One should practice breath control, eating light food and having the senses subdued.
If one should unintentionally harm living beings during the course of a day and night due to ignorance,
a penance of eighteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) is prescribed.
One should perform ten [repetitions] for an offense committed with the eyes, twenty for that which is spoken,
and one should perform three hundred or even one hundred according to the rule for that which is done with the mind.
[63] Manu: Whatever living beings a practitioner unintentionally injures by day or by night,
for the sake of purifying himself from those acts, he should perform six breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) after bathing.
Even three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) performed according to rule by a Brāhmaṇa,
joined with the Vyāhṛtis and the Praṇava, should be known as the supreme austerity.
Just as the impurities of metallic ores are burned away when they are being smelted,
so too are the defects of the senses burned away through the restraint of the vital breath.
Likewise: "One should contemplate the destinies of men arising from the defects of their actions,
as well as their falling into hell and the torments in the abode of Yama."
Separation from loved ones and union with those who are disliked,
as well as being overcome by old age and tormented by diseases.
The departure from this body, the subsequent rebirth in a womb,
and the wanderings of this inner self through thousands of millions of wombs.
The connection with suffering for embodied beings arises from unrighteousness,
while the inexhaustible union with happiness arises from righteousness and purpose.
And by means of yoga, one should contemplate the subtlety of the Supreme Self,
as well as its manifestation within bodies, both high and low.

In the Mahābhārata: One should perform action for the sake of food; one may perform even censurable acts. Food is for the sake of sustaining life; life is for the sake of desiring to know reality (*tattva*); and one should desire to know reality so that one shall not be born again.
[64] Even if adorned with ornaments, one should practice dharma, regardless of which stage of life (*āśrama*) one dwells in.
One should be equal toward all beings; outward signs are not the cause of dharma.
Although the fruit of the *kataka* tree clarifies water,
the water does not become clear merely by uttering its name.
Likewise:
"The twice-born man who renounces the world according to this sequential yoga,
having shaken off all evil in this world, attains the supreme Brahman."

Yājñavalkya says: Even a householder is indeed liberated if he possesses wealth acquired by righteous means, is devoted to the knowledge of reality, is fond of guests, performs ancestral rites, and speaks the truth.
In the Mahābhārata: "Whose words could this be that would be true— that there is no liberation from the planets— spoken by the faithless, the ignorant, those devoid of subtle vision?"
Alas, cessation from worldly life is seen by the ignorant and unlearned, who possess feeble horses, lack true knowledge, and are tormented by their own past actions.
‘Of all’: of everyone. Manu says: "This dharma has indeed been taught for those ascetics of restrained self who have renounced the Vedas; now learn the yoga of action [for others]."
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and likewise the ascetic—
these four distinct stages of life (āśramas) originate from the householder.
All these, when performed in due order according to the scriptures,
lead a Brahmin who acts as prescribed to the supreme goal.
And among all these [stages of life], according to the injunctions of the Vedas and Smṛtis,
the householder is said to be the best, for he indeed supports these other three.
Just as all rivers and streams find their resting place in the ocean,
even so do all those in the [other] stages of life find their resting place in the householder.
Furthermore, this tenfold dharma must always be practiced with diligent effort by the twice-born belonging to all four stages of life.
Fortitude, forbearance, self-restraint, non-stealing, purity, control of the senses, modesty, knowledge, truthfulness, and freedom from anger— this tenfold set is the characteristic of dharma.
Those brahmins who thoroughly study the ten characteristics of dharma,
and having studied them, follow them accordingly, attain the supreme goal.
Practicing the Dharma characterized by the ten marks with a concentrated mind,
and having heard the Vedāntas according to the prescribed rule, the twice-born man, free from debt, should renounce.
Having renounced all ritual actions and cast off the defects of action,
he should dwell happily under the sovereignty of his sons, self-restrained and devoted to the study of the Veda.
Having thus renounced all actions, intent upon his own duty and free from desire,
he destroys his sin through renunciation and attains the supreme goal.
Thus ends the section on the duties of ascetics in the Mokṣakāṇḍa of the Kṛtyakalpataru composed by Śrī Lakṣmīdhara, son of Śrī Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhāra.
8. Now, regarding detachment (*vairāgya*), it is stated in the *Mahābhārata*:
"Furthermore, detachment is the supreme method for this liberation."
And from knowledge alone does dispassion arise, by which one is liberated.
‘The supreme method’ means the highest means. ‘From knowledge’ means from the realization that saṃsāra consists of suffering and so forth.
Now, regarding the causes of dispassion, therein are the various types of ascetics.
In that regard, the Viṣṇu Purāṇa states: "O Maitreya, having understood the threefold suffering, beginning with the internal, the wise man,
possessing the knowledge and dispassion that have arisen, attains ultimate dissolution."
Internal suffering is indeed twofold: physical and likewise mental. Physical suffering is divided into many varieties; hear now about that.
By means of various ailments such as headache, catarrh, fever, colic, fistula-in-ano, cough, asthma, consumption, vomiting, and so forth.
Likewise, the suffering born of the body is divided by those known as eye diseases, dysentery, leprosy, and other ailments; you should now hear about that which is mental.
It is born from desire, anger, fear, hatred, greed, delusion, and despondency;
likewise, it arises from sorrow, envy, humiliation, jealousy, malice, and so forth.
O best of the twice-born, mental suffering also occurs in many ways;
indeed, through such defects as these, suffering is known as internal (ādhyātmika).
The *ādhibhautika* [suffering] of humans is produced by wild animals, birds, and men, as well as by *piśācas*, serpents, *rākṣasas*, reptiles, and so forth.

O best of the foremost twice-born, that suffering arising from cold, heat, wind, rain, water, lightning, and so forth, is called *ādhibhautika* (supernatural). The suffering arising from cold, heat, wind, rain, water, lightning, and so forth, is described by the most excellent of the twice-born as *ādhidevika* (divine). [Note: There appears to be a textual inconsistency in the source regarding the term used; the first half uses *ādhibhautika*, while the second half uses *ādhidevika*. Following the second half: O best of the foremost twice-born, that suffering arising from cold, heat, wind, rain, water, lightning, and so forth, is described as *ādhidevika*.
O best of sages, suffering arising from the womb, birth, old age, ignorance, death, and likewise from hell, is divided into thousands of varieties.
Within the womb, the creature of delicate body is enveloped by much impurity,
encased in the fetal membrane, with the collection of bones in its back and neck bent.
Due to the mother’s consumption of food that is excessively bitter, pungent, sharp, hot, and salty,
and because she drinks too much, the fetus experiences extreme pain as it grows.
He is no longer the master of his own limbs for extending or contracting them;
lying in the great mire of excrement and urine, he is oppressed in every way.
Then, breathless yet conscious, remembering hundreds of previous births,
he remains in the womb in extreme suffering, bound by his own karma.
Being born with a face defiled by feces, blood, urine, and semen,
his skeletal frame is tormented by the *prājāpatya* wind.
Indeed, turned head-downwards by the powerful winds of labor,
the distressed child emerges from the mother's womb with great difficulty.
Having fallen into a great swoon and being touched by the external air,
O best of sages, he experiences a loss of consciousness and is born again.
With his limbs pierced by thorns as if torn apart by saws,
he fell upon the earth like a worm from a festering sore.
He is incapable even of scratching himself, powerless even to turn over;
he obtains even bathing, drinking, and food only through the will of others.
Lying upon a bed of impurity, though constantly being bitten by insects, gadflies, and the like,
he is not capable of warding them off.
The many sufferings of birth, those occurring immediately after birth,
and those pertaining to the physical realm and so forth that one encounters during childhood.

‘The threefold affliction’ (*tāpatraya*) refers to the three types of suffering. ‘One in whom knowledge and dispassion have arisen’ (*utpannajñānavairāgyaḥ*) means one in whom knowledge and dispassion have been produced; here, “knowledge” refers to that which has Brahman as its object. ‘Absolute dissolution’ (*ātyantiko layaḥ*) is liberation (*mokṣa*).
Likewise:
“A man whose internal organ is deluded and shrouded by the darkness of ignorance.”
He does not know from where he comes, who he is, where he is going, or what his nature is.
By what bond am I bound? What is the cause, and what is not the cause?
What is to be done, and what is not to be done? What is to be spoken, and what is not to be spoken?
What is non-dharma and what indeed is dharma? In what does it abide, or how? What is to be done and what is not to be done? Or what possesses virtue and what possesses fault?
Thus, great suffering born of ignorance is experienced by deluded men who are like beasts, being solely devoted to their genitals and bellies.
Ignorance is a state of darkness; O twice-born one, the undertakings of actions and the greed for karma proceed from those who are ignorant.
The wise say that hell is the fruit of the omission of one's duties;
therefore, for the ignorant, there is supreme suffering both in this world and in the next.
A man whose body is worn out by old age, with limbs grown flaccid,
with decaying and falling teeth, and covered with wrinkles, sinews, and veins;
His eyes were completely lost from sight, with only a star-like pupil remaining within the sockets;
a mass of hair protruded from the openings of his nostrils, and his body was trembling.
With all his limbs exposed and the collection of bones in his back bent,
he took little food and had few activities because the fire of his stomach was extinguished.
His movements—walking, rising, lying down, and sitting—are performed with great difficulty;
his hearing and sight grow dim, and his face is defiled by trickling saliva.
With all his faculties no longer under his control and facing death,
he is unable to remember any of the things experienced even moments before.
When a sentence is uttered but once, the aged man experiences great exhaustion;
overcome by the sleeplessness born of labored breathing, coughing, and great fatigue,
he is raised up by one person and laid down again by another.
Treated with contempt and humiliation by his servants, himself, sons, and wife,
and with all his purity exhausted, he craved only recreation and food.
Despised even by his own attendants, with all his kinsmen weary of him,
he experiences his own past conduct as if it were occurring in another birth.
Remembering his youth, he who was once excessively tormented now places his trust [in it];
thus indeed, having experienced these miseries in old age.
[70] Hear also those sufferings which one encounters at the time of death:
the man’s neck, feet, and legs become slack, and he is then overcome by trembling.
At times overcome by dejection, and at other times possessed of a fragment of knowledge,
[he remains attached] to gold, grain, sons, wife, servants, houses, and the like.
"How will these come to be?"— thus he was exceedingly agitated by the sense of "mine," as if pierced in his vital organs by diseases as cruel as saws.
With the bonds of his life being severed as if by the terrible arrows of Death,
his pupils rolled in their sockets and he repeatedly flung about his hands and feet.
With his palate and lips parched, he makes a gurgling sound;
his throat is obstructed by a flood of humors, and he is oppressed by labored upward breath.
And from that, one undergoes a body of torment through suffering;
these and other fierce miseries belong to humans at the time of death.

“Engagements in the commencement of undertakings” here refers to those activities within the scope of forbidden or optional rites. “Omission of duty” is the non-performance of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites.
Devala says: “The suffering of one who is dying, and the suffering of a mother in her [labor] bed...”
For indeed, there is no other comparison in this world than that between those two while they are still alive.
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa: "From dwelling in the womb until the occurrence of rebirth,
every state of embodied beings is indeed nothing but suffering."

[71] Just as one considers the subsiding of hunger and thirst to be pleasure, so too does one consider the subsiding of cold and other such things to be pleasure; yet, due to a childish intellect, that is in fact nothing but suffering.
For those whose limbs are utterly motionless, who seek pleasure through physical exertion,
and whose bodies are shrouded by delusive cognition, even a blow feels like pleasure.
Likewise: by cold, fire becomes a producer of pleasure; by thirst, water [becomes so]; and by hunger, food [becomes so].
For that [pleasure] is indeed produced by the cessation of those [other states] through their opposites.
Likewise,
O Brahmin, there is no known limit to the number of sufferings arising from sinful causes that are experienced by those in hell.
O best of the twice-born, it is not only in hell that there is a succession of sufferings;
even in heaven, O dear one, there is no peace for one who is fearful and subject to decay.
Furthermore, one comes to be in the womb and is born again and again;
having dissolved back into the womb, one is born once more and then passes away.
One dies as soon as born; death is certain in childhood, or in youth, or upon reaching middle age, or even in old age.
As long as it lives, it is overwhelmed by various kinds of sufferings;
it remains like a cotton seed amidst a mass of fibers, the causes of the thread.
In the loss of wealth, as well as in its acquisition and its preservation, men always encounter manifold sufferings; likewise, so it is when their cherished desires fail.
O Maitreya, whatever object arises for men as a remedy,
that very thing becomes the root of the tree of suffering.
[72] Men do not derive such abundant happiness from wives, friends, sons, themselves, houses, fields, wealth, and so forth, as they do from that [other] happiness.
Thus, for those whose minds are scorched by the heat of the sun of the suffering of saṃsāra,
where is there happiness for human beings except in the shade of the tree of liberation?
Therefore, this threefold mass of suffering, which arises for the wise in such states as the womb, birth, old age, and so forth—
The attainment of the Blessed One, characterized solely by the state of bliss consisting of unsurpassed and extraordinary delight, is considered the singular, absolute, and ultimate medicine.
Therefore, wise men should make an effort to attain that;
O Great Sage, it has been taught that both knowledge and action are the means for attaining it.

The meaning is that she is characterized by a state of bliss consisting solely of unsurpassed delight dispelled by the multitude of rays [of her eyes]; she is of the nature of supreme happiness. "Absolute" (*ātyantikī*) means she stands in a high station having transcended everything;
furthermore, Viṣṇu is present there as impermanence (*anityatā*).
Thus, in this supportless time that flows on incessantly,
I do not perceive any such thing that exists as a permanent stability.
The grains of sand in the Ganges, or the streams of rain when Indra pours it down, might be counted in this world; but the grandfathers who have passed away cannot be counted.
In every eon, fourteen lords of the gods perish,
as do the fourteen Manus who are the foremost in all the worlds.
Many thousands of Indras and millions of lords of the Daityas have perished here through time; what then can be said of mere mortals?
[73] And many royal sages, endowed with all virtues,
as well as gods and celestial seers, have met their end through the power of time.
Those who are capable in this world of being the causes of creation and destruction—even they are overcome by time; for time is indeed more powerful.
In the Mahābhārata: "How will you travel alone along this path through the wilderness of darkness— without rest, without support, without provisions for the journey, and without a guide?"
When you are unconscious, with a steady and motionless gaze, devoid of effort and hiccups, yet presided over by labored breathing,
you are led toward a great darkness like a deep abyss.
Then where are wives, where are sons, and where are kinsmen?
For one who is now free from debt and possesses a secure livelihood,
what is the use of kinsmen, friends, or dependents? Abandoning all of them, as well as the acquisition and preservation of property, [one should seek liberation].
Having gone in an instant, it does not return.
O Brahmin, what use have you for wealth, or what use for kinsmen, or what use for a wife, since you are destined to die?
Seek the Self that has entered the cave.
Where have those grandfathers and your father gone?
You behold those of equal birth, age, and form who have been snatched away by death; how is it that you feel no world-weariness? For iron indeed is your heart.
If this person were to see Death stationed upon his own head,
even food would not appeal to him, let alone the performance of forbidden acts.
"My son, one who is about to die will not feel such despair;
however, for one whose faculties are utterly deluded, it will not accomplish his purpose."
Having repeatedly failed to exert yourself when you ought to have been vigilant,
and being distressed by the very things that inspire confidence, alas, my dear son, you are ruined!
Why do you fear death? Death does not release one who is already afraid, nor does it seize one who is unborn. Exert yourself in that which is unborn.
This boat of a body has been purchased by you with the great merchandise of merit;
hasten to reach the far shore of the ocean of afflictions before it breaks apart.
Thus, when the world is in such a state of extreme peril and oppressed by time,
one should establish the mind in liberation by relying upon very great fortitude.

‘Without a guide’ means devoid of instruction regarding the path. ‘A forest of darkness’ means impassable due to darkness. ‘With steady and motionless eyes’ refers to one who is firm, inactive, and whose gaze is fixed. ‘Entered into the cave’ refers to that which is taught in the Dahara-vidyā.
Now follows the censure of sense-objects from the Mahābhārata:
Due to the wickedness of sense objects, the restlessness of the senses,
and the instability of the mind, everyone dwells in hardships.
Pursuing sense objects, one encounters great fear,
like a kapiñjala bird flying into the shade of a hawk while in the heat of the sun.
The attachment of men toward sense objects, cultivated through hundreds of previous births,
is indeed difficult to ward off, just as an old ox is hard to turn away from the crops.
[75] Devala said: "Those things which have been eaten must be eaten again by men"— for one who has seen the reality of this matter, this world appears as a mere repetition.
In the Mahābhārata:
"For delight in the contact of touch is said to last only as long as the flight of an arrow;
this is especially true for seeing, tasting, smelling, and hearing."
Then, at that very moment, an intense sensation arises for him;
for food, whether delicious or tasteless, has alike slipped down from his throat.
For indeed, at the tip of the tongue of every being to be addressed,
there is always peace and conflict, day after day and night after night.
The effort made with the thought "I shall enjoy" is called the perception of fault;
for the downfall of all embodied beings is caused by the tongue and the organ of generation.
Like one afraid of a herd of serpents, like one fearing poison in sweet food,
or like one dreading ogresses, he approaches the acquisition of knowledge.
The phrase "the range of an arrow" (*iṣuprapāta*) is an illustration of a short duration of time.
Likewise: "But the contacts of the senses, O son of Kuntī, which give rise to cold, heat, pleasure, and pain..."
They come and go; endure them with equanimity, O Bhārata.
For that steadfast man, O bull among men, whom these do not disturb,
who is equal in pleasure and pain— he is fit for immortality.
‘Contact with the elements’ (*mātrāsparśāḥ*) refers to connections with sense objects. Dakṣa says: But one whose mind is attached to sense objects does not find liberation.
Therefore, with effort, the yogi should avoid attachment to sense objects.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"The laughter, the baring of bones, the pair of intensely blazing eyes, and the threatening gesture of the woman— "
The breasts and other parts are plump with flesh and dense; that place is the seat of semen—is such a woman not a hell?
In the Mahābhārata:
Even if one possessed a thousand tongues and lived for a hundred autumns, if he were single-mindedly devoted [to silence],
he would pass away without having spoken of the faults of women.
A woman is like glowing coals, and a man is like a jar of clarified butter;
those who are attached to them here are consumed, while those who remain detached have gone to heaven.
One should not conquer sleep by sleeping, nor thirst by drinking;
one should not conquer fire with fuel, nor a woman with desire.
Those very foul-smelling, leaking openings of women which carry impurities are indeed the objects of desire; oh, what a mockery for men!
In whichever parts of the body are utterly loathsome, therein the world remains attached and finds delight; by what means will it attain dispassion?
That which is called "woman" is a transformation of illusion, a personification of anger and envy;
a wise man should avoid that ignoble being from afar, as he would fire or impurity.
Now, regarding the censure of wealth,
it is said there in the Mahābhārata:
"There is suffering in the acquisition of wealth, and suffering in the preservation of what has been acquired."
There is suffering in their loss and suffering in their expenditure; fie on wealth that only increases sorrow!
They delude one in times of prosperity, cause distress in times of adversity, and weary one at the time of acquisition;
when, then, do enjoyments ever bring happiness?
For just as meat is devoured by birds in the sky, by beasts of prey on the earth,
and by fish in the water, so too is the man of wealth preyed upon everywhere.
For those possessed of wealth, there is constant fear from kings, from water, from fire, from thieves, and even from their own kin, just as for living beings there is constant fear of death.
Likewise:
"The wise recognize these as the defects of embodied beings arising from wealth: miserliness, arrogance, pride, fear, and even delusion."
Out of greed for wealth, men have repeatedly adorned themselves and turned themselves into instruments for the benefit of others, just as women do for their own sake.
Likewise:
Prosperities and women are as transient as the crests of waves;
what wise man would take delight in them, which are like the shadow cast by the hood of a snake?
For who indeed would desire prosperity like a flowering creeper of poison? Intoxication, which brings one under the sway of calamity, is like a drink mixed with poison.
She does not delight in virtues, nor does she turn away from the absence of virtue;
like a mad or blind cow, Fortune remains fixed only in some particular place.
Prosperity attends someone who remains inactive and sits still;
yet another, even while performing action, does not attain what is to be gained.
Likewise: "The sovereign ruler of the whole earth and he who is intent on mere travel—
the enjoyment of these two is equal, but their burdens and duties are extensive."
Now, regarding the censure of sons, wives, and so forth, it is said in the Mahābhārata:
"A man accumulates unwholesome karma out of regard for his wife."
Alone one encounters afflictions, suffering in both this world and the next.
Beings submerged in their children, wives, and families perish,
like forest elephants sinking and perishing in the lake-like ocean of mud.
O Lord, upon the loss of a son or the loss of wealth, even for kinsmen and relatives,
one encounters very great suffering that is like a forest fire.
Likewise: "Thousands of mothers and fathers, and hundreds of sons and wives have been experienced in saṃsāra; to whom do they belong, or to whom do we belong?"
Just as one traveling along a road might rest by taking shelter in the shade,
and having rested, go on again— such is the meeting of living beings.
Trees lose their color through their own innate nature;
how then could the separation of one thing from another not occur?
This is not an absolute cohabitation for anyone with anything—
not even with one's own body, let alone with other ordinary people.
For living beings once born, unions and separations are certain; like bubbles upon the waters, they come into being and then cease to be.
Enough with possessions here, for possession is fraught with fault;
for the silkworm is bound by its own cocoon.
As many kinsmen as one makes dear to his heart,
so many spikes of grief are driven into his heart.
For affection is observed to be the root of mental suffering;
through affection a living being is cast away [from happiness] and encounters the yoke of suffering.
Sufferings have affection as their root, and fears are born of affection;
likewise, worldly joy and exhaustion—all proceed from affection.
Now, regarding the refutation of heaven,
it is stated in the Mahābhārata: "One who desires heaven should perform sacrifice"— thus the Veda is constantly heard.
For the fruit is indeed conceived as the apūrva; from that, the sacrifice proceeds.
Moreover, even here in heaven there is a distinction of low, high, and middling;
even there, no contentment exists upon seeing the radiant splendor of others.
The fruit of an action performed is experienced by the doers in heaven;
yet no further action is performed, for it is consumed by the very cutting away of its root.
For those whose minds were pervaded by happiness and who had escaped calamities with their own hands,
there was now a delusion of perception as they fell, and they were overwhelmed by dust.
And when the garlands have withered, there is fear for one wishing to fall;
O Brahmin, these most terrible defects extend as far as the abode of Brahmā.
Those who partake of heaven attain it from that; therefore, one should not desire heaven.
For a man is indeed abandoned by friends, kinsmen, and those of his own kin when his wealth has become utterly exhausted.
Likewise, when his merit is exhausted, all the hosts of gods, including their lords, abandon that man.
"And 'assault arising from passion' (rasajā) means being overcome by the quality of rajas.
In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"Even in heaven there is incomparable suffering, beginning from the time of ascent..."
"From this moment on, I shall fall"—this thought dwells in my mind.
Having beheld even the hells, where great suffering is experienced,
I am restless day and night, thinking, "I shall go to that destination."
9— Now, regarding the avoidance of desire and the like, it is said in the Mahābhārata:
"The tree of desire grows in the heart, arising from an accumulation of delusion within the mind."
It has anger and pride as its great trunk and is covered with the bark of doubt.
Ignorance is its foundation, heedlessness its watering,
while envy is its foliage and past misdeeds its core.
It is a tree with delusion as its trunk and branches, causing the breaking of the limbs of sorrow,
and it is entwined by the creeping vines of thirst that lead to infatuation.
One should forcibly sprinkle the root of that latent tendency (anuśaya) with the supreme sword that is both gentle and sharp, through the power of renunciation and clarity.

‘With gentleness’ means with that which brings peace. Hārīta says: Desire arises from intention (*saṃkalpa*); it increases through expectation; and through affection, it becomes bound. This desire, characterized by longing, is of many kinds; overcome by it, the world—never truly satiated with desires—is submerged in this whirlpool of the cycle of birth and desire. This very fire of desire is such that the Veda declares, "Desire, indeed, is the venerable Vaiśvānara. Its restraint is the absence of intention (*asaṃkalpa*). [82] As stated in the *Mahābhārata*.
By every possible means, one who seeks the highest good must restrain desire and anger,
for those two are intent upon obstructing one's welfare.
Why do you not desire freedom from thirst for the desires of those who lust after sweet things?
O evil-minded one, you see the honey; why do you not see the precipice?
Whatever desires one renounces, by that much is one's happiness fulfilled;
a person who pursues desires perishes along with those very desires.
He who should attain all desires, and he who should renounce them all entirely—
the renunciation of all desires is superior to their attainment.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: Desire should be abandoned by every means; if it cannot be abandoned, then it should be directed toward the desire for liberation, for that indeed is its remedy.
Hārīta says:

Overwhelmed by the fire of anger, one becomes disregarded even by one's own kin, unapproachable, and untrustworthy. One does not deliberate upon what ought or ought not to be done, nor what should or should not be said. Possessed by this passion, one transgresses even against teachers who speak for one's welfare. One leads oneself to the world of hungry ghosts (*preta*), where, after experiencing terrible torments resembling those of hell, one is born among the fierce carnivorous animals. There, one becomes an object of slaughter for all living beings. Eventually attaining human status, one comes to be hated by all people. For anger is of the nature of darkness (*tamas*); its restraint is patience (*kṣamā*).
[83] In the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*: "Anger occurs only in fools; how could it exist in those possessed of knowledge?
For who, my dear, is slain by whom, since the person is the enjoyer of his own good deeds?"
In the Mahābhārata:
"The wise man does not become angry, nor does he become attached, nor does he despond, nor does he speak harshly."
And he does not grieve even in extremely difficult calamities, remaining by his very nature as immovable as the Himalayas.
In the Śrī Rāmāyaṇa: Blessed are those high-souled tigers among men, O tiger among men, who by means of their intellect restrain rising anger, just as one quenches a blazing fire with water.
In the Mahābhārata:
"Now, by what impelled does this man commit sin,
O Vārṣṇeya, even against his will, as if constrained by force?"
The Blessed Lord said:
This is desire, this is anger, born of the quality of rajas;
all-devouring and greatly sinful—know this to be the enemy here in this world.
As fire is covered by smoke, as a mirror by dust,
and as an embryo is enveloped by the amnion, so is this [Self] covered by that.
Knowledge is veiled by this eternal enemy of the wise,
O son of Kuntī, which takes the form of desire and is like an insatiable fire.
The senses, the mind, and the intellect are said to be its seat;
through these, it deludes the embodied soul by veiling its knowledge.
Therefore, O bull among the Bharatas,
first restrain your senses and utterly abandon this evil, which destroys both knowledge and realization.
Likewise, in the *Mahābhārata*:
"Greed alone is the great predator; from greed, evil is born.
From that evil comes descent into the lower realms, and from that one encounters suffering."
O lord of men, greed alone is the foundation for all evils;
through greed, even highly learned men commit sinful deeds.
Anger, greed, malice, slander, and envy— these, O Indra among kings, belong to those who are greedy and of undisciplined mind.
Discontent leads only to unhappiness; through greed, there is a derangement of the senses.
Consequently, his wisdom perishes, like knowledge abandoned through lack of practice.
Devala said:

Now, therefore, we shall explain the faults of sin arising from mind, speech, and body. Among these, there are twelve mental [faults]: delusion, attachment, aversion, pride, greed, intoxication, grief, the sense of "mine," egoism, fear, joy, and the vain pursuit of wealth. And among these, the threefold origin of delusion is the source of all sins.
Ignorance, doubtful knowledge, and false knowledge—this is the triad.
Consciousness consists of mastery over all branches of knowledge, the independent investigation of meanings, and invulnerability to defects; otherwise, it is ignorance.
Wandering between the unwholesome and the wholesome is doubt;
they call false knowledge the perception of benefit in what is harmful.
From unrighteousness arises ignorance, and from ignorance arises doubt;
from both together, a most wicked form of perverted knowledge is produced.
From ignorance comes the attainment of suffering; from doubt one is bound again;
and from false knowledge the deluded man surely falls into the wombs of darkness.
All objects are enveloped by defects, just as the body is;
having placed them in the heart according to their qualities, attachment arises—this is the characteristic of attachment.
From proximity, from ignorance, from volition, from self-conceit,
and from pleasure, passion for sense objects arises in embodied beings.
One desists from [the practice] due to ignorance, aversion, incapacity, affliction, attachment to something else,
separation, time, grief, and [the loss of] merit.
If this passion of a person is turned back by causes such as hatred and the like, it arises again from attachment; it perishes only through knowledge.
Excessive attachment to enjoyments becomes a source of harm,
even through a mere longing for the wives or the property of others.
Anger, intolerance, envy, malice, false reflection,
and being worthy of suffering— these six are declared as faults by those who know faults.
That heat which arises as a disturbance in the heart of a living being,
when there is a desire to do harm to another, is designated by the term "anger."
That which is designated as hatred arising from the fault of perceiving even a slight [unpleasant] sight is the definition of intolerance (amarṣa).
When one, upon seeing or hearing of another's qualities that exceed one's own,
does not rejoice out of malice, that is declared to be envy (abhyasūyā).
He who always seeks to destroy the wealth even of his friends,
being of unfriendly mind and wicked, they call that the characteristic of malice.
When one considers virtuous people who are without fault to be fault-finders,
and regards that [perception] as a false conceptualization, they say that it arises from a defect of disposition.
From greed and from hatred arises the intention and the contemplation of evil deeds;
this should be known as deserving of suffering, for it originates from past misdeeds.
This sixfold fault arises from suffering, from the designation of substance, and from defects;
it ceases through knowledge, the lapse of time, dharma, and joy.
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"What wise person would harbor hatred toward these beings who are all afflicted by the threefold suffering and are thus objects of pity?"
Furthermore, even if one's own power is inferior while other beings are prosperous, one should nevertheless rejoice; for loss is the fruit of hatred.
O dear one, when Govinda— the Supreme Self, the soul of all beings, the Lord of the world, and identical with the universe— is present, where is the talk of friend or foe?
Devala says: Misapprehension of reality, distress, trembling, confusion of knowledge,
perspiration, eye disease, and harshness— these, as well as attachment and hatred, arise from defects.
He who considers himself superior to all everywhere should be known as "equal" (samāna), provided his speech and actions are clear and according to his will.
The thirst and greed that arise upon seeing or hearing of another's food, another's enjoyments, and even another's power;
[87] There is no suffering equal to craving, and there is no happiness equal to renunciation;
therefore, a wise person should abandon craving born of greed.
Even having obtained the entire earth, his thirst is not appeased;
for it increases all the more, like the flame of a fire.
Because it consists of suffering and the like, because it has a miserable end, because it is unrighteous, because it brings no satisfaction,
and because it leads to grief later on, thirst for sensual pleasures is never conducive to the highest good.
Vṛddhaśātātapa says:
Who could ward off the long strides of horses with mere bits of grass,
as if they were the long evening shadows cast before one’s footsteps?
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa: "There is no end to one's desires, whether in a hundred years or even in hundreds of thousands of years."
When each set of desires is fulfilled, there arise yet new desires.
Having gone forth on foot, she became a young woman; she entered into union with a husband and gave birth;
she saw her sons and the offspring born of them.
Yet my inner self still longs for the haughty one.
If I should even behold their offspring, another desire would arise from that;
and when that is fulfilled, yet another birth would follow.
And by whom can the course of one's desires be turned back?
[88] Until death, there is truly no end to my desires; today I have this realization:
the mind of one who is intent on attachment to desires—
Indeed, that which is designated as the ultimate reality is not born.
For a full thousand years my mind was attached to sense objects;
nevertheless, thirst for those very things has not subsided, but rather continues to arise within me.
Therefore, having abandoned these and fixing my mind upon Brahman,
I shall wander with the deer, free from dualities and free from the sense of "mine."
In the Mahābhārata: "For craving is considered the most persistent of all things; it is thought to cause constant agitation, abounding in unrighteousness, terrible, and increasing one's sins."
For hope, O fool, makes a man stand still and not speak;
therefore, having encountered deficiency, death is certain—of this there is no doubt.
Having shown me objects close at hand at every step,
thirst has led me far away, like a goat whose mouth is drawn toward green grass.
Youth is seized by old age, health is struck down by diseases, and life is overtaken by death; craving alone remains free from affliction.
The hair of one who grows old decays; the teeth of one who grows old decay;
everything decays as one grows old, but craving alone does not decay.
Just as the horns of those two grow as they grow in time,
so indeed does craving grow as wealth grows.
In matters that ought not to be done, craving impels a man like a virtuous wife;
yet it is shame alone that protects him from all sins, like a mother.
There is no acquisition of what has not been done, nor is there destruction of what has been done;
yet this world, for no other reason at all, has been made a slave by you, O Craving.
[89] This thirst is a bottomless pit; by whom can it be filled?
For even when great things are poured into it, the pit is merely dug deeper.
Likewise: "One free from hope sleeps in happiness; freedom from hope is the supreme happiness.
Having rendered hope hopeless, Piṅgalā sleeps in happiness."
For one whose mind is contented, there is prosperity everywhere;
indeed, for one whose feet are covered by shoes, the entire earth is as if covered with leather.
There is no end to thirst; contentment is the supreme happiness.
Therefore, the wise desire contentment alone as their wealth in this world.
Whatever rice, barley, gold, cattle, and women exist upon the earth—all that is not enough for even one person; realizing this, one should seek tranquility.
In the phrase “not enough for one,” the word *alam* signifies sufficiency. Devala says:
“That by which one distresses another through these own qualities—lineage, intellect, body, learning, wealth, power, and majesty—that is the characteristic of pride (*mada*) in this world.”
The gods, asuras, and humans who are arrogant due to causes for intoxication are subdued by that very intoxication; therefore, intoxication should be abandoned by the wise.
Exultation, arrogance, and insolence, hypocrisy, pride, and haughtiness,
as well as other such dualistic states, are all conceptualizations born of intoxication.
The suffering that arises in the heart from aversion born of union with the undesired, from affection born of separation from the desired,
or from affliction, is designated as sorrow (śoka).
If all things are impermanent, then grief regarding them is pointless;
or, if they were eternal, from what cause would grief arise?
One established in *sattva* does not grieve in this way, nor does one who is purely in *tamas*.
In brief, it is from passion (*rāga*) that one experiences suffering born of sorrow in this world.
The meaning is that by reflecting in the manner thus described—namely, "one should not grieve in this way"—one does not encounter suffering. As stated in the *Mahābhārata*:
"If Time did not tear apart all beings while I was looking on..."
May my joy, sorrow, and anger indeed increase.
By good fortune, the destruction of beings is like that of rivers in the ocean;
the wielder of the thunderbolt understands this correctly and is not deluded.
I am not the agent, nor are you the agent; rather, he who is the eternal Lord is the agent.
It is this very Time that ripens me, like a fruit that has come to maturity upon a tree.
A man burns what is already burnt, strikes what is already struck;
he perishes when already lost, and obtains what is destined to be obtained.
Grief does not touch a man who is intelligent, whose wisdom is cultivated, who is attentive, free from envy, self-controlled, and has conquered his senses.
Whether one is intelligent or foolish, brave or timid, wise or dull,
weak or strong, destiny attends upon the man.
Devala said: That sense of ownership which one considers as "this is mine" regarding one's own possessions,
while being ignorant of their impermanence— the wise know that as "mamatva" (the notion of "mine-ness").
That which impels one toward actions involving cause and effect through the conceit of "I" is the definition of egoism (ahaṃkāra).
[91] All embodied beings are bound by the notions of "I" and "mine";
through these two, one who is liberated from them is released from the constraints of saṃsāra.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: "In whatever object a man's consciousness arises through the sense of 'mine-ness,' from that very thing it seizes hold of and bestows only sorrows."
The suffering felt when a domestic cock is eaten by a cat is not equal to that felt for a sparrow or a mouse when they are devoid of the sense of "mine."

In the Mahābhārata: "One does not attain happiness without renouncing; one does not find the supreme state without renouncing; and one does not sleep without fear without renouncing. Having renounced everything, be happy."
The country is ruined, the city is burnt, the chief elephant is slain;
yet one suffers through false knowledge over these things which are common to all the world.
The dawn drum of the king is common to all who dwell in happiness;
that sense of "this is mine" which arises toward it brings one joy.
Moreover, Maithila sang this when he beheld a man consumed by fire:
"Indeed, not even a single grain of husk is burnt within me."
It is said that the king himself spoke this.
"Infinite indeed is my wealth; yet look, I possess nothing at all.
Even when Mithilā is ablaze, nothing of mine is burned."
Yaṅkir said:
"Even this self is not mine, nor is the entire earth mine.
Realizing that 'as it is for me, so it is for others,' I have no distress."
I have entered this Brahma; like one entering a cool lake in the heat of summer, I am stilled, I am extinguished, and I abide in absolute bliss.
Whether it belongs to a calf, a cowherd, its owner, or a thief, the milk that one drinks belongs to him; such is the certainty regarding the cow.
Devala said:
One revolves in saṃsāra by thinking "I" and "mine";
one who sees that "I am nothing" and "nothing is mine" is not bound.
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"O sinless one, this [notion] of 'I' and 'mine' is ignorance; likewise, worldly transaction is based upon it. But the ultimate reality is inexpressible; it does not fall within the range of words."
Likewise:
"The notion of a self in what is not-self, and the thought of 'mine' in what is not mine—
this is the seed from which the tree of ignorance arises, existing in two ways."
In this body composed of the five elements, the embodied soul, shrouded by the darkness of delusion and possessed of poor intellect, loudly forms the notion: "I am this."
When the self stands distinct from ether, air, fire, water, and earth,
who can produce a sense of "self" within the body?
For even the physical body is not to be clung to, much less houses, fields, and so forth; what wise person would think "this is mine" regarding that which is bodiless and not the self?
And thus, when [the body] has given rise to sons, grandsons, and so forth, what wise person would claim ownership over that non-self physical frame?
A human being performs every action for the sake of the body's enjoyment;
yet when that body perishes, that subsequent action leads to the man's bondage.
Just as a house made of clay is indeed plastered with clay and water, so too this body is earthen; its condition is that of a corpse being smeared with earth.
The body consists of the five elements, as do the objects of enjoyment;
yet, if these are so, what grounds are there for a person’s pride in this regard?
Devala says:
That agitation which arises in the heart upon hearing of or seeing something that causes harm to oneself when it has presented itself is known as fear.
One should fear as long as the danger has not yet arrived;
but having seen that the danger has arrived, one should strike back like one who is fearless.
"What is to be will surely come to be; there is no deviation from karma. For those who have thus seen reality, fear never arises anywhere.
Upon seeing one's own prosperity or the misfortunes of another,
the joy that arises in the mind is designated as "harṣa" (exultation).
If you reflect upon it and see clearly, there is no room for joy among all past things, nor among momentary riches.
Even neutrality is a fault when others are in distress;
how much more so is rejoicing with a foolish mind at the calamity of another?
He who would vainly contemplate matters that are mutually contradictory with his mind— this they call "vain reflection," which destroys both dharma and action.
[94] He who, out of greed and other passions, wanders aimlessly through the intoxication of wealth, power, and the like,
destroys himself, his intellect, and his actions through futile deliberation.
Therefore, having abandoned far-reaching anxiety and the grief born of action,
one should undertake auspicious deeds in every way in order to attain the eternal state.
A wise person should cut through those knots born of passionate thoughts, firmly fixed within the hearts, by means of the wondrous sword of knowledge of reality.
One should repeatedly contemplate with the mind the means for exhausting one's own faults, the impermanence and impurity of the body, and what is beneficial for all living beings.
These twelve defects born of the mind—
delusion and the rest— are declared to be the causes of misfortune, which delude both gods and asuras.
Through association with that [right conduct], when the mind is guarded, and by means of devotion to knowledge and the Dharma,
as well as through the renunciation of vices and the like, the mental [defilements] come to an end.
Enveloping the intellect on all sides, darkness causes the non-illumination of the mind;
first, delusion born of evil arises in the hearts of embodied beings.
From delusion arises passion; from passion, hatred proceeds.
Through these three, indeed, evil—whether of body or speech—is produced.
Therefore, Hari himself sleeps within the minds of all;
to abandon all defects, one should first renounce these three.
‘Aparasparān’ means one after another, continuously. In the *Mahābhārata*:
“For a person dwelling on sense-objects, attachment to them arises;
from attachment, desire is born; from desire, anger is produced.”
From anger arises delusion; from delusion, the confusion of memory;
from the loss of memory comes the destruction of the intellect; and from the destruction of the intellect, one perishes.
Likewise:
"O King, for a person there is one enemy and no second equal to ignorance."
Enveloped by which, one becomes utterly heedless and performs terrible and most cruel deeds.
Passion, hatred, desire, and delusion; the actions of the wicked;
doubt, anger, and confusion; hypocrisy, envy, and likewise arrogance.
Envy, violence, and stinginess, as well as contempt, sloth, and ignorance— this is designated as thirst, which is the cultivation of delusion.
One should eradicate anger through forbearance and desire by abandoning mental constructions;
through the cultivation of goodness, the wise man ought to eliminate sleep.
One should consume fear through heedfulness by serving the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña);
and one should turn back envy, hatred, and desire through fortitude.
Through the practice of knowledge, the knower of reality should turn back delusion, confusion, and the whirlpool [of worldly existence], as well as sleep and the reflection [of the self].
One wards off calamities and diseases by eating wholesome, digested, and moderate food;
greed and delusion by contentment; and the objects of the senses by the vision of reality.
One should conquer unrighteousness through compassion, and righteousness through equanimity;
one should conquer hope for the future, and deceit by abandoning attachment.
The wise man should overcome attachment through the contemplation of impermanence, hunger through yoga,
pride regarding the self through compassion, and craving through contentment.
Having risen, one should conquer drowsiness; one should conquer discursive thought through firm resolve.
One should abandon excessive speech through silence, and fear through courage.
One should not dwell upon those qualities belonging to things that have already passed;
by disregarding them, one is liberated from the bond of affection.
One should perceive the defects in that wherein passion arises;
one should see it as increasing what is undesirable, so that it quickly ceases to grow.
When physical or mental suffering has arisen,
one should contemplate those [causes] from which it cannot be removed even with effort.
This is the medicine for suffering: that one should not dwell upon it;
for by dwelling upon it, it perishes [for a moment] but then arises yet again.
One should destroy mental suffering with wisdom and physical suffering with medicines;
this is the power of discernment, which for those who are weak becomes equivalent to nothing at all.
Likewise: "In such a way that the supreme attainment of one's goal does not cause excessive joy,
and likewise, in times of calamity, does not cause delusion."
He who experiences pleasure, pain, and likewise that which is intermediate, is a man who bears the yoke.
Whatever state a person may encounter,
if he is tormented by mental confusion therein,
he should thus dispel that mind-born [suffering] when it has grown great.
It causes distress and physical exhaustion.
Holding the genitals and the belly against the chest, the hands and feet with the eyes,
the eyes and ears with the mind, and the mind and speech with knowledge;
Sleep should be abandoned by all means by one who observes the faults of dreaming;
for in sleep, the embodied soul is overwhelmed by passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas).
[97] 10 — Now, regarding the conquest of the senses,
Manu says:
A wise man should exert effort in restraining the senses as they roam among alluring objects, just as a charioteer restrains his horses.
Through attachment to the senses, one undoubtedly incurs fault;
but by fully restraining them, one attains perfection.
Desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of desired objects;
rather, it increases all the more, like a fire fed with clarified butter.
These senses, corrupted by sense-objects, cannot be so effectively restrained by abstinence as they can be constantly by means of knowledge.
That man who, having heard, touched, seen, tasted, or held [an object],
neither rejoices nor desponds, should be known as one who has conquered his senses.
But if among all the senses even one sense is leaking,
through that his wisdom leaks away, like water from the foot of a leather water-skin.
‘Kāma’ means longing. ‘Of desires’ (kāmānām) means of desirable things; ‘objects’ (viṣayāṇām) refers to sound and so forth. ‘Dhṛti’ means a bellows.
As stated in the Mahābhārata:
“Indeed, desire never arises in one who is ignorant of flavors.”
It arises from hearing, or from seeing, or even from touching.
Do you not remember the Vāruṇī wine and the quail birds?
There is nothing to be found here that is more delicious to eat than those two.
‘For one who does not know flavors’ means for one who is unacquainted with the pleasure produced by them.
And likewise:
“The objects of the senses turn away from the embodied one who abstains from food.”
With the exception of taste; even this taste ceases for him upon seeing the Supreme.
For even of a wise man who strives, O son of Kuntī,
the turbulent senses forcibly carry away the mind.
Restraining all these, one should sit disciplined and self-controlled;
for he whose senses are under control, his wisdom is firmly established.
But one who is liberated from passion and hatred, moving among sense objects with senses under his own control, being self-disciplined, attains tranquility.
When there is serenity, the destruction of all sufferings arises for him;
for the intellect of one whose mind is serene quickly becomes firmly established.
When the mind follows after the wandering senses,
it carries away one's wisdom, just as the wind sweeps away a boat upon the waters.

Regarding the phrase "with the exception of taste" (*rasavarjam*), the *Gītā-bhāṣya* states that "taste" (*rasa*) means attachment (*rāga*). Regarding the phrase "having seen the Supreme" (*paraṃ dṛṣṭvā*), it means having directly realized the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). As stated in the *Viṣṇu-purāṇa*: "The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings; [the mind] attached to vices leads to bondage, while [the mind] liberated through the nature of being free from sense-objects leads to release."
In the Mahābhārata: One should uplift oneself by means of oneself; one should not despise oneself.
For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.
The self is the friend of that person by whom the self has been conquered by the self;
but for one who lacks self-mastery, the very self would behave as an enemy in the state of enmity.
For one who has conquered the self and is tranquil, the Supreme Self is fully composed amidst cold and heat, pleasure and pain, as well as honor and dishonor.
[100] 11 — Now, regarding the emanation of reality (*tattva-sṛṣṭi*),
Devala says as follows:

In that regard, for the Sāṃkhyas, there is one root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*). There are seven natures and transformations (*prakṛtivikṛtayaḥ*): the Great One (*mahat*) and the I-faculty (*ahaṃkāra*), the five subtle elements (*tanmātrāṇi*), and sixteen modifications (*vikārāḥ*). These consist of the five sense organs, the objects, and the five specific gross elements; these are the thirteen instruments (*karaṇāni*). Among them, three are internal instruments and ten are external instruments. "The five sense organs" refers to the five cognitive organs and the five active organs, thus making ten. "Objects" refers to form and so forth. "Specific gross elements" refers to earth and so forth. Thus it is said.

Now, the root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) is the unmanifest (*avyakta*); the great one (*mahat*), the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), and the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) are the natures and evolutions (*prakṛtivikṛtayaḥ*). These are: the subtle element of sound, the subtle element of touch, the subtle element of form, the subtle element of taste, and the subtle element of smell. The subtle elements are of two kinds. The sense organs, the mind (*manas*), and the specific gross elements (*bhūtaviśeṣa*) are the modifications (*vikāra*). The eye, ear, nose, tongue, and skin are the organs of cognition (*buddhīndriya*). Form, taste, smell, touch, and sound are their respective objects. The voice, hands, feet, anus, and genitals are the organs of action (*karmendriya*). Speaking, grasping, movement, excretion, and procreation are the functions of the organs of action. Air, fire, water, ether, and earth are the specific gross elements. The ten organs, along with the intellect (*buddhi*), ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), and mind (*manas*), are the instruments (*karaṇa*). Among these, the mind, intellect, and ego-sense are the internal instruments (*antaḥkaraṇa*), while the ten organs are the external instruments. And the organs are also [included therein].

The Unmanifest (*avyakta*), characterized by the equilibrium of the *guṇas*, is synonymous with *pradhāna*, *prakṛti*, and *vidhātṛ*. The Great One (*mahat*), characterized by determination (*adhyavasāya*), is synonymous with *buddhi*, *mati*, and *upalabdhi*. The subtle elements (*tanmātra*) are characterized by mere existence; the senses (*indriya*), characterized by their own respective favors, are called *akṣa*. The mind (*manas*) is characterized by volition (*saṃkalpa*). The specific objects of the senses, characterized as the objects of the senses, are synonymous with the *bhūtas*. Thus [the categories] are explained.

The primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is the first of all. From primordial nature arises the Great One (*mahat*); from the Great One, the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*); from the ego-sense, the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the sense organs; and from the subtle elements, the specific gross elements (*viśeṣa*). This is the sequence of evolution.

"Characterized by the equilibrium of the qualities" means that the equilibrium of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* is a state of non-modification (*avikṛtitva*). That which has this as its characteristic is thus described. "The first of all" means the foremost among everything. [This refers to] Yama.
The mind, intellect, ego, ether, air, fire, water, and earth—
these are the eight primary natures (prakṛtis), while the other sixteen are their transformations (vikāras).
The ear, eye, tongue, nose, and skin, as well as volition;
and sound, form, taste, touch, smell, speech, hands, and the anus.
The feet and the generative organ—these are the sixteen further modifications.
The wise say that this is the knowledge of the twenty-fourfold [principles].
The twenty-fifth is the unmanifest; the twenty-sixth is the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
Having known this, ascetics of tranquil intellect are well liberated.
