One who knows the twenty-five principles [attains] that which is the supreme state of Viṣṇu.
Yājñavalkya says: The emergence of the intellect (buddhi) is unmanifest; from that arises the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra);
and from the ego-sense arise the subtle elements (tanmātra) and the rest, each possessing one additional quality [in succession].
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are their qualities;
whichever among these has emerged from which [element], that dissolves back into that very same [element].
‘Ekottaraguṇāni’: the elements, beginning with space, each possess one additional quality in successive order. As stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"That which is the unmanifest cause is called Pradhāna by the best of sages."
The subtle primordial nature (prakṛti) is declared to be eternal, consisting of both the existent and the non-existent.
The unmanifest is not any other support; it is immortal, undecaying, and eternal.
It is devoid of sound and touch, and is not composed of form and the other [sensory qualities].
That source of the world, consisting of the three qualities, is without beginning, origin, and decay;
by it all was indeed pervaded at the outset, following the dissolution.
O learned one, those who know the declarations of the Vedas, who are self-restrained and expounders of Brahman,
recite this very same meaning which establishes the Pradhāna.
There was neither day nor night, neither sky nor earth;
there was no darkness, nor was there light, nor anything else— only the One, perceivable by the intellect through the ear and other senses.
That Brahman, consisting of primordial matter, became the Person.
That which was manifest while established in primordial nature (prakṛti) becomes transcended during the dissolution;
therefore, this process of re-absorption is called "prākṛta" (pertaining to primordial nature).
O twice-born one, the Blessed Time is without beginning and its end is not known;
therefore, these restraints regarding heaven, stability, and the end have been utterly cut off.
Then, O Maitreya, when that equilibrium of the qualities has subsided and the Puruṣa remains distinct, that form of Viṣṇu which is the very nature of Time prevails.
Then that Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Self, consisting of the universe,
all-pervading, the Lord of all beings, the Soul of all, the Supreme Lord—
At the time of creation's arrival, Hari, by his own will, entered both Pradhāna and Puruṣa— the perishable and the imperishable— and caused them to vibrate.
Just as a fragrance causes agitation to the mind by its mere presence, even without performing any service, so too is this Supreme Lord.
O Brahmin, that very Puruṣa is considered both the agitator and the object of agitation;
through contraction and expansion, he remains established even in the state of Pradhāna.
And likewise, through their modifications and their essential natures such as the form of Brahmā and others,
Viṣṇu, the Lord of all lords, exists both in his manifest form and in that same manner.
Therefore, O sage, best of the twice-born, from that state of equilibrium of the guṇas, when presided over by the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña),
there arises at the time of creation the manifestation of the guṇas.
The principle of Pradhāna, having manifested, enveloped the Mahat;
and that Mahat is threefold: Sāttvika, Rājasa, and Tāmasa.
Together with the principle of Pradhāna, [the intellect] is enveloped like a seed by its skin:
the Vaikārika, the Taijasa, and the Bhūtādi which is Tāmasa.
This threefold ego-sense was born from the principle of Mahat;
it is the cause of the elements and the senses because it possesses the three qualities, O great sage.
Just as the Great Principle (mahat) is enveloped by the Primal Nature (pradhāna),
so too the Origin of Elements (bhūtādi), undergoing transformation while conjoined with the Self, then produces the triad.
From the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra), he emitted space, which is characterized by sound;
then Bhūtādi enveloped that space, which consists of mere sound.
But space, undergoing transformation, produced the subtle element of touch;
from it arose the powerful wind, and touch is considered its quality.
Space, consisting of the subtle element of sound, enveloped the subtle element of touch;
then, through its transformation, wind produced the subtle element of form.
Light arises from wind; it is said to have the quality of form.
From that, wind—consisting of touch alone—envelops the subtle element of form.
And light, undergoing transformation, produced the subtle element of taste;
from that, the waters came into being, which indeed serve as their support.
The waters, being agitated, enveloped the subtle element of form;
and the waters, becoming further disturbed, produced the subtle element of smell.
Since a composite arises from that, its quality is considered to be odor;
because it exists within each respective [subtle element] as a mere-measure (*tanmātra*), it is therefore remembered as "mere-measure" (*tanmātratā*).
The subtle elements (tanmātras) are non-specific (aviśeṣa); for that reason they are so called. They are neither peaceful, nor terrible, nor deluded, nor are they specific (viśeṣin).
This [group] known as the gross elements and subtle essences arises from the tamasic ego;
they say the sense organs are taijasa, while the ten deities are vaikarika.
The eleventh here is the mind, as well as the gods who are products of transformation;
moreover, the skin, eye, nose, tongue, and the ear as the fifth are present here.
O twice-born Maitreya, for the sake of attaining sound and the other sense objects, the intellect indeed impels the anus,
the genitals, the hands, the feet, and speech as the fifth.
They declare their functions to be emission, craftsmanship, motion, speech, and action;
likewise, [the elements are] space, wind, fire, water, and earth.
O Brahmin, because they are endowed with the qualities beginning with sound, each succeeding one more than the last,
and because they are calm, dull, or fierce, they are therefore known as the "specifics" (viśeṣas).
Having diverse powers and being separate from one another,
they were unable to create living beings without a collective union, as they had not come together in their entirety.
Having come together in mutual conjunction and being mutually dependent,
they form a single composite whole, attaining complete unity.
And because they are presided over by the Puruṣa and through the favor of the Unmanifest,
those principles beginning with Mahat and ending with the Viśeṣas produce the cosmic egg.
O one of great intelligence, from the elements arose the Egg, which was vast and rested upon the water; it was uniform, like a bubble on the water, and yet contrary to the sequence [of creation].
The primordial, unsurpassed abode of Viṣṇu, whose nature is Brahman, is there;
in that place, the Lord of the World, though his true form is unmanifest, assumes a manifest form.
Viṣṇu himself remained in the form of Brahmā;
Meru became his amnion and the mountains his chorion.
The waters of his womb were the seven oceans;
mountains, islands, and oceans, along with light, constituted the collection of worlds belonging to that Self.
Within that egg, O Brahmin, were contained the gods, asuras, and humans;
it was then enveloped on the outside by water, fire, air, ether, and the principle of cosmic ego (bhūtādi).
O Brahmin, the Mahat-tattva, along with Bhūtādi, is likewise enveloped by the tenfold-folded Egg; and the Great One (Mahān) is encompassed by all those together with the Unmanifest (Avyakta).
By these seven natural coverings, the egg is enveloped,
just as the seed within a coconut fruit is enclosed by its outer husks.
There, Hari, the Lord of the Universe himself, partaking of the quality of rajas,
becomes Brahmā and proceeds with the creation of the world.
And having created [the world], the Lord Viṣṇu, whose prowess is immeasurable, protects it age after age as long as there is the differentiation of time; he is the enjoyer of the essence of beings.
Because he performs the acts of creation, preservation, and dissolution, the one Lord Janārdana alone assumes the designations of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
The Creator creates himself; Viṣṇu protects that which is to be protected; and at the end, the Lord himself, as the Destroyer, withdraws all.
Earth, water, fire, air, and space,
as well as all the sense organs and the internal organ— that which is called the world is indeed the Puruṣa.
He alone is the Lord of all beings, whose form is the universe, since he is imperishable;
for the creation and so forth, which abide within the elements, serve his purpose.
He alone is the object of creation and He is the creator;
He alone protects and is protected.
With all forms, through the states of Brahmā and the others, He is the entirety of existence.
Viṣṇu is the most excellent, the giver of boons, and the one worthy of choice.
[Thus: When the transformation beginning with the Great Principle (mahat) and ending with the specific elements (viśeṣa) has been dissolved,
and when that process of reabsorption (pratisaṃcara) has been set in motion by Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Time.
The waters indeed first swallow up the quality consisting of smell belonging to the earth;
then, its smell having been taken away, the earth becomes fit for dissolution.
When the subtle element of smell has perished, the earth becomes of the nature of water;
and that quality which belongs to water is dissolved by light.
Likewise: Light dissolves into wind; wind dissolves into space;
space, in turn, devours the source of the elements (bhūtādi), and the Great One (mahat) likewise devours that.
O twice-born one, O great sage, Prakṛti swallows Mahat along with these [tattvas],
when it is characterized by the equilibrium of the guṇas and is neither deficient nor excessive.
[108] It is declared that *prakṛti* is the cause, the primary matter (*pradhāna*), the supreme source;
thus this entire *prakṛti* consists of both the manifest and the unmanifest.
O Maitreya, that manifest nature dissolves into that unmanifest;
likewise, the Person (puruṣa) is one, pure, imperishable, eternal, and all-pervading.
Even that portion of the Supreme Self, O Maitreya, which belongs to the Being of all beings,
is such that in that Lord of all, there exist no conceptual constructions of name, genus, and the like.
When the object of knowledge consists of pure existence, being of the nature of consciousness and the supreme Self,
that is Brahman, that is the supreme abode, and he is the Supreme Self and the Lord.
That Viṣṇu is indeed all this, from which the ascetic does not return;
he is the primordial nature (prakṛti) which I have described as having the form of both the manifest and the unmanifest.
Both of these, including the individual soul (puruṣa), dissolve into the Supreme Self;
and the Supreme Self is the support of all, the Supreme Lord.
He is celebrated by the name Viṣṇu in the Vedas and in the Vedāntas.
In the Mahābhārata:
"From the Imperishable (akṣara) first arose wind; from wind, light; from that, water;
from water, the world (jagatī) was produced; and within the world, the universe (jagat) is born."
Now follows the consideration of the body; regarding the succession of gods, humans, and animals, Devala says:

Their specific bodily forms are of three kinds: [the divine body] is radiant, fragrant, uncreated, stainless, unwinking, free from sweat, devoid of hunger, thirst, sleep, and laziness; it possesses form, strength, and armor according to its will, is vigorous, pure, supremely excellent, and caused by meritorious deeds—this is the body of a deity. The human body is impermanent and impure, the abode of all diseases, a vessel of suffering, subject to many afflictions; it is a framework of bones bound together by veins and sinews, smeared with flesh, covered by skin; it is filled with food-juices, excrement, blood, fat, muscle, marrow, semen, bile, wind, phlegm, intestines, rectum, bladder, liver, spleen, moisture, sweat, urine, feces, and worms; it has nine apertures, is constantly discharging fluids, extends to the hair, down, and nails, is foul-smelling, requires constant grooming, and is subject to old age and death—such is the human body. The body of the animal womb is perpetually agitated, lacks refinement, is characterized by suppressed secretions, is subject to hunger and thirst, has senses directed toward delusion, is the path of evil deeds, ignorance, and incapacity—such is the body of the animal womb.
Likewise: desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, hunger, thirst, effort, fear, birth, and death— these are common to all embodied beings.
[110] All living beings necessarily take delight in their own wombs;
for those possessed by the unreal, there is no such thing as birth—this is the certainty.
The body of those who undergo the womb-experience is impure, exceedingly foul-smelling, devoid of essence, a vessel of suffering, unstable, and full of manifold misery.
In this world, bathing, eating, and other such activities merely sustain this body, which is filled with feces, urine, and worms, a dwelling place of disease, and always afflicted.
Whether lying down, walking, standing, or sitting, living beings never wish to abandon their own kind, each according to its respective order.
Having abandoned the body, the embodied being does not even desire the station of Indra;
therefore, even a worm finds great delight in its own kind among living creatures.
‘The construction of its strength according to one’s desire’: that is, where the collection of parts possesses the power of a genus according to one’s wish.
[It is] a structure with bones for pillars, bound together by sinews, plastered with flesh and blood, covered with skin, foul-smelling, and filled with urine and excrement.
One should abandon this abode of the elements, which is beset by old age and sorrow, a dwelling place for disease, afflicted, full of passion, and impermanent.
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa: "Where is this body, which is merely a collection of phlegm and other such [impurities], and where are qualities such as beauty, splendor, fragrance, and loveliness?"
If a fool feels attachment toward this body— a mere collection of flesh, bone, blood, fat, pus, sinews, feces, and urine— he will find himself even in hell.
[111] Manu says: All stationary beings are born from sprouts; they grow from seeds or from stems.
Herbs are those that perish at the ripening of their fruit and are endowed with many flowers and fruits.
Those which bear fruit without flowers are known as *vanaspati*;
those that bear both flowers and fruit are known as *vṛkṣa*.
Various clusters and shrubs, as well as species of grasses, creepers,
climbing plants, and spreading vines are thus proclaimed.
Enveloped by manifold darkness caused by their past actions,
these beings possess internal consciousness and are endowed with pleasure and pain.
In the Mahābhārata: "In the bodies of all mobile beings, there are five elements which, when individually distinguished, cause the body to move."
Skin, flesh, bone, marrow, and sinew as the fifth—
this is reckoned here as the body composed of earth.
Heat, fire, as well as anger, the eye, and likewise warmth—fire also causes decay; these are the five fires within embodied beings.
The ear, the nose, the mouth, the heart, and the stomach—
these five elements in the bodies of living beings arise from space.
Phlegm, bile, sweat, fat, and blood— thus water exists perpetually in five forms within the bodies of living beings.
Through *prāṇa* the living being breathes out; through *vyāna* it always breathes about;
*apāna* moves only downward, while *samāna* is situated in the heart.
From *udāna* one breathes out and a differentiation of sound arises;
these five winds thus cause the embodied being to move.
Now follows the discrimination between the self and the body; regarding this, Śaṅkha says:
A wise person should understand these five great elements: earth, water, fire, air, and space.
One should know that the ear, the eye, the sense of touch, the tongue, and the nose—
these five alone are the organs of perception within this body.
The mind, the intellect, the self, and likewise the unmanifest—
these four are said to be superior to the senses.
A wise person should always recognize these five objects of the senses: sound, form, touch, taste, and likewise smell.
The hands, feet, the generative organ, the tongue, and likewise the anus—
these are the five organs of action always present in this little body.
These twenty-four principles have indeed been described;
likewise, know that Self to be the twenty-fifth principle, the Puruṣa.
If the hundredth part of the tip of a hair were further divided a thousandfold,
the living being (jīva) is said to be subtler even than that hundredth part.

In the Viṣṇupurāṇa: "The supreme power of Viṣṇu is declared to be one; likewise, the other is called the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field); another, known as *avidyā* and *karman*, is held to be the third power."
O King, impelled by that [power], the all-pervading power of the Knower of the Field experiences the entire succession of the miseries of saṃsāra.
And because it is concealed by that [power], O King, the power known as the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is perceived in all beings according to a gradation of degrees.

"Viṣṇu’s power is supreme," which is of the nature of Brahman and is called the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña); "the inferior" is of the nature of the individual soul (jīva), known as Māyā, ignorance (avidyā), and karma.
Manu says: "The one who causes this self to act is designated as the Knower of the Field."
But he who performs actions is called the "elemental self" (bhūtātman) by the wise.
The inner self, known as the *jīva*, is distinct and innate to all embodied beings;
by means of it, one experiences all pleasure and pain throughout successive births.

The word "self" (*ātman*) is used here in a figurative sense because this body, which is of the nature of a physical form, exists for the sake of the self. The "causer" (*kārayitā*) is the one who impels the activities consisting of motion by means of his own effort. The "elemental self" (*bhūtātman*) is the body because it is a composite of the elements such as earth and so forth. The "inner self known as the living soul" (*jīvasaṃjño 'ntarātmā*) is another; this very thing is the inner self in the form of the internal organ, the mind (*manas*), and it is called the "living soul" (*jīva*). It is [called the inner self] "because it exists for that purpose," meaning because it serves the purpose of that [body] as the internal organ. The expression "by which one experiences" (*yena vedayate*) is indicated using the instrumental case, signifying an instrument. It is "innate" (*sahaja*) because of its connection with that [body] until the attainment of liberation. As stated in the *Mahābhārata*:
In that regard, he who is indeed the Supreme Self is traditionally held to be eternally devoid of qualities;
he is to be known as Nārāyaṇa, for he is the Self of all and the Puruṣa.
One is not smeared by the fruits of action, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water;
however, that other one, whose nature is action, is joined with both liberation and bondage.
Furthermore, he is joined with the group of seventeen as well.
‘By the seventeenfold’: by this group consisting of the ten sense organs, the mind, the intellect, and the five vital airs (prāṇas) beginning with prāṇa.
Likewise, they call that [the soul] the conscious quality of the individual self (jīva).
He constantly acts and dies;
beyond that, those who know the field say he was the one who clothed the seven worlds.
And likewise in the Mahābhārata;
and thus Bharadvāja said:
"If fire, wind, earth, ether, and water [are present] within embodied beings..."
O sinless one, tell me this: what are the characteristics of the individual soul (jīva) therein?
If the wind breathes, if the wind alone moves about, and if it merely makes the sound "śvas" when speaking, then the living soul (jīva) is purposeless.
[115] If that which has become hot is indeed cooked by fire, and if fire itself undergoes decay, then the living soul (jīva) is purposeless.
When a person is dying, the life-principle (jīva) is not perceived at all;
it is simply the wind that leaves him, and the state of warmth perishes.
If the living being were like the wind, or if its union were with the wind,
it would be seen like a whirlwind and would depart along with the hosts of Maruts.

“If it were visible like a circle of wind” is the refutation of the position that the living being (jīva) is comparable to the wind. Regarding the position that “the living being is a conjunction with the wind,” the meaning of “it would be visible like a circle of wind” is that it is not perceived by touch, unlike the mass of wind at the time of departure. As for the statement, “he would go along with the hosts of winds,” he would go toward whatever direction the masses of wind travel; however, this is not so, because the attainment of heaven or hell through the power of merit and demerit is established by scripture. Likewise, Bhṛgu said:
“In this regard, there is nothing common to all five.”
The inner self alone sustains the body;
it perceives odors, tastes, sounds,
touch, form, and whatever other qualities there may be.
The inner self, which consists of the five elements, displays the five qualities; pervading all limbs,
it experiences both sufferings and pleasures here.
But the body does not know its separation from that.

“There is nothing here common to the five”: in this body, among the five elements, there exists no single element that is common [to all] and capable of synthesizing various objects such as odors. Yet there is a synthesizer of various objects, and there is the synthesis of many things. There is a synthesizer of various objects and there is the synthesis of many things; therefore, the meaning is that there exists an inner self (antarātman) distinct from these, which is the synthesizer of odors and so forth. It flows and it runs. “Other qualities” refers to pleasure and the like. Yājñavalkya said: “Just as the great elements are real, so indeed is the self.”
And who else could see with one eye what was seen by the other?
Who indeed understands speech after hearing it again and again?
Whose is the memory of a past object, and who is the creator of a dream?
Proud on account of birth, form, age, conduct, learning, and so forth,
one is capable [of acting] toward objects such as sound, either through action or even by means of the mind.
Likewise: "By means of the Vedas, the scriptures, and specialized knowledge; by birth and by death;
by affliction, by departure, and likewise by arrival; indeed, by truth and by falsehood."
[He was distinguished] by excellence, by pleasure and pain, by auspicious and inauspicious actions,
and by the fruits arising from omens, the knowledge of birds, and the conjunctions of planets.
[117] By means of the movements of the stars and constellations, whether occurring while awake or in dreams,
as well as by space, wind, light, water, earth, and darkness;
Through the periods of the Manvantaras, through the attainment of the Yugas, and even through the fruits of the Manvantaras,
one perceives the Self as the knower and likewise as the cause of the world.
Egoity, memory, intelligence, aversion, intellect, happiness, fortitude,
the transition between different sense organs, desire, and death and life.
Heaven, dreams, the impelling of inherent natures, the movement of the mind,
the blinking of the eyes, consciousness, and the grasping of the five elements are all dependent upon the Self.
Since these marks of the Supreme Self are observed,
therefore there exists a Self beyond the body, the all-pervading Lord.

‘With one eye’: having seen an object with the visual faculty (*cakṣurindriya*), one discerns it with another, the tactile faculty (*sparśanendriya*). Thinking, “I who saw it, I now touch it,” one thus discerns the self (*ātman*) as the knower through these means.
As stated in the *Mahābhārata*: “Just as someone, having taken up an axe...”
Just as one might not see smoke or fire within the wood [if it were concealed],
so too people do not perceive that which is other than this, being hidden by the body, the belly, the hands, and the feet.
Just as when one rubs other pieces of wood together and sees both smoke and fire within the wood,
so too is that person of excellent intelligence because of his possession of the true faculties.
He perceives his own supreme, eternal nature.
Just as one sees one's own limb fallen upon the earth as something other than oneself within a dream,
so too does one endowed with the ear and other senses, being well-disposed and possessed of sound intellect, perceive [the self].
Then, from that subtle body, another subtle body proceeds.
When he later remembers for a long time those vital breaths and qualities that were previously presented by the senses,
once those senses have been destroyed— then...
Supreme power arises from the form of the intellect.
Just as one does not perceive all sensory objects simultaneously in their entirety within a short time,
so that wise man moves according to his capacity.
Therefore, he alone is the one supreme embodied being.

Just as the side or the back of the Himalayas is not seen by human beings, yet it does not follow that it does not exist; so too, [the Buddha] has not been seen before by humans, yet he is not non-existent for that reason.
In the same way, that subtle Self of beings, possessing the nature of knowledge, has never before been seen by the eyes; yet it does not follow from that that it does not exist.
The living soul does not depend on the body;
when that [body] is destroyed, it is not destroyed, just as fire is not extinguished when the fuel has been consumed.
Indeed, there is no destruction of the living soul upon the destruction of the body;
the ignorant say falsely, "He is dead," for the living soul merely passes into another body.
The dissolution of his body occurs at the end of five ten-year periods.
Just as the flames of fire, the gusts of wind, the rays of the sun, and the waters in rivers go forth and return in a continuous stream;
In the same way, however, the bodies of embodied beings [are distinct from them].
Likewise: "Just as the embodied one passes through childhood, youth, and old age in this body, so too does he attain another body; the wise man is not deluded by this."
Likewise: "The non-existent has no being; the existent has no non-being.
The limit of both these has been perceived by the seers of reality."
But that by which all this is pervaded is indeed indestructible;
no one is able to effect the destruction of this immutable one.
These bodies are said to have an end, belonging to the eternal, indestructible, and immeasurable embodied self; therefore, fight, O Bhārata!
He who perceives this as a slayer, and he who thinks of it as slain—both of them do not understand; this does not slay, nor is it slain.
It is never born, nor does it ever die; having come into being, it will not cease to be again. Unborn, eternal, everlasting, and ancient is this [Self].
It is not slain when the body is slain.
How, O Pārtha, can that person— who knows this Self as imperishable, eternal, unborn, and immutable— cause anyone to be slain or slay anyone?
Just as a person, having cast off worn-out garments, takes others that are new,
even so does the soul, casting off worn-out bodies.
The embodied soul enters other new bodies.
Weapons do not cut this, nor does fire burn it;
water does not moisten it, nor does the wind dry it up.
This is indivisible, this is ungraspable, and it is indeed neither moistened nor dried away;
eternal, all-pervading, stable, immovable, and ancient.
This is said to be unmanifest, unthinkable, and unchangeable.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: Or she, Madālasā, under the pretext of lulling him to sleep, spoke to her son, a young child lying on his back,
who was crying without fear.
O father, you are pure; indeed, that name was given to you only out of convention just now. This body composed of the five elements does not belong to you.
Why is it that you do not weep for him? For what reason?
Nor does Your Lordship, who are born in all beings, weep when this sound reaches the mass of the earth,
even as it is conceptualized through various qualities and the like.
And from the qualities [arise] the elemental [substances] within all the sense organs.
Just as the elements of men, though initially very weak, attain growth through food,
water, drink, and so forth, so it is with this [embryo].
For you there is no increase, nor is there any decrease.
When this garment of your own is being worn away,
do not suddenly fall into a state of delusion;
for this body [is sustained] by auspicious and inauspicious karmas.
Enveloped by the sheaths, he is deluded by intoxication and the like.
Sometimes "father," sometimes "son," sometimes "mother," sometimes "beloved";
sometimes "mine," and sometimes "not mine."
You may lead the multitude of beings in many ways.
Likewise:
the vehicle is on the ground, and the body is situated in the vehicle;
and within the body, another—the Puruṣa—is established.
Alas, this delusion is such that one does not feel toward others as one feels toward one's own body with excessive possessiveness.
Likewise:
"Just as there is a distinction between a gnat, a fig, a blade of grass, a reed, a fish, and water,
even though they exist as one, so too would there be a distinction between the field and the self."
[122] ‘Even in the case of oneness,’ that is, even when there is the conceit of oneness due to the force of their conjunction;
as stated in the *Mahābhārata*: “Know thus the distinction between the subtle *sattva* and the *kṣetrajña*.”
"One [element] emits the qualities; one does not emit the qualities."
Then, having truly released the firm knot of the heart consisting of intellect and mind,
one should dwell in happiness, liberated and with doubts severed.
Yājñavalkya said: This self has never at any time been released from egoism, the mind, the movement [of the senses], the fruit of action, and the body.
Just as the continued existence of a lamp depends on the combination of the wick, the support, and the oil,
so too is its transformation observed, such as the premature exhaustion of its life-force.
When, having become as small as an atom, he moves about while remaining within the seed-syllable, he enters into union with it; then he casts off his physical form.
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa: "Then, at the time of departure, the heat provoked by occasional defects is indeed stirred up within the body by a violent wind."
Then, having pervaded the body, it indeed obstructs all the humors (doṣas),
piercing the seats of the vital breaths (prāṇas) and further passing beyond the vital points (marmans).
Due to cold, the wind becomes aggravated and moves upward;
it then resides in the locations of the vital breaths (prāṇa) of all living beings.
When knowledge is enveloped by darkness and the activities are shrouded,
that individual soul cannot be directed by the vital breath (mātariśvan) due to its lack of a substratum.
That living being, though being driven by his own karmas,
again correctly maintains that eightfold vital function through his own heroic efforts.
Thus the body is indeed abandoned, and then it becomes breathless;
thus, being forsaken by the vital breaths, it is designated as "dead."
Just as those with impaired vision perceive the clouds in the sky and the firefly separately during the rainy season, so it is from that [state].
The Siddhas behold such a living being with their divine eye.
In the Mahābhārata,
the Blessed Lord said:
"An eternal portion of My very self, having become a living soul, exists in the world of the living."
The mind draws forth the senses, with the mind as the sixth, which abide in their own nature.
Whatever body the Lord acquires, and whatever [body] He departs from,
He takes these with Him and goes forth, just as the wind carries fragrances from their source.
Presiding over the ear, the eye, the sense of touch, the tongue, and the nose,
as well as the mind, this [self] enjoys the objects of the senses.
Whether it is departing, or staying still, or enjoying experiences endowed with the qualities of nature, the deluded do not perceive it; those who possess the eye of knowledge perceive it.
Likewise:
"The intellect, presided over by the Puruṣa, operates among those objects;
sometimes it finds pleasure, and sometimes it grieves."
It never exists with either pleasure or pain,
just as the senses cease from their respective functions due to exhaustion.
A man indeed sleeps because of the withdrawal of the senses;
yet, due to the cessation of the senses, the mind remains unceased.
If he indulges in sense objects alone, one should know that to be a vision in a dream.
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa: "Due to the failure to perceive reality, the threefold reality is always bound by the *prākṛta* face as well as the *vaikārika* face."
Bound by the third [type of gift], namely sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), one increases excessively;
thus these three are declared to be bonds caused by ignorance.
The perception of permanence in the impermanent, the viewing of pleasure in suffering, the notion of self in what is not-self, and the conviction of purity in the impure.
And the increase of passion and hatred—that is declared to be ignorance.

Devala says: There are three types of bondage: *prakṛtibandha* (bondage by primordial nature), *vaikārikabandha* (transformative bondage), and *dakṣiṇābandha* (bondage by sacrificial fees). Among these, bondage through the eight principles beginning with the Unmanifest (*avyakta*) is *prakṛtibandha*. Bondage of the senses toward the objects of the senses is *vaikārikabandha*. Bondage through sacrifices such as *iṣṭāpūrta* is *dakṣiṇābandha*. In this regard, among the *prakṛtis*, the cause of bondage for the gods is [their own nature]; for those in the stages of life (*āśramins*), it is through sacrificial fees; and for others, it is through transformative qualities, virtues, and ignorance. [125] As stated in the *Mahābhārata*:
Sattva, rajas, and tamas— these qualities born of nature bind the imperishable embodied soul within the body, O mighty-armed one.
In that regard, O sinless one, sattva, being pure, illuminating, and free from affliction, binds by attachment to pleasure and by attachment to knowledge.
Know that passion consists of attachment and arises from thirst and clinging;
it binds the embodied soul, O son of Kuntī, through attachment to action.
Know that *tamas* arises from ignorance and deludes all embodied beings;
it binds them, O Bharata, through negligence, laziness, and sleep.
Sattva attaches one to happiness, O Bhārata, and rajas to action;
rajas [attaches] to sattva and tamas, and likewise tamas to sattva and rajas.
When light arises in all the gates of this body,
one should then know that the quality of goodness (sattva) has increased.
Greed, activity, undertaking of actions, harshness, and longing—
these arise when rajas has increased, O bull of the Bharatas.
Lack of illumination, lack of activity, negligence, and even delusion—
these arise when darkness has increased, O joy of the Kurus.
But when the embodied soul meets its end while sattva is predominant,
then it attains the stainless worlds of those who know the Highest.
Having gone to dissolution in rajas, one is born amidst attachments to action;
likewise, having dissolved in tamas, one is born in the wombs of the deluded.
[126] They say that the fruit of well-performed action is sattvic and stainless;
the fruit of rajas, however, is suffering, and the fruit of tamas is ignorance.
From *sattva* arises knowledge, and from *rajas* arises greed;
from *tamas* arise negligence and delusion, as well as ignorance itself.
Those established in sattva go upward; those characterized by rajas stay in the middle;
and those of tamas, abiding in the conduct of the lowest quality, go downward.
Manu says: One should know that *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are the three qualities (*guṇa*) of the Self (*ātman*),
by which the Great One (*mahat*) remains pervading all these states without exception.
Whichever of these qualities predominates in the body in its entirety,
it then makes that embodied being consist primarily of that quality.
Goodness is knowledge, darkness is ignorance, and passion is said to be attachment and aversion;
this is their pervasive nature, which rests within all beings.
That which is conjoined with suffering and is disagreeable to oneself, one should know that to be passion and aversion; it constantly afflicts embodied beings.
But that which is joined with delusion, whose nature consists of manifest objects,
and which is inconceivable and unknowable— one should understand that to be *tamas*.
In that regard, whatever one perceives within oneself as conjoined with joy,
tranquil and appearing pure— that should be understood as the *sattva* element.
[127] Furthermore, I shall explain in its entirety the arising of the fruits of these three qualities— the foremost, the middling, and the lowest.
Study of the Vedas, austerity, knowledge, purity, restraint of the senses, performance of dharma,
and contemplation of the Self— these are the characteristics of the quality of sattva.
Delight in undertaking activities, lack of fortitude, adherence to ignoble deeds,
and constant indulgence in sense objects— these are the characteristics of the rajasic quality.
Greed, sleepiness, lack of fortitude, cruelty, atheism,
violation of moral conduct, mendicancy, and negligence are the characteristics of the quality of darkness (tamas).
And for these three qualities residing in the three [states],
this should be known as the concise definition of their characteristics in their respective order.
Whatever action one feels ashamed of having done, ashamed of doing, and ashamed of being about to do—
that should be known by the wise as entirely characterized by the quality of tamas.
That action by which one attains abundant fame in this world,
yet does not grieve over failure, should be known as rajasic.
That which one does not wish to know entirely, that for which one feels shame when practicing,
and that by which one's own self is satisfied— this is the characteristic mark of the quality of a virtuous being.
Desire is said to be the characteristic of *tamas*, while purpose is said to be that of *rajas*;
the characteristic of *sattva* is righteousness (*dharma*). Their preeminence follows this sequence.

"Sattva" refers to knowledge (*jñāna*), and so forth. "Knowledge" is discernment (*viveka*); "ignorance" (*ajñāna*) is delusion (*moha*). "The form of both" is *rajas*. By the term "attachment and aversion," the conjunction with the actions of both is expressed. This is their common characteristic, pervasive among all living beings. "Inconceivable" (*apratarkya*): "tarka" means inference; it is beyond that scope. "Sāttvika characteristic" means this is the defining mark of the quality of *sattva*. "Delight in undertaking" (*ārambharatitā*) is the state of being devoted to the commencement of actions, whether they are for specific desires or for visible worldly ends. "Unsteadiness" (*adhairyam*) is the lack of mental composure even when faced with a slight cause for distress. "Improper action" (*asatkārya*) is acquisitiveness (*parigraha*). "Practice of conduct contrary to the world and the scriptures" is the persistence in enmity even over a minor offense. "Fractured conduct" (*bhinnavṛttitā*) is the ruin of one's character (*śīla*). "Begging" (*yācita*) is the habit of begging.

In the Mahābhārata: Foods that increase longevity, vitality, strength, health, happiness, and joy; which are savory, unctuous, substantial, and pleasing to the heart—these are dear to those of sattvic nature.
Bitter, sour, salty, excessively hot, pungent, dry, and burning foods are desired by those of the rajasic nature; they bestow suffering, grief, and disease.
Food that is stale, tasteless, putrid, and long kept,
as well as that which is leavings or impure— such food is dear to those of a tamasic nature.
Likewise:
"One who is free from attachment, devoid of egoism, endowed with fortitude and perseverance,
and remains unchanged in success or failure— such an agent is said to be characterized by goodness (sāttvika)."
A doer who is passionate, desirous of the fruits of action, greedy, violent by nature, impure,
and possessed by joy and grief, is proclaimed to be of the rajasic type.
One who is undisciplined, vulgar, stubborn, deceitful, malicious, lazy,
despondent, and procrastinating is said to be a doer of tamasic nature.
Hear from me, O Dhanañjaya, the threefold division of the intellect and of fortitude according to the gunas, as it is being declared in its entirety and in detail.

O Pārtha, that intellect which understands both engagement and withdrawal, what should be done and what should not be done, fear and fearlessness, as well as bondage and liberation— that intellect is sāttvika.
O Pārtha, that intellect by which one understands dharma and adharma, as well as what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, incorrectly, is of the nature of passion (rājasī).
That intellect which, enveloped by darkness, O Pārtha, perceives unrighteousness as righteousness and all things in a perverted manner, is tāmasī.
That resolve by which one sustains the activities of the mind, the vital breaths,
and the senses through unwavering yoga— that, O Pārtha, is sattvic resolve.
But that resolve by which one holds fast to dharma, pleasure, and wealth, O Arjuna,
while desiring the fruits through attachment— that resolve, O Pārtha, is rajasic.
O Pārtha, that resolve by which the dull-witted person does not abandon sleep, fear, grief, despondency, and even intoxication— that is of the nature of darkness (tāmasī).
But now hear from me, O bull among the Bharatas, about the threefold happiness,
in which one finds delight through practice and reaches the end of suffering.
That happiness which is like poison at first but like nectar in its result, born from the clarity of one's own intellect, is declared to be *sāttvika*.
That pleasure which arises from the contact of the senses with their objects, which is like nectar at first but like poison in its consequence, is known as rajasic.
That pleasure which, both at the beginning and in its consequence, deludes the self and arises from sleep,
laziness, and negligence, is declared to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).
There is no being on earth, nor again in heaven among the gods,
that is free from these three qualities born of nature.
Now, regarding the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman,
Yājñavalkya says as follows:
Just as sparks fly forth from a heated mass of iron,
even so do [beings] indeed emerge from the Self, from the very presence of the Self.
In that regard, the self indeed performs some action by itself, some by its own nature, and some—
consisting of both dharma and adharma— through habituation.
The cause, the imperishable, the agent, the knower, Brahman, the possessor of qualities,
the controller, the unborn— he is proclaimed as "born" due to the assumption of a body.
Just as at the beginning of creation he emits space, air, fire, water, and earth—
each possessing one additional quality— so too does he take them up when coming into being.
Through oblation the sun is nourished; from the sun comes rain, and from that the plants.
That food, in the form of essence, attains the state of semen.
When a man and a woman unite and the semen and blood are pure,
the Lord, himself the sixth, simultaneously takes up the five elements.
The sense organs, mind, vital breath, knowledge, lifespan, happiness, fortitude,
retention, impulsion, suffering, desire, and indeed the ego-sense;
Effort, form, color, likes and dislikes, existence and non-existence—
all this is born of that beginningless one who desires a beginning.
Just as Bharata describes his own body with various colors,
so too does the self assume bodies born of karma, taking on manifold forms.
Just as space, though one, appears distinct within jars and other vessels,
so too the Self, though one, appears manifold like the sun reflected in many water bowls.
Likewise,
all the organs of perception, the mind, the organs of action,
as well as the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), the intellect (buddhi), and the elements beginning with earth.
The unmanifest Self is declared to be the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) of this field;
it is the Lord of all beings, who is both being and non-being, and that which is beyond both being and non-being.

‘They arise from themselves’: those who identify with the gross body are born under the influence of their own auspicious and inauspicious karma. ‘He does something of his own’: whatever he performs independently for the sake of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful. ‘By nature’: that which one performs due to the influence of limiting adjuncts such as caste, as in the case of a camel’s habitual tendency to eat thorns. ‘Whatever’: acts such as giving, study, and so forth. ‘The possessor of qualities’ (guṇī): one endowed with the qualities of *sattva* and the rest by way of their power. ‘The master’ (vaśī): one who is independent. ‘The five elements’: the five gross elements (*bhūta*). ‘Fortitude’ (*dhṛti*): stability of the mind. ‘Existence’ (*bhava*): the attainment of wealth, sons, and so forth; its opposite is non-existence (*abhava*). ‘Bharata’: an actor. ‘All’: together with their objects, such as sound and the rest.
In the Mahābhārata:
"O son of Kuntī, this body is designated as the 'field' (kṣetra).
Those who know this call him who understands it the 'knower of the field' (kṣetrajña)."
And know Me also as the Knower of the Field in all fields, O Bhārata;
that which is the knowledge of the Field and the Knower of the Field is, in My view, true knowledge.
Likewise: "The supreme Brahman is without beginning; it is said to be neither being nor non-being.
It has hands and feet everywhere, and eyes, heads, and faces on all sides."
Possessing ears everywhere in the world, it stands encompassing all;
likewise, it is the witness, the consenter, the sustainer, the enjoyer, and the Great Lord.
And he is also called the Supreme Self, the Supreme Person within this body.
Likewise,
O son of Kuntī, because it is beginningless and devoid of qualities, this supreme Self is immutable; though dwelling within the body, it neither acts nor is it tainted.
Just as space, though all-pervading, is not defiled because of its subtlety,
so too the self, though dwelling everywhere within the body, is not defiled.
[133] Just as the one sun illumines this entire world,
so too, O Bhārata, does the Knower of the Field illumine the entire field.
Likewise: "This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth;
it is seen by subtle seers through their sharp and subtle intellect."
Likewise: "Someone beholds this as a marvel; likewise, another speaks of it as a marvel."
And another hears of this as something wonderful; yet even having heard it, no one at all truly knows it.
Yājñavalkya said: If this is so, O Brahmin, how is it that he is born into sinful wombs?
How does that Lord become joined with undesirable states of being?
And how is it that one endowed with sense organs does not possess prior knowledge? Why is it that even though the gods are omnipresent, they do not perceive [everything]?
Likewise,
one who is possessed by both passion and darkness, wandering here,
joined with undesirable states, enters into the cycle of existence.
[134] Just as a dirty mirror is incapable of reflecting forms,
so too an immature faculty is incapable of self-knowledge.
Just as in an unripe *urvāru* gourd, even though it possesses a sweet taste, that taste cannot be perceived;
so too, knowledge is not attained within the self when the faculties are unripened.
The embodied soul experiences sensation within its own innate body, which is the substratum of all;
yet the disciplined yogi does not experience any of those sensations.

‘If this were so’: if the self alone assumes the state of a living being (*jīva*), then it would be born in sinful wombs such as those of pigs and the like. To the three questions posed by the words ‘If this were so,’ etc., he gives the answers in sequence, beginning with ‘By passion and by darkness,’ and so forth. Regarding ‘in bitter cucumbers’: in the *tikta-karkaṭikā* (bitter gourd). Regarding ‘in its own body’: in a body acquired through its own karma. Regarding ‘the yogi who is disciplined,’ etc.: the yogi who is disciplined becomes the knower of all sensations; the meaning is that he is not a sufferer of pain. [This is stated] in the *Brahmapurāṇa*.
This supreme Self is indeed one, yet it appears divided into two;
in this world, both the enjoyer and the object of enjoyment are that very same Supreme Lord.
The insentient body, senses, and qualities perform actions when they are in equilibrium;
the conscious one who presides over them is the tranquil self, and he does not act.
An insentient weapon moves when a village is nearby;
likewise, the body and the collection of instruments act when presided over by that [consciousness].
When the sun has risen, the world performs its activities; the sun itself performs none of them, nor does it cause anything else to do so anywhere.
[135] However, this is the very nature of both the sun and the world:
it is pure consciousness, like the sun; and the sense organs are likewise like the world.
Even for one awakened by consciousness, yet still stupefied by the sense of "mine," there arises in the mind a mental disposition toward the power of pleasure and pain.
In the state of being a seer, a doer, and an enjoyer of actions—
whether superior, inferior, or middling— one acts like a fool, thinking "mine" and "I."
Although omnipresent, it remains within the body and conforms to that knowledge; being perfectly pure, it assumes the color of various kinds of pigments.
The crystal is not those [reflections], nor have they arisen from it, nor is it produced by them;
just as the reality (tattva) is fashioned by the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of rajas and tamas.
The All-pervading Lord bears its burden; it is not yours, nor do you belong to it.
Moving when it moves and remaining still when it stands still, it is like the reflections of the sun and moon in water.
The self, however, is not perceived in the collection of the senses, nor is it truly so;
for the invisible Rāhu becomes visible within the orbs of the moon and the sun.
The self is all-pervading and is seen as abiding within the intellect;
in pure vision, the world perceives its own honor through that which is devoid of consciousness.
This self beholds itself within you, whose intellect is stainless;
likewise, it beholds the castes and stages of life, as well as dwelling in heaven or even in hell.
These do not exist anywhere for the Person, the Supreme Self;
yet the form of the world is perceived, though it is unreal, false, and like a deception appearing as real.
Just as water exists in a mirage, so too do rays of light appear in the desert sands; indeed, the one sun alone is seen in many ways within various receptacles of water.
The Supreme Self alone shines forth, established in all substrates;
it is Brahman itself, situated both within and without the bodies.
Just as space is perceived within jars but not otherwise, so it is with that intellect by which one thinks, "I am the body. [136]
Through the delusion of self in what is not-self, that bondage of saṃsāra arises;
but one who is devoid of all conceptual constructions is pure, awakened, and free from old age and death.
The Lord is eternally tranquil, all-pervading like space, and of the nature of consciousness;
just as sugar, jaggery, and candied sugar are all produced from the juice of sugarcane.
Likewise, the various states and divisions of the self here are manifold in form:
the vital breath (prāṇa), the non-conscious (avijñāna), the inner ruler (antaryāmin), and the changeless one (avikāraka).
One should [know] one's own self as having place, time, body, and fire, along with its states and designations,
and as possessing infinite divisions such as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), like a net.
Having sported, Hari himself withdraws [the world],
always accompanied by the three— beginning, middle, and end— which are unattainable and born of delusion.
The Viśva and Taijasa states are veiled by waking, dreaming, and deep sleep;
but the Turya is the Supreme Self, the unmanifest and eternal state.
The waking state is to be known as that which is like being awake while fully alert;
and the dream state belongs to one who is situated within the subtle channel in the space of the heart.
The abandonment of the body, senses, and qualities is the state of deep sleep;
the awakening to all states of being is called the fourth state (turya), which is pure consciousness alone.
Just as the sky is not defiled by smoke, clouds, or dust,
so the Puruṣa is not tainted by the transformations (vikāras), even though he is touched by the material elements (prakṛti).
Just as when the space within a single jar is defiled by impurities such as smoke,
other jars situated far away do not become soiled anywhere at all.
Likewise, when one living being is defiled by various pairs of opposites, other living beings are not anywhere rendered impure by that.

‘Edible things’ (*bhojya*) refer to the collection of transformations produced from earth and the other elements. ‘Weapon’ (*śastra*) refers to iron. ‘The mind follows its own nature’ means it conforms to that inherent nature. ‘In the intellect’ (*dhiyi*) refers to the principle of the Great One (*mahattattva*). ‘Possessing a designation’ (*abhidhānavat*) means having names such as Devadatta and so forth. ‘Situated at a distance’ refers to the spaces within jars (*ghaṭākāśa*). Likewise:
“The various classes of individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) are born from that very same single consciousness.”
Like rays of light spread out from iron blazing with fire.
The Self of all beings is devoid of division, abandonment, conjunction, birth, death, and meeting; it abides within all things like space within jars.
But the person who is attached to it is bound by the power of Prakṛti,
just as a man of good character is bound by the fault of association with a thief.
Frost, bubbles, and foam are the three innate qualities of water;
likewise, smoke is the innate quality of fire—this illusion (māyā) is always innate to Viṣṇu.
One should contemplate this non-dual Brahman— which is entirely devoid of fruit, eternal, and free from delusion— as being the very nature of the illusory duality.
In the Mahābhārata,
the Blessed Lord said:
"Know that both Prakṛti and Puruṣa are indeed beginningless."
And know that both the transformations and the qualities arise from primordial nature (prakṛti).
Nature is said to be the cause in the agency of action and its instrument;
the Puruṣa is said to be the cause in the experience of pleasure and pain.
For the person, situated in material nature, experiences the qualities born of nature;
attachment to these qualities is the cause of his births in good and evil wombs.

[138] *Prakṛti* (Nature) is by its very nature devoid of specific characteristics (*alakṣaṇā*), being beginningless in the form of a continuous flow; for saṃsāra is beginningless, consisting as it does of "creation again, dissolution again. The *puruṣa*, though a portion of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) and beginningless, has never at any time been manifested in reality, even while remaining non-different from Him. Regarding the phrase "by action and ignorance": the effect is the body, and the causes are the senses; *prakṛti* is the cause in their agency and manifestation. By this it is stated that the entire range of objects of experience arises from *prakṛti*. "Abiding in *prakṛti*" means abiding in the aggregate of effects and causes. "He experiences those born of *prakṛti*" means he experiences pleasure, pain, and delusion produced from *prakṛti*. "Attachment to the *guṇas*"—that is, to the effects and causes characterized as such—is the misconception, the notion of "I" and "mine," which is the cause for attaining good and evil wombs. "Good wombs" are those of gods and so forth; "evil wombs" are those of animals and so forth; and "middling wombs" are humans.
Likewise: "Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind,
intellect, and ego— thus is my nature divided eightfold."
O mighty-armed one, know that this is My lower nature; but distinct from this, know My other, higher nature, which is the soul (jīva), by which this entire world is sustained.
Understand that all beings have this as their source;
I am the origin and likewise the dissolution of the entire universe.
[139] There is nothing else whatsoever higher than Me, O Dhanañjaya;
all this is strung upon Me like clusters of gems upon a thread.
Whatever states of being there are—whether characterized by goodness (sāttvika), passion (rājasa), or darkness (tāmasa)—know them to proceed from Me alone; yet I am not in them, but they are in Me.
Deluded by these three states consisting of the qualities, this entire world does not recognize Me, who am beyond them and imperishable.
For this divine illusion of Mine, consisting of the gunas, is difficult to overcome;
but those who take refuge in Me alone cross over this illusion.
The evil-doers, the deluded, the lowest of men, do not seek refuge in me;
their wisdom has been carried away by illusion, and they have taken hold of a demonic nature.
In this same way,
by me, whose form is unmanifest, all this world is pervaded;
all beings dwell in me, yet I do not abide in them.
And yet the beings do not dwell in Me; behold My divine yoga!
My Self, the source of all beings, sustains all beings but does not dwell within them.
Just as the great wind, omnipresent and eternal, rests always in space,
even so understand that all beings rest in Me.
O son of Kuntī, at the end of a kalpa all beings go to my own nature;
again, at the beginning of a kalpa, I send them forth.
Taking hold of my own nature,
I send forth again and again this entire multitude of beings, which is powerless under the sway of nature.
And those actions do not bind me, O Dhanañjaya,
for I sit as if indifferent, unattached to those actions.
Under my supervision, Nature brings forth the world of the moving and the unmoving;
by this cause, O son of Kuntī, the universe revolves.
Fools disregard me when I have assumed a human form,
being ignorant of my supreme nature as the Great Lord of all beings.
Futile their hopes, futile their actions, futile their knowledge, and devoid of discernment,
they have taken refuge in a delusive nature that is both demonic and asuric.
But the great-souled ones, O Pārtha, having taken refuge in the divine nature, worship me with undistracted minds, knowing me as the imperishable source of all beings.

Though I am unborn and my nature is imperishable, and though I am the Lord of all beings, yet by taking hold of my own material nature, I manifest myself through my own divine power of illusion (māyā).
Whenever there is a decline of righteousness, O Bhārata,
and a rise of unrighteousness, then I manifest myself.
For the protection of the virtuous, for the destruction of the wicked,
and for the sake of establishing righteousness, I manifest myself age after age.
‘*Jīvabhūtām*’ means that which has attained the state of being the individual soul; the consciousness abiding as the enjoyer. ‘*Protam*’ means woven or strung together.
As stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
“This entire universe is the expansion of Viṣṇu, who is the self of all beings.”
Therefore, the wise should regard [all things] as non-different from the self.
Likewise: "Those of dull intellect, perceiving this entire world— which is in its true nature pure consciousness— as being in the nature of material objects, wander in the deluge of delusion."
The luminaries are Viṣṇu, the worlds are Viṣṇu, the forests, the mountains, and the quarters are Viṣṇu;
the rivers and the oceans— he alone is everything.
O best of brahmins, that which exists and that which does not exist—
Since the Blessed One is of the nature of consciousness, possessing all forms yet not a substantial entity,
he [appears] as the various distinctions of mountains, oceans, earth, and so forth.
Know them to be the manifestations of consciousness.
But when all knowledge is pure, possessing its own innate form, free from defects through the exhaustion of karma,
then indeed [cease] the fruits of the tree of volitional construction.
There arise for us distinctions between entities among things.

Is there anywhere any entity that is devoid of beginning, middle, and end, eternally of one form, and yet which, O twice-born, undergoes transformation? For what has come into being [cannot remain so].
That is not so there; for how could there be reality?
The earth becomes a jar; from the jar come shards;
from the shards, powdered dust; and from that, atoms—[all this] by people whose certainty regarding the self is stilled by their own karma.
It is perceived; tell me, what is the truth in this matter?
Therefore, O twice-born one, there is no collection of objects whatsoever, anywhere or at any time, apart from consciousness;
consciousness alone exists through the differentiation of its own karma.
It is approached in many ways through various modes of conduct.
Knowledge is pure, stainless, free from sorrow, with all greed and other passions cast away and devoid of conceptualization;
it is the one, the truly one, the supreme, the Lord of the highest.
That Vāsudeva exists from whom nothing whatsoever [is separate].
Thus have I explained to you the true nature of existence; knowledge is the truth, while everything else is unreal.
This, however, is that which constitutes conventional worldly practice.
And it has also been stated there that those [elements] are dependent upon the worlds.
In the sacrifice, the animal, the fire, all the officiating priests,
the Soma, the gods, and the desire consisting of heaven—
thus is seen the path dependent on ritual action.
And the enjoyments of the earth and so forth are their fruits.
And whatever I have told you regarding this world,
one subject to karma indeed wanders everywhere therein;
having understood this, [one realizes] that [the Self] is certainly immovable and of a single form.
One should perform that by which one indeed enters Vāsudeva.

‘Of the nature of knowledge’ (*jñānasvarūpa*): knowledge is the nature of consciousness (*cit*), and the world has that as its essence, just as a pot is of the nature of clay. ‘The unintelligent’ (*abuddhayaḥ*) are those who do not know reality. ‘Of the nature of objects’ (*arthasvarūpa*): that which is the inherent nature [of things], by virtue of having material causes such as primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and so forth—that is its true form. ‘In the flood of delusion’ (*mohasaṃplave*): in the ocean of false knowledge. The meaning is that whatever exists and whatever does not exist—all that which is the nature of being—is He alone. ‘And not consisting of material substance’ (*na ca vastubhūtaḥ*): not that which is composed of earth and the other elements. ‘There is no differentiation of substance among substances’: it is not the case that pots and the like arise from a differentiation of substance while earth and the other elements already exist with their own inherent natures; rather, the meaning is that they arise through the power of volition (*saṃkalpa*).

And thus says the Śruti: "By his mere volition (saṃkalpa), the ancestors attend upon him. This has been explained in the Vedānta Sūtra under the aphorism: "But [it is] from volition alone, because of that scriptural statement. Regarding the phrase "the other is unreal" (asatyam anyat), the meaning is that everything other than Brahman is unreal; it undergoes change and perishes. In the verse beginning with "The true state is thus," it is stated that because the time for ritual action (karma) is impermanent, one must exert effort toward attaining Vāsudeva through knowledge. Thus ends the section on detachment (vairāgyaparva) in the Mokṣakāṇḍa of the Kṛtyakalpataru.
[144] 15 — Now follows the application of knowledge and action; regarding this, it is stated in the Mahābhārata:
For regarding liberation, a threefold steadfastness has been observed by the great seers of old;
some people who are learned in the scriptures of liberation declare that steadfastness in knowledge is the path.
Other ascetics of subtle vision declare that steadfastness in action alone is the goal; yet there are those who, having abandoned both of these—knowledge and action—follow knowledge exclusively.
In the third [chapter], this conclusion was proclaimed by that Great-Souled One. Likewise,
Śuka said:
Regarding this Vedic statement, "Perform action" and "Renounce action"—
in which direction do they go by means of knowledge, and in which do they go by means of action?
I truly wish to hear this;
may you explain it to me according to its true nature—that which exists in mutual incompatibility and opposition.
Thus addressed, the son of Parāśara replied to his son:
"I shall explain these two syllables, my son, which consist of action and knowledge."
Listen with a one-pointed mind, my son, for this distinction between them is indeed subtle: the direction they go to by means of knowledge, and that which they reach through action.
A living being is bound by action, but is liberated through knowledge;
therefore, ascetics who have seen the further shore do not perform ritual action.
Through action, one is born after death as a embodied being consisting of sixteen parts;
through knowledge, one is born eternally as the imperishable, for one's true nature is indeed imperishable.
But some men of very little intelligence praise karma; therefore, they remain devoted to it, seeking to bring under their control the various bodies born of it.
But those who have attained supreme understanding and perceive the subtleties of Dharma do not regard action as real, just as one drinking from a river does not notice the well.
One obtains the fruit of action—happiness and suffering, existence and non-existence;
through knowledge one attains that state, having gone to which one does not grieve.
Wherever one goes, one does not die; wherever one goes, one is not born;
wherever one goes, one does not decay; and wherever one goes, one does not grow old.
‘Those who perceive the subtlety of dharma’ means those who understand the supreme means for attaining steadfastness (*dhṛti*) through its gradations. As Manu says:
"But this is the supreme dharma: that one perceives the Self through yoga.
‘Existence and non-existence’ refers to birth and death. ‘By knowledge’ means by the knowledge of Brahman.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa,
the son said:
"O father, thus wandering in this perilous wheel of saṃsāra..."
This knowledge, which is the cause for attaining liberation, has been obtained by me.
It is understood here that all this which is designated as Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman is awakened by the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman; thus says Yogiyājñavalkya. [146]
Liberation comes from thorough understanding; this is the characteristic of laziness.
The unwise do not desire action that consists of bodily affliction.
Through the union of knowledge and action, one attains the Supreme Puruṣa; it cannot be accomplished through their separation. Therefore, one should rely upon both.
Knowledge is primary, but not devoid of action;
action is primary, but not devoid of wisdom.
Therefore, accomplishment arises only from the union of both.
For a bird does not fly with only one wing.
‘It would not succeed’ means it would not be liberated. ‘Both’ refers to knowledge and action.
Bṛhaspati says:
Truth, sacrifice, austerity, and charity—this is the characteristic of Dharma.
From the Dharma come both happiness and knowledge; from knowledge, liberation is attained.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"O King, by the performance of meritorious and non-meritorious acts,
and likewise by not performing obligatory duties out of a lack of desire [to do so]," [one experiences their results].
Due to the non-accumulation of new karma and the exhaustion of previously acquired karma,
one incurs bondage through action and assumes a body again and again.
‘From not acting out of desire’ means from not performing actions motivated by desire; as Manu says:
“That which leads to happiness and worldly prosperity, and that which leads to the supreme good.”
Vedic action is of two kinds: that which leads to worldly involvement and that which leads to its cessation.
Action performed with desire for results, whether in this world or the next, is called "pravṛtta" (engaged); but action free from desire and preceded by knowledge is taught as "nivṛtta" (disengaged).
By practicing active karma, one attains the nature of the gods;
but by practicing renunciation, one transcends the five elements in the fifth stage.
Seeing oneself in all beings and all beings in oneself,
one who sacrifices to the Self attains self-sovereignty.
Even having abandoned those duties as they have been described, the best of the twice-born should be diligent in self-knowledge, tranquility, and the study of the Vedas.
This is the complete equipment of a twice-born man, especially of a Brāhmaṇa;
for having attained this, the twice-born man has indeed accomplished his purpose, and not otherwise.

In the phrase “conducive to the arising of happiness” (*sukhābhyudayika*), the suffix *ṭhan* is used in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*), meaning that which has the arising or production of happiness as its fruit. “Conducive to the supreme good” (*naiḥśreyasika*) refers to that action for which the supreme good—namely, liberation (*mokṣa*)—is the purpose. “Engaged and disengaged actions” are said to be, respectively, the causes for the engagement in and the cessation from saṃsāra. “Having become one’s own nature” (*sātmatām*) means having attained an identical capacity. Regarding “sovereignty” (*svārājyam*): that which shines or manifests by itself is a self-ruler (*svarāṭ*), namely Brahman; the state of being that is sovereignty (*svārājya*). The meaning is that one attains the state of Brahman. (As stated) in the *Mahābhārata*.
O sinless one, in this world I have previously declared two kinds of perfection:
through the yoga of knowledge for the followers of Sāṃkhya, and through the yoga of action for the yogis.
[148] A person does not attain freedom from action by abstaining from actions,
nor does he achieve perfection merely through renunciation.
For indeed, no one ever remains even for a moment without performing action;
for everyone is driven helplessly to act by the qualities born of nature.
He who sits restraining the organs of action but continues to dwell upon the objects of the senses with his mind, being deluded in soul, is called a hypocrite.
But he who, O Arjuna, having restrained the senses with the mind,
engages in the yoga of action through the organs of action without attachment— he is superior.
Perform your prescribed duty, for action is indeed superior to inaction;
even the maintenance of your body would not be possible through inaction.
This world is bound by action other than that performed for the sake of sacrifice;
therefore, O son of Kuntī, perform action for that purpose, free from attachment.

"In this world," meaning in this context concerning the path to liberation (*apavarga*). "Firm foundation" (*niṣṭhā*) means stability. "By the yoga of knowledge for the Sāṃkhyas": those who have correctly discerned and directly realized the reality of the Self are the Sāṃkhyas; their state is said to be primarily characterized by [knowledge]. Ritual action (*karman*), as it is obtained according to the rules prescribed for one's stage of life (*āśrama*), certainly exists for them as well, for the sake of maturing knowledge and for the avoidance of transgression. "By the yoga of action for the Yogins": this refers to those possessed of the yoga of purity (*sattva*) who perform action for the sake of propitiating the Lord; their state is primarily characterized by action, because [action] is a means to the higher realization that directly perceives the Self. And so it has been said:
Knowledge arises for men through the destruction of evil karma,
so that they may behold the Self within themselves, as if in the surface of a mirror.

‘In the self’ means in the intellect (*buddhi*). The destruction of evil results from dharma, according to the Vedic revelation: “One removes evil by dharma; seek to know Brahman through austerity. Since knowledge also exists in a general form, there is no distinction such that one or the other is primary; thus, there is no [exclusive] conjunction. [149] Through the union of knowledge and action, one attains the Supreme Person. They may be accomplished separately; therefore, one should resort to both.

This is according to the statement of the *Yogiyājñavalkya*: "Liberation comes from knowledge alone. Thus, the view that no Vedic (*śrauta*) or Smārta ritual action should be performed because they cause bondage has been refuted. By the passage beginning with "Not by abstaining from actions does one attain freedom from action" (*naiṣkarmyam*), the meaning is that *naiṣkarmya*—the state of being free from merit and demerit—is liberation (*mokṣa*). "From renunciation" (*saṃnyasanāt*) means by taking up the highest stage of life (*uttamāśrama*). "Unattached" (*asaktaḥ*) means devoid of attachment to results. Regarding the phrase "other than action for the sake of sacrifice" (*yajñārthāt karmaṇo 'nyatra*), by the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*), the Lord of Sacrifice (*yajñapuruṣa*) is meant, according to the Vedic text: "Viṣṇu is indeed sacrifice. Therefore, the meaning is that action other than that performed for the purpose of propitiating the Lord leads to bondage, whereas action for the sake of heaven and such results is what causes bondage.
And so it is said:
"Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give away,
and whatever austerity you practice, O son of Kuntī, perform that as an offering unto Me."
In this way, you shall be liberated from the bonds of action through their very fruits, whether auspicious or inauspicious;
with your self disciplined by the yoga of renunciation, you will be freed and come to Me.
‘Whatever you do,’ such as bathing and so forth; ‘whatever you eat’—here, eating refers to the form of the oblation to the vital breaths (*prāṇāhuti*). Likewise:
“Your right is to action alone, never to its fruits.”
Do not let the fruit of action be your motive, nor let there be attachment in you toward inaction.
Established in yoga, perform actions while abandoning attachment, O Dhanañjaya;
becoming the same in success and failure—that state of equanimity is called yoga.
For action is far inferior to the yoga of wisdom, O Dhanañjaya;
seek refuge in wisdom. Miserable are those whose motive is the fruit of action.
One endowed with wisdom casts off both good and evil deeds in this very world;
therefore, apply yourself to yoga, for yoga is skill in actions.
For the wise, endowed with discernment, having abandoned the fruit born of action,
being liberated from the bondage of birth, go to the state that is free from all suffering.

“‘In action alone’ means that your authority (*adhikāra*) lies in action alone as prescribed for your stage of life (*āśrama*), because it is an obligatory duty, and not in the fruits of action. To clarify the meaning of the phrase ‘let there be no authority for you in the fruits,’ he says: ‘Do not become the cause of the fruit of action. One who desires the fruit of action is a ‘cause of action,’ meaning a performer of action. ‘May you not be so’—this implies that you must not entertain a desire for the fruit. ‘Let there be no attachment to inaction’ does not mean that you should not have attachment toward performing action; rather, the meaning is that actions must indeed be performed. To the question of how, then, actions should be performed, he says ‘established in yoga,’ and so forth. Those obligatory actions such as the *saṃdhyā-vandana* (twilight worship) and others, perform them while being ‘established in yoga’: having abandoned attachment to the fruit, and having become equanimous by remaining free from joy or dejection regarding the success or failure of the result of the action. Furthermore, when action is performed for the sake of propitiating the Lord, there is no inequality. The meaning is that the Lord alone is the agent and the action is of His nature; thus, the action being performed partakes in being the cause for attaining Him. This very state of equanimity is called ‘yoga.’”

Action devoid of knowledge is far inferior to this action endowed with the intellect of equanimity. “Seek refuge in the intellect” means take recourse to the intellect. “Those whose motive is the fruit”: those for whom the fruit is the cause of their engagement are so described. “Endowed with the intellect” means performing action with the understanding that it is for the sake of worshipping the Lord. The meaning is that one abandons both the auspicious and inauspicious actions already undertaken. “Apply yourself to yoga” means strive for the yoga of equanimity. “Skill in actions” refers to this: the dedication of action to Brahman and the absence of intention regarding its results. “Born of action” means born of auspicious and inauspicious action; “having abandoned the fruit,” they go to the abode of Viṣṇu, which is free from birth and devoid of all afflictions—this is the meaning.
Likewise: "Actions do not smear me, nor do I have a longing for the fruit of action;
he who understands me thus is not bound by actions."
Knowing this, even the seekers of liberation in the past performed action;
therefore, you too should perform action, as it was performed by those of old, even more so than before.

"Actions do not taint me"—meaning, actions do not smear me because I have no longing for the fruit of action. In the same way, any other person who, having abandoned thirst for the results in his own undertaking, engages in action with the thought "this is for the Supreme Lord," he too is not bound by actions; this is the meaning.
Likewise, Arjuna said:
O Kṛṣṇa, you praise renunciation of action, and yet again you praise yoga;
tell me with certainty which one of these two is the better.
The Blessed Lord said:
Both renunciation and the yoga of action lead to the supreme good;
however, of these two, the yoga of action is superior to the renunciation of action.
He should be known as a perpetual renunciant who neither hates nor desires;
for one free from the pairs of opposites, O mighty-armed one, is easily liberated from bondage.
The ignorant, not the wise, speak of Sāṃkhya and Yoga as distinct;
even by being properly established in one, one obtains the fruit of both.
The state that is attained by Sāṃkhya is also reached by those through Yoga;
he who sees Sāṃkhya and Yoga as one truly perceives.
But renunciation, O mighty-armed one, is difficult to attain without yoga;
the sage disciplined in yoga attains Brahman before long.
One who is disciplined in yoga, whose self is purified, who has mastered the self and conquered the senses,
and whose self has become the self of all beings, is not tainted even while acting.
The disciplined knower of reality should think, "I do nothing at all," while seeing,
hearing, touching, smelling, eating, walking, sleeping, and breathing.
