Speaking, releasing, grasping, opening, and even closing the eyes—
one should maintain the awareness that it is the senses alone that operate upon their respective objects.
He who performs actions by dedicating them to Brahman, having abandoned attachment,
is not smeared by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
Having abandoned attachment, yogis perform action with the body, mind, intellect, and even with the senses alone, for the sake of self-purification.
The disciplined one, having abandoned the fruit of action, attains peace that is final;
the undisciplined one, acting out of desire and attached to the fruit, is bound.

"Karmayoga is superior to the renunciation of action (*karmasaṃnyāsa*). This means that compared to the renunciation of performed actions unto the Lord—which has been described—that Karmayoga is superior, wherein Brahman alone is the agent, as well as the other factors of action and the action itself. How so? For renunciation has duality as its object, whereas Karmayoga has non-duality as its object; the meaning is that it is directly based on right vision (*samyagdarśana*). "Free from the pairs of opposites" (*nirdvandva*) means devoid of the pairs such as attachment and aversion. "Established in renunciation" (*saṃnyāsasthiti*) means that what is practiced apart from the yoga of renunciation leads to suffering and not to the direct realization of Brahman. "He attains Brahman before long" means he realizes Brahman directly in no long time. "Yoked in yoga" (*yogayukta*) means established in the vision of non-duality. "Pure in self" (*viśuddhātman*) means one whose intellect has been made stainless. "Self-conquered" (*vijitātman*) means one who has mastered the fluctuations of the mind. Regarding the phrase "the senses in the objects of the senses": one should maintain the thought, "The senses operate upon these objects of the senses; I have no agency here. The meaning is that one yoked in yoga should think thus. "He attains peace that is final" (*śāntim āpnoti naiṣṭhikīm*) means he attains absolute happiness.
Likewise,
Arjuna said: "O mighty-armed one, I desire to know the true nature of renunciation."
And [tell me] of renunciation, O Hṛṣīkeśa, separately, O slayer of Keśin.
The Blessed Lord said:
The wise know the renunciation of actions performed for the sake of desire as *saṃnyāsa*;
the discerning call the relinquishment of the fruits of all actions *tyāga*.
Some wise men say that action should be abandoned as being full of fault;
others say that action consisting of sacrifice, gift-giving, and austerity should not be abandoned.
Listen to my certain conclusion regarding renunciation, O best of the Bharatas;
for renunciation, O tiger among men, is proclaimed to be of three kinds.
Sacrifice, charity, and austerity—action is not to be abandoned; it must indeed be performed.
For sacrifice, charity, and austerity are the purifiers of the wise.
But even these actions, O Pārtha, must be performed after abandoning attachment and the fruits; this is my firm and supreme conviction.
But the renunciation of obligatory action is not appropriate;
its abandonment through delusion is declared to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).
If one should abandon action merely because it is suffering out of fear of physical exhaustion,
he performs a passionate renunciation and shall not obtain the fruit of renunciation.
O Arjuna, when prescribed action is performed simply because it is duty,
having abandoned attachment as well as the fruit, that renunciation is considered to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika).
He does not hate unwholesome action, nor does he cling to the wholesome;
he is renounced, filled with compassion for all beings, wise, and one whose doubts have been severed.
For it is not possible for one who bears a body to abandon actions entirely;
however, he who renounces the fruits of action is called a "renouncer."
The threefold fruit of action— unpleasant, pleasant, and mixed—
accrues after death to those who do not renounce, but never to those who have renounced.

"Having abandoned attachment" means having abandoned the fruits such as worship and other results that are for the sake of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*). "Of the obligatory" refers to the daily (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites. "He does not find evil in the gods" means he does not regard them as instruments of suffering, such as insults, abuse, or beatings. "He does not hate" means he remains tranquil, thinking, "I am experiencing the fruit of past karma. "In the auspicious" refers to the means of attaining happiness, such as honor and worship.
Likewise: "He who performs the necessary action without depending on the fruit of action..."
He is both a renunciant and a yogi; he is not one who has merely abandoned the sacred fires, nor is he one who has simply ceased from action.
That which they call renunciation, know that to be yoga, O Pāṇḍava;
for no one becomes a yogi without having renounced all purposeful intention.
For a sage who desires to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the means;
likewise:
"But that man who should find delight only in the Self, and who is satisfied with the Self..."
And for one who is content in the Self alone, there is no duty to be performed.
He has no purpose whatsoever here through action, nor any through inaction;
nor does he have any dependence on any being for any object of desire.
Therefore, perform always your prescribed duty without attachment;
for by performing action without attachment, a person attains the Supreme.
For Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone;
you should likewise act, having regard for the maintenance of the world.
Whatever a superior person practices, that very thing other people also do;
whatever standard he sets, the world follows that.
O Pārtha, there is nothing whatsoever in the three worlds that must be done by me;
there is nothing unattained to be attained, yet I continue to engage in action.
For if I were not to engage unweariedly in action at any time,
O Pārtha, men would follow my path in every respect.
These worlds would perish if I were not to perform action;
I would be the author of confusion and would destroy these beings.
Just as the ignorant act while attached to action, O Bhārata,
so should the wise man act without attachment, desiring the welfare of the world.

The wise man, acting with disciplined composure, should not create a disturbance in the minds of the ignorant who are attached to action; rather, he should encourage them toward all actions while performing them himself.

He whose delight is in the Self alone, and not in sense-objects, is "one who delights in the Self" (*ātmarati*). He who is satisfied with the Self alone, and not by food, flavors, and so forth, is "satisfied with the Self" (*ātmatṛpta*). He who finds contentment in the Self alone is "contented with the Self" (*ātmasaṃtuṣṭa*); for him, there is no further task to be accomplished through the acquisition of wealth. Since one who has attained the supreme light is beyond worldly activity, he has no duty to perform. Because the grounds for qualification no longer exist, there is no purpose to be served by the non-performance of prohibited acts—namely, the non-arising of sin that would otherwise result from their performance. "Dependence on objects" (*arthavyapāśrayaḥ*) refers to the expectation of some motive; since for one who follows worldly conduct, the renunciation of action cannot arise, the Lord says "therefore, being unattached," and so forth, to urge him to perform the necessary action while remaining free from desire for the fruits of action. "By action alone"—not by the renunciation of action—one should cause the world to be sustained; that is, one should practice it.
Likewise:
"Renouncing all actions in Me with a mind focused on the Supreme Self,
become free from desire and possessiveness, and fight, rid of all feverish distress."
"With an inward-turned mind" means by means of the vision of non-difference, [realizing] that "all this—the entire aggregate of effects and instruments—is indeed Brahman.
Likewise: "Having abandoned attachment to the fruits of action, ever-contented, and without support..."
Even though he is fully engaged in action, he does nothing at all.
Free from desire, with mind and self controlled, having renounced all possessions,
one who performs action solely for the sake of the body incurs no sin.
Content with whatever comes by chance, transcending the pairs of opposites, and free from envy—
one who is the same in success and failure is not bound even while acting.
For one who is free from attachment, liberated, whose mind is established in knowledge,
and who performs action as a sacrifice, all action is entirely dissolved.
The offering is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman, poured by Brahman into the fire of Brahman;
by him who is absorbed in the work of Brahman, Brahman alone is to be attained.

‘Free from desire’ (*nirāśīr*) means one whose attachment to results has departed. ‘With mind and self controlled’ (*yatacittātmā*) means one whose inner being is restrained. ‘The aggregate of causes and effects’ refers to the mere physical body, that which is to be accomplished by the body. It is action prescribed by the scriptures alone, devoid of [attachment to] results. ‘He incurs no sin’ means he does not incur *saṃsāra*; the ellipsis is “by means of passion, hatred, and so forth” for one who is liberated. [158] ‘For sacrifice’ means for the Supreme Self. ‘Offering to Brahman’ (*brahmārpaṇam*): by the etymology “that by which [the offering] is offered,” it refers to the sacrificial ladle (*sruc*), the dipping-spoon (*sruva*), and so on. ‘With the concentration that action is Brahman’ (*brahmakarmasamādhinā*) means with the meditative absorption in the thought that action itself is Brahman. And likewise:
Having mentally renounced all actions, the self-controlled embodied being dwells in happiness within the city of nine gates, neither acting nor causing others to act.
The Lord creates neither agency nor actions for the world, nor the connection with the fruits of action; rather, it is inherent nature that operates.
The All-pervading Lord does not take upon himself the sin of anyone, nor indeed their merit;
he does not bring about union with the fruits of action, for it is nature that operates.
The omnipresent Lord does not take upon Himself the sin or even the merit of anyone;
knowledge is veiled by ignorance, and by that, living beings are deluded.
But for those whose ignorance regarding the Self has been destroyed by knowledge,
that knowledge reveals the Supreme, just like the sun.
With their intellects fixed on That, with their selves absorbed in That, established in That, and having That as their supreme goal,
they go to the state from which there is no return, their impurities shaken off by knowledge.
Likewise:
"O scorcher of foes, the sacrifice of knowledge is superior to the sacrifice consisting of material objects;
for all action in its entirety, O Pārtha, culminates in knowledge."
Know that through prostration, inquiry, and service;
the wise who have seen reality will instruct you in that knowledge.
Having known this, O Pāṇḍava, you shall not again enter into such a state of sacrifice;
by means of it, you shall see all beings without exception within yourself, and then within me.
Even if you are the most sinful among all evildoers,
you shall cross over all wickedness by means of the boat of knowledge alone.
[159] Just as a well-kindled fire reduces fuel to ashes, O Arjuna,
so does the fire of knowledge reduce all actions to ashes.
Indeed, there is nothing in this world as purifying as knowledge;
one who is perfected through yoga finds that within oneself in due course of time.
The man of faith, devoted to it and with senses restrained, attains knowledge;
having attained knowledge, he reaches supreme peace without delay.
The ignorant, the faithless, and the doubting soul perish;
for the doubting soul, there is neither this world, nor the next, nor happiness.
O Dhanañjaya, actions do not bind one who has renounced action through yoga, whose doubts have been cut away by knowledge, and who is self-possessed.
Therefore, having cut asunder with the sword of self-knowledge this doubt residing in the heart which has arisen from ignorance, take recourse to yoga; arise, O Bhārata!
Likewise: Just as seeds scorched by fire do not sprout again,
so too the Self is never again joined with all things once they have been consumed by knowledge.
[160] 16— Now, regarding the causes for the knowledge of the Self, Yājñavalkya says:
The recitation of the meaning of the Vedas, sacrifice, celibacy,
austerity, self-restraint, pure fasting, and independence are the causes for the knowledge of the Self.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Having studied the Vedas and having grasped their meaning with his intellect, he is also a knower of words."
And having heard the Dharmaśāstra of the Mīmāṃsakas,
one realizes that this self is difficult to attain within the three worlds.
By means of non-violence, detachment from the senses, Vedic rituals,
and the practice of severe austerities, they attain that state in this world.
Austerity and knowledge are the supreme means for a Brahmin to attain the highest good;
through austerity he destroys impurity, and through knowledge he partakes of immortality.
In the Mahābhārata: "Knowledge arises for men through the destruction of sinful karma;
they behold the Self within the self, as if in the surface of a mirror."
In the Matsya Purāṇa: This very yoga of action is the means for accomplishing the yoga of knowledge;
without the yoga of action, knowledge does not exist for anyone here in this world.
Yājñavalkya says: Service to the teacher, discernment of the Vedic scriptures,
the performance of those prescribed duties, association with the virtuous, and auspicious speech.
The cessation of the pursuit of women and the vision of the Self in all beings;
the renunciation of possessions and the wearing of worn-out saffron robes.
Avoiding lethargy and indolence arising from the contact between the senses and their objects,
maintaining a constant awareness of the body, and perceiving evil in worldly activities.
The destruction of rajas and tamas, purity of sattva, freedom from desire, and self-restraint—
perfected by these means, he becomes fit and attains immortality.
Through the establishment of mindfulness of reality, through the application of being, through the exhaustion of karmas, and through proximity to the virtuous, the yoga of the good proceeds.

‘Enumeration of the body’ (*śarīraparisaṃkhyāna*) means reflecting upon it with a focus on defects such as its impurity and instability. ‘In activities’ (*pravṛttiṣu*) refers to perceiving the faults in actions such as coming and going, namely the subtle killing of living beings. ‘From the recollection of reality’ (*tattvasmṛteḥ*) means from the contemplation of the reality of the Self. ‘From the presence’ (*upasthānāt*) means from focused attention.
[As stated] in the *Mahābhārata*, the Blessed One said:
Humility, freedom from hypocrisy, non-violence, patience, uprightness,
service to the teacher, purity, steadfastness, and self-restraint.
Detachment from the objects of the senses, as well as the absence of egoism,
and the perception of the defects and suffering inherent in birth, death, old age, and disease.
Non-attachment and absence of clinging toward children, wife, home, and so forth;
and constant equanimity of mind amidst the occurrence of the pleasant and the unpleasant.
And unwavering devotion to me through the yoga of exclusive concentration;
the habit of resorting to solitary places; and a distaste for the assembly of crowds.
Constancy in the knowledge of the inner self and the vision of the goal of the knowledge of reality—this is declared to be knowledge;
that which is otherwise than this is ignorance.

‘Self-restraint’ (*ātmavinigraha*) is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind. ‘Non-attachment’ (*asakti*) is dispassion (*vairāgya*). ‘Absence of clinging’ (*abhiṣvaṅga*) is the lack of devotion to worldly objects. ‘Perception of the goal of the knowledge of reality’ (*tattvajñānārthadarśana*) is the investigation of the scriptures for the sake of self-knowledge. ‘This is knowledge’ (*etaj jñānam*) means this is the means to knowledge.
Likewise: “There is no wealth like this for a Brāhmaṇa.”
Just as oneness, truthfulness, and the absence of "mine-ness," so too are steadfastness in virtue, laying aside the rod, uprightness,
and the gradual withdrawal from all activities.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"Attachment should be abandoned with all one's soul; yet, if it cannot be abandoned, it should be directed toward the virtuous, for association with the good is indeed a medicine."
In the Mahābhārata,
the Blessed One said: Fearlessness, purity of being, steadfastness in the yoga of knowledge—
Generosity, self-control, sacrifice, study of the Vedas, austerity, and uprightness;
Non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, renunciation, tranquility,
absence of backbiting, compassion toward all beings, lack of greed, gentleness, and freedom from cowardice and crookedness.
Splendor, forgiveness, fortitude, purity, freedom from malice, and absence of arrogance—
these, O Bhārata, belong to one born with the divine fortune.
Deceit, arrogance, self-conceit, anger,
as well as harshness and ignorance— these, O Pārtha, belong to one born to the demonic nature.
The divine endowment leads to liberation; the demonic is considered to lead to bondage.
‘Tejas’ means sovereignty. Likewise:
“The Lord dwells, O Arjuna, in the heart-region of all beings.”
Causing all beings to revolve, mounted on a machine by means of his illusory power.
Go to him alone for refuge with your whole being, O Bhārata;
through his grace you shall attain supreme peace and the eternal abode.
Thus has this knowledge, more secret than the secret, been declared to you by me;
having reflected upon it in its entirety, do as you wish.
Listen again to my supreme word, the most secret of all secrets;
because you are dearly beloved to Me, I shall therefore speak what is for your benefit.
With your mind become My devotee, sacrifice to Me, and bow down to Me;
you shall come to Me alone—this I promise you in truth, for you are dear to Me.
Renouncing all duties, take refuge in me alone;
I shall liberate you from all evils, do not grieve.
"Having renounced all duties"—this means: "Having abandoned all duties, perform my worship. This statement is intended primarily to establish the preeminence of the worship of the Blessed One.
Likewise: "I am the source of all; from me everything proceeds."
Thinking thus, the wise, filled with devotion, worship me.
With their hearts set on me and their lives surrendered to me, awakening one another and constantly speaking of me, they find contentment and offer salutations.
To those who are constantly devoted to Me and worship Me with love,
I grant that yoga of discernment by which they come to Me.
Out of compassion for them alone, I, abiding within their own being, destroy the darkness born of ignorance with the radiant lamp of knowledge.
Yājñavalkya says: Indeed, he (the Self) is to be sought after by all the stages of life in this very manner;
furthermore, He is to be seen, reflected upon, and heard by the twice-born.
165] 17—The *Sapallavyoga*. Now, regarding the *yoga*: on this point, Devala says:

For gods and humans, there are two kinds of human goals (*puruṣārtha*): prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). Of these, prosperity has been described previously as being of two kinds. The supreme good consists of Sāṃkhya and Yoga. Knowledge of the twenty-five principles is Sāṃkhya. Yoga is the stabilization of the mind upon the intended object after withdrawing it from sense-objects. In both cases, liberation (*apavarga*) is the fruit. As stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"That particular movement of the mind which depends upon personal effort..."
The union with that Brahman is designated as yoga.
Dakṣa says:
Having rendered the mind free from activity and having unified the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) with the Supreme Self, one is liberated; this is called the primary yoga.
In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"O King, this [nature] of ignorance has been described by me to you;
there exists nothing other than yoga that brings about the destruction of the afflictions."
Yogiyājñavalkya says: Having abandoned all duties, one should take refuge in the dharma of yoga;
for all other duties are indeed flawed, as they cause rebirth.
In this, there is no loss through transgression, nor does any obstacle exist;
even a very little of this dharma protects one from great fear.
‘Overstepping’ (atikramaḥ) means non-commencement; here, ‘destruction’ (nāśaḥ) refers to fruitlessness.
As it is said in the Mahābhārata: “Just as large fish, having broken through the net, [re-enter] the water again...”
In that same way, through yoga, those whose impurities have been removed attain that state.
Just as powerful fish, being "unblinking," break through the net and,
freed from all bonds, reach the clear path; so too shall they attain the stainless way.
O King, those endowed with strength, having broken through the bonds born of greed by means of yoga, go along the supreme path to the stainless Śiva.
Just as small birds, having encountered the enemy-subduing Jaja, are captured there when they lack the strength, but are released when endowed with power; so it is with men.
O scorcher of the foe, yogas bound by the fetters born of karma likewise perish when they are weak, but those endowed with strength are liberated.
Just as a careful archer, being fully concentrated, hits the target,
so too the yogi who is properly disciplined attains liberation without doubt.
Just as there might be a certain terrible forest, abounding in snakes and reptiles,
full of chasms, devoid of water, difficult to traverse, and thick with thorns.
A man might safely traverse a path that is devoid of food, consisting mostly of wilderness, with its trees scorched by forest fires, and infested with robbers.
Whosoever among the twice-born resorts to the path of yoga and practices it,
that path is remembered as having many defects, even though it leads to peaceful cessation.
Likewise:
"Even one of inferior caste, or a woman seeking righteousness—
even these two shall go by this path to the supreme goal."
Likewise:
For one who is not disciplined, there is no wisdom; for one who is not disciplined, there is no meditative cultivation.
For one who does not cultivate, there is no peace; for one who lacks peace, how can there be happiness?
Likewise: "The yogi is superior to the ascetics; he is even superior to those who possess knowledge;
and the yogi is superior to the performers of ritual action. Therefore, O Arjuna, become a yogi."
Even among all yogis, he who, endowed with faith, worships me with his inner self absorbed in me, is considered by me to be the most disciplined.
Now, regarding the limbs of yoga,

it is stated in the Mahābhārata: "Restraint (yama), observance (niyama), posture (āsana), breath control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna), and absorption (samādhi) are the eight limbs of yoga."
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"The Self must first be known by the self through yoga, for that is difficult to conquer.
One should exert effort toward its conquest; hear from me the means for that."
One should burn away defects by means of breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and sin by means of concentrations (dhāraṇā);
one should abandon attachments through withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra) and ungodly qualities through meditation (dhyāna).

‘Defects’ (*doṣān*) refers to perspiration, trembling, and so forth; ‘associations’ (*saṃsargān*) refers to connections with sense objects; ‘non-sovereign’ (*anīśvarān*) means ordinary or natural. Devala states:

“Passions” (*kaṣāyāḥ*) are said to be attachment, aversion, and delusion. Their removal is achieved through austerity characterized by restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*), as well as through fivefold knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). This is the “ripening of passions” (*kaṣāyapācana*).

In the Viṣṇupurāṇa: "The yogi, free from desire and maintaining a serene mind, should practice celibacy, non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, and non-possessiveness, while bringing about his own fitness."
One who possesses self-mastery should constantly perform study, purity, contentment, and austerity,
and likewise direct the mind toward the supreme Brahman.
These five Yamas and five Niyamas have been proclaimed;
when performed with desire, they bestow distinguished fruits, but for those free from desire, they grant liberation.

Having established himself there upon one of the seats and so forth, the self-controlled ascetic should further apply himself to the qualities known as the restraints (yamas) and the observances (niyamas).

In the *Vāyupurāṇa*: "Having assumed the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), or the upright posture (*ūrdhvāsana*), or likewise the auspicious cross-legged posture (*svastikāsana*), the yogi should practice yoga, having made his mind intent upon that."
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: "The restraint of the prāṇa and apāna breaths is declared to be prāṇāyāma. In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
Indeed, that which brings the vital air called *prāṇa* under control through practice is to be known as *prāṇāyāma*; it is both with seed (*sabīja*) and without seed (*abīja*).
‘With seed’ (*sabīja*) means having the mantra and so forth as its object of focus.
Bṛhaspati says:
“Having assumed the posture, having restrained the vital breaths, and likewise having recollected the *ṛṣi* and the other [constituent parts of the mantra]...”
With eyes closed and observing silence, one should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma).
One should recite the Gāyatrī together with the Vyāhṛtis, the Praṇava, and the Śiras three times while restraining the breath; that is called prāṇāyāma.
One should practice the three [breaths] of inhalation, retention, and exhalation of the vital air;
meditating upon Brahmā, Keśava, and Śambhu, one shall be liberated from bondage.
One should meditate on the Grandfather (Brahmā) as red, Viṣṇu as having the luster of a blue lotus,
and Hara (Śiva) as white and three-eyed, the one who enables crossing over the ocean of saṃsāra.
He perceives past and future objects, those that are distant or concealed,
as well as the positions of the moon, sun, stars, and planets— this is the perfection of his knowledge.
But when the yogin attains consciousness equal in power [to that of the object],
then that state of breath control (prāṇāyāma) is known as "consciousness" (saṃvit).
That by which his mind and the five elements attain clarity—
namely, the sense faculties and the objects of the senses— is known as *prasāda*.
"The five elements" refers to the five gross elements, beginning with earth. Likewise:
"Ten and two breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) are declared to be one concentration (dhāraṇā)."
Two types of concentration (dhāraṇā) are known as yoga by the yogis who perceive reality.
In the same way, for the yogi who is thus engaged in yoga and whose self is disciplined,
all defects perish and he becomes established in his own true nature.
He beholds the supreme Brahman as distinct from the material qualities (guṇas),
as well as space and the other elements down to the atom, and likewise the stainless Self.
In this manner, the yogi, restrained in diet and devoted to breath control,
having mastered his posture, should ascend to the stage that has been conquered, as if ascending to his own home.
The unconquered earth, being assailed by faults, delusion, and likewise disease, causes [the practitioner] to increase them; therefore, one should not ascend to an unconstructed stage.
And here, the means has been taught by the yogis and supreme sages,
by which defects such as disease do not arise for the yogi.
Just as those seeking water might slowly sip it through lotus stalks and the like,
so should the yogi, having conquered fatigue, drink the vital air.
[173] First, on the navel and the abdomen; then the third above that;
on the throat, the mouth, the tip of the nose, the eyes, the middle of the eyebrows, and the crown of the head.
When [the mind] is somewhat [stabilized] upon another [object], concentration (dhāraṇā) is considered supreme.
Having attained these ten concentrations, one attains equality with the Imperishable (akṣara).
Prāṇāyāma is declared to be the complete restraint of the vital breaths;
it is to be known as dhāraṇā (concentration), by which the mind is held steady.
When the senses, which do not turn away from sounds and other objects,
are withdrawn by means of yoga through self-restraint, that is therefore known as pratyāhāra (withdrawal).

"Unrestrained" means attached to their own objects. "By yoga" means by the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind, according to the definition in the *Pātañjala* [Yogasūtra]: "Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind. Devala states:
Pratyāhāra (withdrawal) is the re-applying of the mind—which has fallen away from yoga due to its subtlety, fickleness, lightness, or strength—back to its [proper] object.
In this context, "object" (artha) refers to the self (ātman).
As stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"The knower of yoga should restrain the senses that are attached to sound and the other objects."
Devoted to withdrawal (pratyāhāra), one should perform actions that conform to the mind.
Nor does one become a yogi who accomplishes yoga by means of those senses which are not brought under control, even while perceiving that supreme self through them.
Devala says:
Dhāraṇā is so called because it sustains (dharaṇāt) the body, the senses, the mind, the intellect, and the self. Hārīta says:

The fixing of the mind within the body—in the heart, the forehead, the supreme light of the Self that is Brahman, the sun, the earth, the sky, or in water—is called *dhāraṇā* because the mind is held there in a single stream, like a vessel filled with water.

“Internal body” (*antardeha*) refers to the heart and so forth; or externally, it refers to the Supreme Brahman and other such objects characterized by qualities such as being free from evil (*apahatapāpman*). The fixing of the mind upon these is *dhāraṇā*. Regarding the phrase “like water in a vessel”: just as water contained within a vessel remains only in that vessel, so too, when these [objects] are present, the movement of the mind—its stability in one particular location—is born from *dhāraṇā*. And thus, it is not like the common [notion] of the mind [merely following its object]. Accordingly, the *Pātañjala-sūtra* states: “*Dhāraṇā* is the fixing of the mind in a place, as with a vessel. — Śaṅkha.
The restraint of the mind is called *dhāraṇā* by those who know it; as stated in the *Viṣṇu Purāṇa*:
"By means of breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) one [subdues] the vital airs, and by means of withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), the sense organs."
Then, one should bring the mind under control and establish it upon a virtuous object of focus.
In the Mahābhārata:
"O high-minded one, it is easy to stand upon the sharpened edges of razors,
but it is difficult for those of unrefined self to remain steady in the concentrations of perfect yoga."
[175] Since a failed concentration does not lead to a fortunate rebirth,
it is like a man devoid of sight among men, O King.
But he who, O son of Kuntī, abides in the concentrations according to the rule,
completely abandons death, the suffering of birth, and even pleasure.
Among the practices of yoga, meditation alone is the supreme strength for practitioners;
nevertheless, those who know the Vedas say that meditation is of two kinds.
The one-pointedness of the mind, as well as breath control (prāṇāyāma),
and a continuous flow of cognition in that form alone, free from longing for anything else.
O King, that meditative absorption (dhyāna) is accomplished by means of the first six factors;
for it is indeed the grasping of the very nature of that [object] as free from conceptual construction.
The meditative absorption (samādhi) belonging to one who is devoted to meditation with the mind is thus described.
Now, regarding the regulation of food and other matters, it is stated in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
Alms, rice-gruel, buttermilk, milk, or barley-meal;
or fruit, roots, cooked grains, husks, oil-cake, and flour.
Thus, these indeed are the auspicious foods that bring about the success of yogins.
In the Mahābhārata:
"One is disciplined in the eating of grain-particles and in the eating of oil-cake."
A yogi who is intent on avoiding unctuous substances shall attain strength.
O subduer of enemies, by consuming barley as food for a long period of time,
that yogi of purified soul will at some point attain strength.
Having remained for fortnights, months, and seasons, and likewise moving through the planets,
the yogi, having drunk water mixed with milk, shall attain power.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa: "The Cāndrāyaṇa is remembered as the most excellent of all observances for yogis;
one should perform it once, twice, thrice, or four times, according to one's capacity."

In the Mahābhārata, within the Mokṣadharma section: "One who is self-restrained, moderate in food, and has conquered the senses attains the station of Brahman, which is supreme and eternal beyond primordial nature."
Likewise:
"The holy life is difficult to practice; hear from me the means for that.
A superior twice-born man should restrain [the senses] when they are set in motion and aroused."
One should not listen to talk about women, nor should they be looked upon when naked;
for from seeing them even by chance, passion may enter those who are weak.
If passion arises, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance; three times during the day one should enter the water.
And having submerged oneself, even in a dream, one should mentally recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times.
In this way, one burns away the evil consisting of internal passion three times.
"The weak" refers to those who have not conquered their senses. "And in sleep" means when the arising of passion for women occurs; thus is the meaning in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*.
In empty spaces, in dwellings, and in caves, the yogi,
ever-disciplined, should always properly undertake meditation.
In a place noisy with sounds, near fire or water, in a dilapidated cow-pen,
at a crossroads, on a heap of dry leaves, by a river, in a cremation ground, or where reptiles dwell.
A knower of reality should avoid practicing yoga in these places: in a dangerous location, on the bank of a well, at a shrine, on an anthill, or in a heap of refuse.
In the Mahābhārata: "Freed from all attachments, moderate in diet, and having conquered the senses,
one should fix the mind upon the Self during the first and last parts of the night."
O lord of men, one should not apply oneself to yoga during the voiding of urine, the voiding of feces, or while eating;
at all other times, one should apply oneself to it with devotion.

In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: "O King of kings, a yogi intent on attaining perfection should practice yoga neither when bloated with food, nor when hungry, nor when exhausted, nor when his mind is distracted."
One intent on meditation should not practice yoga during times that are too cold, nor too hot, nor in a forest environment characterized by wind.

And since the existence of a sentient being is impossible when both place and time are excluded, there can be no perception of a non-existent thing in yoga; therefore, one should avoid that [non-existence].
Listen to me as I describe those defects that arise as obstacles for one who, out of folly, applies himself while disregarding these faults.
Deafness, dullness, loss of memory, muteness, blindness, and fever arise instantly; likewise do they arise for one who is joined with ignorance.
178] Now follows the treatment of defects; regarding this, it is stated in the Vāyu Purāṇa:
I shall describe the treatment for those [disturbances] and for the humors (doṣas) in their proper order,
so that those humors arising from breath control (prāṇāyāma) may be pacified.
Having eaten a smooth gruel that is very hot, one should maintain [the heat] therein;
by this sequential application, the vāta-gulma is destroyed.
Then, for one who has begun to tremble in all limbs, this medical treatment should be performed as a remedy for that whirlpool.
One should perform this treatment so that well-being is attained;
having mentally paralyzed the mountain within the body, one should hold it there.
One should apply it to the chest, the seat of the vital essence (rasa), and the region of the throat;
likewise for obstruction of speech, in the organ of speech, and similarly for deafness in the two ears.
‘Of one who has begun’ means of one who has set out. ‘Having made it firm, he should hold’ means he should hold the mountain.
In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*: “If a non-human being should enter within the yogin...”
By means of the concentration on wind and fire, one should utterly consume this [impurity] residing within the body.
"Non-human being" refers to a *rakṣasa*, *piśāca*, or similar entity. In the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"In the event of affliction by a black snake, one should wear [the mantra] on the heart and the belly."
Having placed the Great People, austerity, and truth within his heart, he should indeed maintain them.
[179] Having drunk a *pala* of poison, one should then hold the *viśalyā* [mantra];
having visualized the entire earth together with its mountains, one should hold it in the mind.
Having placed within his heart the oceans as well as all the deities,
the knower of yoga, equipped with a thousand jars, should perform the ritual bath.
When the water reaches the neck, one should maintain concentration on the crown of the head;
seated against the current, one should hold the entire body [in concentration].
One should drink anthill earth using cups made from withered arka leaves;
for this is the prescribed method of treatment, beneficial for yogins in its gradual stages.
But it has been explained in brief according to the reasons seen in Yoga;
now follows the procedure of Yoga therein, in the Mahābhārata.
The yogi, dwelling in solitude, alone, with mind and self controlled, free from expectations and possessions, should constantly discipline himself.
Having established a firm seat for oneself in a clean place—
neither too high nor too low, covered with cloth, a deerskin, and kusha grass, one over the other.
Having made the mind one-pointed there, with the activities of the mind and senses restrained,
let him sit upon his seat and practice yoga for the purification of the self.
Holding the body, head, and neck erect and motionless, remaining steady,
gazing at the tip of his own nose, and not looking around at the directions.
With a tranquil self, free from fear, and established in the vow of celibacy,
one should sit disciplined, with the mind restrained, the heart fixed on Me, and intent on Me as the supreme goal.
In the *Vāyupurāṇa*: Having first uttered the syllable *oṃ* and having paid homage to the moon and the sun,
one should assume the *svastika*, the *padma*, or likewise the *ardhāsana* posture.
With both knees together, or with one knee raised, or even with the feet crossed in the *svastika* posture, having assumed a balanced and firm seat, he should draw both feet together.
Having covered the testicles with his two heels, and likewise the generative organ,
he then [withdrew] the senses from their objects, the mind, and the five vital airs.
Having restrained [the senses] through their collective withdrawal, one should undertake the practice of pratyāhāra;
for he who withdraws desires from every side, just as a tortoise draws in its limbs.
Thus, delighting in the Self and established in solitude, one pure in both external and internal aspects, having filled the breath, beholds the Self by means of the self.

One should begin the practice of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) by applying [the gaze] from the navel up to the throat. Yājñavalkya says: With the feet placed flat upon the thighs, one should rest the right hand upon the left.
Lifting the face slightly upward and bracing it with the chest.
With eyes closed, established in *sattva*, one should not let the teeth touch the teeth;
with the tongue fixed motionless against the palate, the mouth should be closed and the body perfectly still.
With the collection of his senses fully restrained, sitting on a seat that is neither too low nor too high,
he should undertake breath control (prāṇāyāma) twice or even thrice.
‘Established in sattva’ means free from desire, anger, and so forth.
— Devala.

In a temple, an empty house, a mountain cave, a riverbank, a cavern, or a forest—whichever among these is pure, free from affliction, and secluded—one should prepare a comfortable seat for the mind. Therein, having taken light food, being free from disease, and being pure, one should keep the head, neck, hands, and feet steady; holding the body straight, without pressing upon the penis and testicles, and occupying either the *svastika*, *bhadraka*, or *maṇḍala* posture, facing north or east, not touching the teeth with the teeth, and with the eyes neither fully opened nor closed, the gaze fixed steadily and slightly lowered between the nose and the mouth, having withdrawn all the senses and directed the vital breaths upward, the contemplation of that [Reality] with the mind is *dhyāna*.
In the Mahābhārata: "Yoga is not for one who eats too much, nor for one who does not eat at all;
nor for one whose habit is excessive sleep, nor for one who is ever awake, O Arjuna."
For one who is moderate in diet and recreation, disciplined in actions,
and regulated in sleep and wakefulness, yoga becomes the destroyer of suffering.
And likewise, that which is the Self of one who is tranquil, self-controlled, devoted to solitude, delighting in the Self, and mature—that is indeed the Divine; of this there is no doubt.
Dakṣa says:
The activities of the mind—such as bitterness, delusion, distraction, shame, and fear—are fully described; one should bring [the mind] under control when it is free from them.
The village where that Great-Souled One dwells, along with its five families,
cannot be conquered by gods, asuras, or humans.
One who seizes the kingdoms of others by force is not called a hero;
he who has conquered the collection of his senses by means of his mastery over the senses is called a hero by the wise.
In the Mahābhārata, the Blessed Lord said:
"Having abandoned all desires born of volition without exception,"
Having restrained the entire collection of senses from all sides by the mind alone.
One should gradually come to rest through the intellect held with firmness;
having established the mind within the Self, one should not think of anything at all.
From whatever cause the restless and unsteady mind wanders away,
from that very cause one should restrain it and bring it under control within the Self alone.
Thus constantly disciplining the self, the yogi, freed from all taints,
easily attains the supreme bliss of union with Brahman.
One whose self is disciplined by yoga perceives the Self abiding in all beings and all beings in the Self; he sees the same everywhere.
He who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me—
for him I am not lost, and he is not lost to me.
The yogin who, established in unity, worships me as abiding in all beings—
though he exists in every manner— he dwells in me.
O Arjuna, he who, by comparison with himself, sees equality everywhere—
whether it be pleasure or pain— that yogi is considered supreme.
[183] Arjuna said:
O Madhusūdana, regarding this yoga of equanimity which has been taught by you,
I do not perceive its steady persistence because of the mind's restlessness.
For the mind, O Kṛṣṇa, is restless, turbulent, powerful, and obstinate;
I consider its restraint to be as difficult as that of the wind.
The Blessed Lord said:
Without doubt, O mighty-armed one, the mind is restless and difficult to restrain;
yet, O son of Kuntī, it is brought under control through practice and dispassion.
It is my conviction that yoga is difficult to attain for one whose self is uncontrolled;
however, it can be achieved through the proper means by one who strives with a self-subdued mind.

"I do not perish" means I do not become hidden. "Existing in every way," whether in me, or in the modification of the intellect, or in the phenomenal world (prapañca), by means of the cognition of Brahman—"existing with the mind"—the meaning is that he exists in me alone.
Likewise: "The sage, having withdrawn the collection of his senses and sitting like a log of wood..."
One should not perceive sound with the ear, nor should one experience touch.
One should not perceive form with the eye, nor likewise tastes with the tongue;
the knower of yoga should abandon even all things that are excellent through the practice of yoga.

The energetic man, discerning in regard to the group of five, should not desire these things that agitate the group of five; having joined the darkness within his mind, he should remain vigilant toward the group of five.
One should steady the wandering mind, which is agitated by the five objects of the senses—
mindless of saṃsāra, without support, and flickering at the five gates.
On the path of prior meditation, the steadfast one should always meditate on the inner mind;
for when he unifies both the senses and the mind, [he attains concentration].
[184] Thus the path of meditation has been fully described by me;
therein, that mind which was previously obstructed, along with the self as the sixth, is contained within.
It will flash across to the ends of the ocean like lightning from a cloud;
it is as unstable in every way as a drop of water resting upon a leaf in the world.
In this very way, his mind becomes concentrated on the path of meditation;
for a brief moment, it remains poised upon the path of stability.
Furthermore, the mind becomes like the wind, wandering through the paths of the wind;
it is free from despondency, devoid of afflictions, free from lethargy, and without envy.
Furthermore, one who knows the yoga of meditation should steady the mind through meditative absorption;
then investigation, analysis, and discernment arise.
While the sage was striving for the first meditation within himself,
his mind became afflicted despite his desire for composure.
A sage should not fall into despondency; he should indeed act for his own welfare.
O Bhārata, he should himself alone control both his mind and his five senses.
Having first attained the path of meditation, one attains peace through constant practice;
that is achieved neither by human effort nor by any destiny whatsoever.
He who has thus restrained his self will attain that very happiness;
endowed with that happiness, he will be established in the practice of meditation.
‘Having condensed,’ meaning having withdrawn [the senses]. ‘The skillful’: those by whom the world has been brought under control and by whom the self has also been brought under control.
Since they [arise] from the sense organs and their objects, I shall explain their conjunction in its entirety.
Yoga does not arise from dwelling in the forest, nor from reflecting on many scriptures;
yoga will not belong to anyone through vows, sacrifices, or austerities.
[185] Indeed, yoga does not arise from the lotus posture, nor from gazing at the tip of the nose;
nor indeed does it ever come about through a purity that exceeds the requirements of the scriptures.
For one who is occupied with the affairs of the world, there can be no yoga through various deceptive practices such as silence, mantras, or numerous crooked arts.
Through application, as well as through practice, by means of certainty regarding that very [object],
and by not becoming weary again and again— yoga is accomplished, and not otherwise.
Through the diversion of contemplating the self, through the play of purification, and through equanimity toward all sentient beings, yoga is accomplished; not otherwise.
But he who is always paired with the Self, likewise sporting with the Self,
constantly blissful in the Self, and ever absorbed in the Self alone;
Contented with the Self alone, his mind fixed on nothing else;
for one who is satisfied with the Self alone, yoga is perfected, and not otherwise.
One who is thus engaged even in dreams, and especially while awake—
one whose conduct is such as this is considered the best and most excellent among the exponents of Brahman.
Yājñavalkya says: Having made the mind, intellect, memory, and senses focused on no other object,
one should meditate upon that Lord who dwells within the heart like a lamp.
By reciting the imperishable Sāma-Gāyatrī according to the prescribed rule,
one who is attentive attains the Supreme Self through such practice.
The Aparāntaka, the Ullopya, the Madraka,
the Prakarī, as well as the Āvaiṇaka, the Sarobindu, and the Uttara are the song-forms (gītakas).
The *ṛggāthā*, the *pāṇikā*, those composed by Dakṣa, and the *brahmagītikā*—this is the *geya*; because it causes practice toward that [truth], it is designated as "liberation."
One who knows the true principles of playing the lute, is proficient in the musical scales and modes,
and understands the rhythmic cycles, attains the path of liberation without effort.
If one who knows song does not attain the supreme state through singing,
he becomes an attendant of Rudra and rejoices together with him.

‘Aparāntaka-ullopya’: therein are the *prakarya*, the *reṇakas*, that which is accompanied by *svarabindu*, and the *uttara*. These seven songs known as *prakaraṇas*, along with the four *gītikās* beginning with the *ṛggāthā*, constitute this collection of songs such as the *parāntaka* and others. It should be understood that this is designated as "liberation" (*mokṣa*) because it is contemplated as the Supreme Self and serves as a means to liberation; for through the cultivation of that [contemplation], one attains eagerness by means of establishing one-pointedness. Regarding the phrase ‘it is heard’ (*śrūyate*): the *śruti* is of twenty-two kinds, and these reside within the notes (*svaras*). To explain: *ṣaḍja*, *madhyama*, and *pañcama* each have four *śrutis*; *ṛṣabha* and *dhaivata* each have three *śrutis*; and *gāndhāra* and *niṣāda* each have two *śrutis*. As for the *jātis*, there are six pure *jātis* and eleven born of mixture (*saṅkara*), thus making eighteen types in total. Regarding the phrase ‘if he is a knower of song’ (*gītajña*): the meaning is that if a knower of song, being established in yoga, is somehow liberated from obstacles, he then attains the status of an attendant of Rudra.
[187] 18. The definition of what is appropriate is found therein in the Mahābhārata.
But one should observe the characteristics of one who is disciplined, O Great King:
like a lamp filled with oil that burns in a windless place.
Likewise, the wise say that one who is joined [in yoga] has an immovable, upward-pointing crest;
he is like a stone struck by drops arising from a cloud.
One who is thus disciplined cannot be shaken; such is the characteristic of one so joined, even by the sounds of conchs and drums, or by various songs and instrumental music.
That one who is disciplined does not tremble while performing [these acts]—this is the illustration:
like one holding a vessel filled with oil beneath [him] with both hands.
Terrified and threatened by those with swords in their hands, he should ascend the steps with self-restraint;
out of fear of them, he should not let even a drop fall from the bowl.
Likewise, for one who is crossing over with a one-pointed mind,
and likewise because of the stability of the sense faculties and their state of immobility.
One should observe the characteristics of a sage who is thus disciplined;
being disciplined, he perceives Brahman, which is supreme and imperishable.
Situated in the midst of great darkness, resembling a blazing fire—
by means of this alone one departs, having abandoned the body which is without a witness.
After a long time, O King, this eternal Śruti was thus established:
"Having steadied the collection of senses with the mind, O Lord of Mithilā."
Having made the mind steady by means of the intellect, one should remain as motionless as a stone.
One should be as unshakable as a pillar and as motionless as a mountain;
those who know the application of the rules declare that one is then "yoked" through such discernment.
He does not hear, nor does he smell; he does not take delight, nor does he see;
he does not perceive touch, nor does his mind form conceptual constructions.
He does not conceive anything nor does he perceive anything, like a piece of wood;
then, having returned to his primordial nature, the wise call him "yoked."
Likewise:
"When the disciplined mind abides in the Self alone,
free from longing for all desires, then one is said to be 'yoked'."
As a lamp standing in a windless place does not flicker— this is the simile taught for the yogi of restrained mind who practices yoga of the self.
Where the mind, restrained through the practice of yoga, comes to rest;
and where, beholding the Self within the self, one finds contentment.
That absolute bliss which is perceivable by the intellect and beyond the senses—
he who knows it, remaining established therein, does not deviate from reality.
Having obtained which, one considers no other gain to be superior to it;
established in which, one is not shaken even by heavy suffering.
One should know that the separation from the union with suffering is designated as yoga;
that yoga must be practiced with determination by one whose mind is free from obstacles.
Likewise:
"The yogi whose self is satisfied with knowledge and realization, who is steadfast and has conquered the senses,
for whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are the same— he is said to be disciplined."
‘Kūṭastha’ means unchanging.
Now, the nature of the object of meditation.
Viṣṇu.

With his feet placed upward on his thighs, having laid his left hand upon his right, with his tongue pressed against the palate and his gaze fixed on the tip of his nose, not looking toward the quarters, free from fear and with a tranquil mind, he should contemplate that which transcends the twenty-four principles (tattvas). (1) He is eternal, beyond the senses, and devoid of qualities; transcending sound, touch, form, taste, and smell; present everywhere, yet exceedingly vast. (2) He is all-pervading, yet exceedingly subtle. (3) He has hands and feet everywhere; eyes, heads, and mouths everywhere; and the power of all the senses everywhere. (4) Meditating thus, (5) for one devoted to meditation, the manifestation of Yoga occurs within a year. (6) Now, if one is unable to fix the mind upon the formless, then, having meditated first on each preceding element among earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intellect, self, the unmanifest, and the Puruṣa, and having gained a firm focus there, one should abandon each in turn and meditate on the next. (7) In this manner, one should begin the meditation on the Puruṣa. (8) If one is incapable even of this, one should meditate on the Puruṣa like a lamp in the center of the downward-facing lotus of the heart. (9) If one is incapable even of that, one should meditate on You, Vāsudeva—wearing a crown, earrings, and a mace; marked with the Śrīvatsa; Your chest adorned with a forest garland; of gentle form, four-armed, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus. (10) Whatever one meditates upon, that one attains; such is the secret of meditation. (11) Therefore, having abandoned everything perishable, one should meditate only upon the Imperishable.
And there is not even a single syllable that exists apart from the Puruṣa. Having attained Him, one becomes liberated.
Because the Great Lord, having pervaded the entire city, lies within it, he is therefore called "Puruṣa" by those who contemplate the principles of reality. || 15 ||
During the first and last watches of the night, the yogi, ever vigilant,
should meditate upon the Supreme Person Viṣṇu, who is beyond the material qualities and the twenty-fifth principle.
It is accessible through the self of all principles, yet devoid of all principles;
it manifests through the qualities of all the senses, yet is devoid of all the senses;
it is unattached and yet the sustainer of all, devoid of qualities and yet the experiencer of qualities.
It is outside and within all beings; it is both the unmoving and the moving.
Because of its subtlety, it is incomprehensible; it is far away, yet it is near.
It is undivided, yet it exists as if divided among all beings;
it is the form of the past, the future, and the present, both devouring and procreating.
That is said to be the light of even the lights, beyond darkness;
it is knowledge, the object of knowledge, and that which is attainable through knowledge, seated in the heart of all. 20.
Thus, the field, as well as knowledge and the object of knowledge, have been described in brief.
My devotee, having realized this, attains to my own state of being. (21)
[191] In the Narasiṃha Purāṇa, Maheśvara said:
"O best of sages, the supreme nectar has been known; it is a profound secret, a mystery."
I shall speak that which destroys suffering in the heart and removes the fear of all bonds.
The fourfold collection of beings, from blades of grass up to the four-faced Brahmā—
the entire world of moving and non-moving things— is rendered as if in deep sleep by his māyā.
If anyone awakens through the grace of that Viṣṇu,
he crosses over saṃsāra, which is difficult even for the gods to cross.
Intoxicated by the pride of wealth and power, and turned away from the knowledge of reality,
one sinks into the great mire of worldly existence like an aged cow.
But for one who binds himself with actions like a silkworm,
I do not see his liberation even in hundreds of millions of births.
Therefore, O Nārada, one should always properly worship Viṣṇu, the imperishable God of all gods, while meditating with a concentrated mind.
He who always meditates upon that Viṣṇu— who is all-encompassing, without beginning or end, unborn, established within his own self, omniscient, and immovable— is liberated.
By constantly meditating upon Viṣṇu— who is self-grasped, imperishable, eternal, devoid of qualities, beyond darkness, all-seeing, and everlasting— one is liberated.
Constantly meditating upon Viṣṇu as Vāsudeva— who is free from conceptual construction, free from appearance, free from proliferation, and free from affliction— one is liberated.
By constantly meditating upon Viṣṇu— the stainless, supreme, peaceful, infallible creator of beings, the womb of the Vedas, and the all-pervading lord— one is liberated.
One who always meditates upon Viṣṇu— nirvāṇa, which is free from all existence, immeasurable, signless, and faultless— is liberated.
The immortal, supreme bliss, free from all evil—Brahman, who is to be known as Śiva and Viṣṇu; by constantly meditating upon him, one is liberated.
By constantly meditating upon Viṣṇu— the Lord of Yoga, known as the Ancient One, dwelling within the cave of one's own body, immeasurable, and immutable— one is liberated.
By constantly meditating upon that Lord Viṣṇu— who is free from the auspicious and the inauspicious, who transcends the six waves, and who is the stainless object of knowledge— one is liberated.
By constantly meditating upon Viṣṇu— who is forever free from all dualities, devoid of all suffering, and beyond the reach of discursive thought— one is liberated.
Nameless, without lineage, non-dual, the fourth, the supreme state—
by constantly meditating upon that Viṣṇu who dwells in the hearts of all, one is liberated.
One who constantly meditates with one-pointed mind upon Viṣṇu— who is formless, whose resolve is truth, who is pure like space, and supreme— is liberated.
By constantly meditating upon Viṣṇu— who is the soul of all, established in his own nature, whose form is self-consciousness, pure, and the single syllable— one is liberated.
By constantly meditating upon Viṣṇu— who transcends time, who knows the three periods of time, who is the Lord of the universe, the witness of the world, and superior to all— one is liberated.
The universe is established in Viṣṇu, and Viṣṇu is established in the universe;
by constantly meditating upon Viṣṇu, the unborn Lord of the universe, one is liberated.
Likewise:
Nārāyaṇa, seated upon a lotus-throne, dwelling in the center of the orb of the sun, should always be meditated upon.
Wearing armlets, crocodile-shaped earrings, and a crown, adorned with necklaces, possessing a golden body, and bearing the conch and discus.
[193] Śaṅkha said:
"The vision of the God of gods, who resides within the heart, occurs through the yoga of meditation (dhyāna).
Meditation has been described; therefore, I shall now proclaim the auspicious yoga of meditation."
All deities reside in the heart; the vital breath is established in the heart;
the luminaries and the sun are in the heart; everything is established in the heart.
Making one's own body the lower fire-drill and the *praṇava* the upper fire-drill,
through the practice of the friction of meditation, one shall behold Viṣṇu abiding in the heart.
The Moon is situated in the midst of the Sun; Fire is situated in the midst of the Moon;
Being (sattva) is situated in the midst of Radiance; and the Imperishable (Acyuta) is situated in the midst of Being.
Smaller than the smallest, greater than the greatest, the Self is hidden in the cave of this living being;
he who is free from sorrow beholds it as consisting of light.
The greatness of the Lord through the grace of the Sustainer.
This divine [Self], however, is made manifest to mortals as if by means of veils;
for those enveloped by the veil of ignorance, the sacred revelation is perceived through the senses and their objects.
This indeed is the Puruṣa Viṣṇu, eternal, both manifest and unmanifest;
he is the Ordainer and the Disposer, the Pradhāna, the partless Śiva.
I know this great Puruṣa, resplendent as the sun, beyond darkness;
having known him, one indeed does not fear death.
There is no other path for going there.
In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*: "Because words turn back without reaching it, along with the mind— that which is unmanifest, due to its being beyond perception, profound, and difficult to attain."
The knot of the heart is broken, all doubts are cut asunder,
and his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen.
Yājñavalkya says: Then the wise man, practicing concentration (dhāraṇā), should fix his mind upon that Lord who resides in the heart like a lamp, and there he should hold the self.
Likewise:
seventy-two thousand channels named Hitā and Ahitā have issued forth from the heart; in their midst is that which has the luster of the moon.
The mandala of that center is the self, immovable like a lamp;
that is to be known, and having known it here, one is not born again.
In the Narasiṃha Purāṇa:
"In this world, the sins of one devoted to the practice of yoga are destroyed;
therefore, becoming intent on yoga, one should meditate during the intervals between daily rites."
Having first brought under control the breath through *prāṇāyāma*, the senses through *pratyāhāra*,
and the mind— which is otherwise difficult to subdue— through *dhāraṇās*.
One should meditate upon the single cause, blissful, of the nature of consciousness, free from ailment, subtler than the subtle, the support of the universe, and imperishable.
Seated alone in a secluded place, one should meditate with delight upon the subtle Self, which resides within a lotus and possesses the luster of molten gold.
One should contemplate: "I am he who knows the minds of all living beings, who dwells in the hearts of all, and who is the knower of all that is to be known."
Meditation is said to last as long as there is the happiness of attaining the Self;
beyond that, one should perform the actions prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti.
Just as a chariot is useless without horses, and a horse is useless without a chariot,
so too is austerity for one who lacks knowledge, and knowledge for one who lacks austerity.
Just as food combined with honey, or honey combined with food,
so too are austerity and knowledge, when united, a great medicine.
Just as the movement of birds flying in the sky depends upon both wings,
even so is the eternal Brahman attained through both knowledge and action.
A Brahmin endowed with knowledge and austerity, who is devoted to yoga,
quickly abandons the two bodies and becomes liberated from bondage.
As long as the supreme state has not been attained by way of the path of the gods,
the destruction of the subtle body (liṅgadeha) does not occur anywhere.

"In the interval between obligatory rites" means during the intervals between obligatory actions; the sense is that it occurs precisely at the time for obligatory duties. "By the Āraṇas" means by the Upaniṣads.
Likewise, by the power of the dispassion that has arisen, the yogin—
Constantly meditating on the Supreme Brahman while engaged in ritual action,
he abandons the body— which is essentially truth and consists of the nature of consciousness and bliss— and attains the station of Viṣṇu.
Yogiyājñavalkya says:
"The designation of Brahman is traditionally held to be threefold: *Oṃ*, *Tat*, and *Sat*.
By means of these, the Brāhmaṇas, the Vedas, and the sacrifices were ordained in ancient times."
Therefore, having uttered "Om," the acts of sacrifice, gift-giving, and austerity,
as prescribed by the ordinances, proceed constantly among those who discourse on Brahman.
And its measures are three: the manifest, the unmanifest, and likewise the other, the subtle.
One should know it as the internal, the elemental, and the divine.
It is the syllable Om, the Praṇava, the Savior, the Imperishable, the Supreme Praṇava.
The Udgītha, as well as Āditya, Haṃsa, and the all-pervading Nārāyaṇa,
are understood from the scriptures through these and other synonymous terms.
It is designated as Oṃkāra; it is threefold, consisting of three syllables, and having three deities.
It is the triple Brahman, existing in three states, pertaining to the three times, and established in three ways.
Truth (satya), passion (rajas), and darkness (tamas) are the qualities; by these they are known as the "three qualities" (triguṇa).
Furthermore, the letter 'A', the letter 'U', and the letter 'M' constitute the triad of syllables (akṣara-traya).
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are declared to be the three deities;
and from fire, wind, and the sun, it is designated as the three measures (trimātra).
The Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman are thus proclaimed as the triple Brahman;
likewise, Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svar are situated in the heart, the throat, and the palate.
Established in the fourth vital breath, as well as in the sun and in the three [worlds],
it is called the "three times" because it encompasses the past, the present, and the future.
He is described as one whose consciousness is internal, one whose consciousness is external, and one whose consciousness is unified;
he is threefold in nature, consisting of the Gārhapatya, Dakṣiṇāgni, and Āhavanīya fires.
It is traditionally taught that it exists in three states— quiescent, terrible, and deluded—
and it is traditionally taught that it possesses three genders— female, male, and neuter.
Having understood the syllable Oṃ in its threefold nature, the twice-born is liberated;
each of these measures (mātrā) therein is indeed further divided in many ways.
The entirety of speech is woven warp and woof within them;
its first form is Speech (vāk), its essence is Being (sattva), and it is Fire (hutāśana) on the earth (bhūḥ).
Viṣṇu: The gross state of waking is to be known by those who know the reality of yoga as Brahmā, the intermediate space, the mind, the Unborn, and that which is designated as Soma— the syllable *U*.
Mātrā, consisting of dream and conceptualization, is the creation; it is the second designation.
Raudrī, designated by the syllable *ma*, known as the vital breath (*prāṇa*), is the third, characterized by darkness (*tāmasī*).
That great sleep called deep slumber withdraws the entire world;
it is the primordial, supreme, and subtle state, the very essence of the unmanifest Lakṣmī.
The gentle one is known by the designation "ma"; what are its connections?
A, u, and ma are the three morae, and the letter *ma* consists of half a mora.
The three measures (mātrās) dissolve into the half-measure; of this there is no doubt.
The half-measure, however, dissolves into the measureless (amātra), which is free from affliction.
When the letter *a* is compressed, it becomes the letter *u*;
when the letter *u* is compressed, it becomes the letter *m*.
When the letter *ma* is pressed, there then arises the half-mora;
when the tongue is pressed, one then becomes free from support (*nirālamba*).
Whether it be of one measure, two measures, or three measures, or even the whole;
short, long, or protracted—the tranquil arises through the tranquil mind.
Having become one whose mind is concentrated and intent upon meditation on reality,
he who meditates upon the syllable Om is known as "one devoted to the inner self" (ādhyātmika).
Just as leaves are completely pierced through on all sides by a pin,
even so all words are indeed pierced through by the syllable *praṇava*.
The Śruti declares that the Puruṣa, indeed, is the Lord (Īśvara), untouched by afflictions, karma, its fruition, and likewise by latent impressions.
Its denoted object is said to be the Lord, and its designator is remembered as the *praṇava*.
When known through the designator, the denoted object itself becomes gracious.
For that purpose, the Praṇava should be constantly chanted and meditated upon by the wise;
when the Lord Puruṣa is worshipped through it, he becomes fully propitious.
For just as a cow, upon hearing the lowing of her calf, goes toward her calf with a lowing sound,
so too does Brahman proceed when offered the *praṇava*.
The speech quickly returns to the mouth of the speaker.
Two Brahmans are to be known: the Brahman of Sound and that which is the Supreme Brahman.
One who is proficient in the Brahman of Sound attains the Supreme Brahman.
That which originates within the body, is impelled by the *udāna* breath,
is to be articulated as speech, functions through the ear, and functions as sound— that is called the organ of hearing (*śrotra*).
The supreme Brahman is the Word-Brahman; when that has dissolved, there is the Imperishable. One who desires yoga within oneself should always meditate upon that Imperishable.
The letter *a*, the letter *u*, and the letter *m*— which is indeed Viṣṇu—
along with the conjunction of three and a half measures (*mātrās*), constitute the fivefold *praṇava*.
He who is the sound proclaimed at the beginning of the Vedas and established at the end of the Vedas— He who is beyond that which is dissolved into primordial nature (prakṛti), He is Maheśvara.
When one knows that bliss of Brahman from which words turn back, unable to reach it along with the mind, one fears nothing whatsoever.
The syllable Om is the bow, the self is the arrow, and Brahman is said to be its target.
One must pierce it with undistracted mind; like the arrow, one becomes absorbed in that.
Making one's own body the lower fire-drill and the vital breath itself the upper fire-drill,
one may behold the God hidden within, through the practice of churning with meditation.
Someone desiring to propitiate Viṣṇu indeed practices devotion;
for the sake of accomplishing that propitiation, they likewise employ an image as a manifesting medium.
Having fashioned an image out of elements such as wood or stone, one should install it with devotion, faith, and reverence; by this, Viṣṇu becomes pleased with that person.
When the Self is worshipped with the syllable Oṃ, it becomes perfectly serene;
this is the most excellent object of focus, this is the supreme object of focus.
Having understood this object of focus, one becomes fit for becoming Brahman.
The Lord has an unseen form; he is to be grasped through contemplation and consists of mind.
"Oṃ" is his supreme name; invoked by it, he becomes gracious.
Therefore, having first uttered "Oṃ," one who is intent upon that should apply himself;
for waking, dreaming, and deep sleep are its stages.
[200] Thus, he may possess external wisdom, internal wisdom, or dense wisdom—there are three kinds.
External wisdom is at the opening of Viṣṇu’s right eye; internal wisdom, however, is within the splendor of the mind.
The wise one is established in three ways within the body: in the ether, in the heart, and in the intellect; Vaiśvānara is always present in the gross body through the internal activities of light.
The Ānandabhuja and the Prājña—thus one who understands enjoyment knows it to be threefold:
the Viśva is gross in every respect, while the Taijasa is indeed differentiated.
And likewise, O wise one, understand Ānanda as the threefold satisfaction;
that which is proclaimed as the food to be enjoyed and the enjoyer within the three abodes.
But he who attains both, while enjoying, is not defiled;
that which consists of sound, the syllable Om, is merely the gross form to be uttered.
This supreme Oṃkāra is said to be uttered without measure (amātra);
it assumes three and a half measures in their proper sequence.
Those who contemplate Brahman declare that very Supreme Brahman to be one's own Self.
That which was previously indicated as being established in the letter *au* at the beginning,
is this supreme state that transcends both syllables and words.
Having reached that which they do not return from, those who have taken refuge in the Supreme Oṃkāra fix their minds there, while the body remains as a mere subtle vehicle (liṅga).
It consists of volition, determination, and that which is called egoism;
it is subtle, presided over by consciousness, and likewise accompanied by the subtle elements.
Having extracted the syllable Oṃ from the heart by means of the lotus-stalk,
one should join it to the supreme space called Ananta, which is devoid of all conceptual constructions.
In that state, one should understand both the mind and the syllable Oṃ;
this is declared to be the yoga practiced until one has attained that stainless state.
One should yoke the mind to the syllable *oṃ*, and likewise the syllable *oṃ* to the *praṇava*;
having established the *praṇava* in Brahman, one should not think of anything at all.
[201] Life-forceless, stainless, pure, soundless, it is designated as Brahman.
From that the life-force arises, and again it dissolves into that very same place.
"For one who is constantly disciplined in the *praṇava*, no fear exists anywhere. Manu says:
"Composed in meditation, one should perceive everything—both the existent and the non-existent—within the Self."
Seeing everything within oneself, one does not direct the mind toward unrighteousness.
The self alone is all the deities; everything is established within the self.
For the self indeed produces the connection with action for these embodied beings.
One should place space within the cavities, wind within movement and touch,
the supreme fire within the digestive heat and sight, and cohesion and form within the solid bodies.
One should worship the Moon in the mind, the Quarters in the ears, Viṣṇu in the feet,
Hara in strength, Agni in speech, Mitra in excretion, and Prajāpati in procreation.
One should know Him as the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), the ruler of these, subtler even than the subtle, radiant like gold, and attainable through the intellect in deep sleep.
Some call this Agni, some Prajāpati;
some Indra, others Prāṇa, and still others the eternal Brahman.
Pervading all beings with its five forms,
this [Self] perpetually causes them to revolve like a wheel through birth, growth, and decay.
Thus, he who perceives the Self within all beings by means of his own self,
having attained equanimity toward all, reaches the eternal Brahman.

It is appropriate that one should perceive the entire connection between action and its fruit within the Self. Regarding this, he states the specific method: “One should merge space into spaces. One should contemplate external space as being one with the space of the nine cavities within the body. Likewise, one should contemplate the oneness of external air with the bodily air which is the cause of movement and touch; the oneness of the supreme light known as the Sun with the digestive heat in the stomach and the ocular fire which causes the digestion of food and drink; the oneness of external waters with the bodily fluids; the oneness of the Moon with the mind; the oneness of the ten directions with the sense of hearing; and the oneness of Viṣṇu with the power of the feet. Having thus contemplated the oneness of the elemental (adhibhautika) and divine (adhidaivika) realms with the internal (ādhyātmika) earth and other elements, one should know the Supreme Self—the ruler of all beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, the ordainer of their respective orders—as described in the Brāhmaṇa passage beginning, “Under the command of that Imperishable, O Gārgī. This Supreme Self is subtler than even an atom because of its formlessness; it is pure in nature like gold; and its essential form is comparable to the consciousness of deep sleep because it is free from the six waves of mental fluctuation. Just as the nature of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) remains in deep sleep when all distinctions of pleasure and pain have subsided, such is the state of the Supreme Self at all times. Ritualists worship this Supreme Self as Fire.

Others, however, on account of the scriptural statement regarding his creatorship—“from him alone all selves emerge”—meditate upon him in the form of Prajāpati known as Manu. Still others, due to his possession of sovereign power, meditate upon him in the form of Indra. Yet others, based on the scripture, “One should meditate upon the *udgītha* as breath,” meditate upon him as the self of breath (*prāṇa*). Others, moreover, [meditate upon him] as the Supreme Self; the meaning is that “this Supreme Self, having encompassed all living beings with the five elements beginning with earth which constitute the body, repeatedly subjects them to birth, maintenance, and destruction according to the exhaustion and arising of their own acquired karma.”
In the Mahābhārata:
"O lord of men, having withdrawn the entire collection of the senses into the mind,
and likewise having pervaded the mind within the ego (ahaṃkāra)..."
[203] Having thus enumerated the ego-sense within the intellect, and the intellect within primordial nature (prakṛti), one should then meditate upon the Absolute alone.
Free from passion, stainless, eternal, infinite, pure, and without blemish;
that supreme reality which is stable, indivisible, undecaying, and immortal.
"Both eternal and immutable, that supreme Brahman is Īśāna.
[As stated] in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"Brahman is the substratum of the mind; and it is twofold by way of its essential nature."
O King, he is both embodied and formless, and both supreme and non-supreme.
O King, while all the specific cognitions and activities remain unexhausted,
this entire universe appears as something else, divided by distinctions, to the various perceptions.
That knowledge in which all distinctions have subsided, which is pure existence alone, beyond the reach of words, and to be realized by the self— that is equal to Brahman.
And that is the supreme form of Viṣṇu, the formless one— the primordial, imperishable,
