and defining characteristic of the Supreme Self, which is both the universal form and its opposite.
Since that [subtle form] cannot be contemplated by one engaged in yoga, O King,
one should therefore contemplate the gross form of Hari, which is the object of the universe.
The venerable Hiraṇyagarbha, Vāsava, and Prajāpati;
the Maruts, Vasus, Rudras, Bhāskaras, stars, and planets.
The Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Daityas, and all other divine species;
humans, animals, mountains, oceans, rivers, and trees.
[204] Furthermore, all the elements, including the earth, are the five causes of beings;
everything from Pradhāna down to the Viśeṣas consists of both the sentient and the insentient.
One-footed, two-footed, many-footed, and footless—
this embodied form, which consists of the threefold contemplation, is the very nature of Reality.
And all this entire universe, this world of moving and non-moving beings,
is endowed with the power of Viṣṇu, whose very nature is the Supreme Brahman.
O King, all these forms have been described in their entirety;
for they are joined with its power, just as they are with the sky.
O Great-minded One, the second form of Viṣṇu is that which is to be meditated upon by yogis;
it is the formless aspect of Brahman, which is called "Being" (sat) by the wise.
O King, that form in which all these objects are established is indeed considered the universal form (viśvarūpa) of Hari; it is a different form altogether.
O Lord of Men, He, whose form consists of all powers, by His own sport brings about among living beings the various activities of gods, animals, humans, and others.
For the benefit of the worlds, that activity of the Immeasurable One is not born of karma; it is all-pervading and characterized by an unimpeded nature.
O King, that form of the Universal Form (Viśvarūpa) should be meditated upon by one devoted to yoga for the sake of purifying the self and destroying all impurities.
Just as fire with its flames raised up burns dry wood when fanned by the wind,
so does Viṣṇu, abiding in the mind, burn away all the impurities of yogis.
Therefore, one should effect the stabilization of the mind upon the form of all the powers therein; that indeed should be known as pure *dhāraṇā*.

O King, for the sake of the liberation of yogins, there is the mind which is the auspicious substratum, all-pervading, and of such a nature; it transcends the cultivation of the three realms of existence.
But others, O tiger among men, those who are the supports of the mind,
such as the gods and the rest, are all impure and have their origin in karma.
When the mind is fixed upon the embodied form of the Blessed One, which is free from all dependence,
this indeed should be known as *dhāraṇā*, wherein the mind is held steady.
Having meditated upon that embodied form of Hari, O lord of men,
listen to how concentration (dhāraṇā) without a support is accomplished.
With a serene and beautiful face, eyes like lotus petals,
lovely cheeks, a broad forehead, and radiant as gold.
Adorned with beautiful earrings resting as far as his ears,
he had a neck like a conch shell, a broad chest marked with the Śrīvatsa sign.
With a belly marked by folds and a deeply sunken navel,
one should likewise visualize Viṣṇu with either eight long arms or four.
One should meditate upon Him, whose thighs and shanks are symmetrical, whose lotus-like feet and hands are perfectly steady, who is of the nature of Brahman, and who is clad in pure yellow garments.
Adorned with a crown, beautiful armlets, bracelets, and other ornaments,
he was equipped with the Śārṅga bow, conch, mace, discus, sword, and a rosary.
The yogi, having concentrated his own mind, should contemplate [the object] with total absorption until,
O King, the meditative retention (*dhāraṇā*) becomes firmly established right there.
Whether speaking, standing still, or performing other actions according to one's own will.
When she does not depart from the mind, then the wise one should consider her as perfected;
thereafter, he should visualize her as being devoid of the conch, mace, discus, Śārṅga bow, and other such emblems.
One should contemplate the form of the Blessed One, serene and holding a rosary;
when that concentration is thus established, it remains steady.
The wise one should then again meditate upon that deity as having only a single limb, devoid of ornaments such as the crown and armlets.
Having done that, one should then become intent upon the resolution regarding the whole.
Likewise,
Maitreya said:
"Just as this entire world exists in the form of ornaments and weapons,"
The Blessed Lord Viṣṇu sustains it; you ought to explain that to me.
Parāśara said: Having paid homage to the immeasurable Viṣṇu, the sovereign lord,
I shall relate to you that which was told to me by Vasiṣṭha.
The Blessed Lord Hari bears the self of this world, which is untainted, stainless, and devoid of qualities, in the form of the Kaustubha jewel.
Bearing the Śrīvatsa mark and resting upon Ananta,
Pradhāna and Buddhi also abide in Mādhava in the form of a mace.
The Lord sustains the twofold ego— the one consisting of the elements and the one consisting of the senses—
abiding in the form of a conch and in the form of a sword.
The mind, which is of the nature of Viṣṇu’s discus and whose speed completely surpasses the wind, remains situated in the hand of Viṣṇu.
O twice-born one, that Vaijayantī garland of the wielder of the mace, which consists of five forms, is indeed a collection of the causes of the elements, and it is truly the garland of the elements.
Janārdana indeed sustains all those numerous senses, consisting of both intellect and action, which are entirely of the nature of corpses.
And that which the Unmanifest bears is the supreme sword, exceedingly pure and consisting of knowledge;
yet that knowledge remains situated within the sheath of ignorance.
In this way, the person, primordial matter, intellect, ego,
the elements and so forth, the mind, and all the senses [are merged] in Hṛṣīkeśa.
O Maitreya, both knowledge and ignorance are entirely dependent upon this [Brahman],
which possesses the nature of weapons, ornaments, and forms, yet is devoid of material form.

Hari, assuming a form of illusion (māyārūpa), sustains for the welfare of living beings both the primary matter (pradhāna) along with its transformations, as well as the individual soul (puruṣa) and the entire universe.
The lotus-eyed Supreme Lord sustains all this:
whatever is knowledge and whatever is ignorance, as well as that which is real and that which is unreal and imperishable.
O Maitreya, Lord of all beings, all that was done by Madhusūdana; Dakṣa,
having indeed turned all the senses outward, made them inward-facing.
One should employ the collection of the senses by means of the mind alone, through one's own self.
One should place that which is born of the field (kṣetraja), liberated from all states of being, into Brahman;
this is both meditation (dhyāna) and yoga—everything else is merely an expansion of books.
That fruit which arises from the conjunction of four is impermanent;
but that which arises from the conjunction of two is eternal, stable, and immutable.
[208] That which does not exist for the whole world is contradicted by saying that it exists;
when so described, it does not remain in the heart of another.
For that Brahman is easily perceived, just as the face of a young maiden;
yet one who is not a yogi does not know it at all, just as one blind from birth does not perceive a jar.
For one whose nature is constant practice, that indeed becomes easily perceived;
yet, because of its subtlety, that supreme, eternal Brahman is indefinable.
‘Of four’ refers to the self, the mind, the objects, and the senses. ‘Of two’ refers to the self and the mind. As stated in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
“By means of the qualities (*guṇa*), the senses, and the body, as well as by the elements, the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), and the classes [of beings]...”
For I am indeed eternally untouched by pleasures and pains.
I am the nature of consciousness, stainless and all-pervading; I am the seer and the hearer in every respect, as well as the smeller, the toucher, the embodied one, and the taster.
I am eternally both the agent and the non-agent, the perceiver devoid of a body;
through the possession of sovereign power, though I am one, I abide as many.
All this space that exists, pervading the stationary and the moving—this entire world is indeed the Self; for, O ascetic, it is both partless and possessed of parts.
When the yogi becomes firmly established through such meditation,
then, liberated from the thicket of the body, he becomes the Supreme Lord.
When both the auspicious and the inauspicious have been exhausted and the individual soul has been burnt away through births,
it goes to the Supreme Self, that highest abode of Viṣṇu.
For liberation there would be no going anywhere else whatsoever,
nor any place or supreme abode where yogins go.
Ignorance is bondage, while liberation is the dissolution into Brahman;
having abandoned all conceptual constructions, the mind becomes motionless, established in the Self.
Having done this, the yogi becomes tranquil like a fire whose fuel has been consumed;
with unfathomable intellect, he may move about upon the earth as if in flight.
Having approached one's own self, which is devoid of destruction and origination,
at whatever time the yogi knows his own self as absolute;
From that time onward, he is designated as one liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
In the Mahābhārata: "Those who, fixing their minds on Me, worship Me with constant discipline,
endowed with supreme faith— they are considered by Me to be the most perfectly disciplined."
But those who worship the Imperishable, which is indefinable,
unmanifest, all-pervading, unthinkable, immovable, unchanging, and eternal—
Having fully restrained the collection of their senses and possessing equal intelligence toward all,
those who delight in the welfare of all beings attain Me alone.
The affliction of those whose minds are attached to the unmanifest is greater;
for the goal of the unmanifest is attained with difficulty by embodied beings.
But those who, having renounced all actions in Me, are intent on Me alone,
and worship Me while meditating with undivided yoga;
I am the deliverer from the ocean of death and worldly existence for those whose minds are absorbed in me; I become so, O Pārtha, before long.
Fix your mind on me alone; establish your intellect in me.
Thereafter you shall dwell in me alone; of this there is no doubt.
[210] Furthermore, O Dhanañjaya, if you are unable to fix the mind steadily upon Me,
then seek to reach Me through the yoga of practice.
If you are unable even to practice, become intent upon performing actions for Me;
by performing actions for My sake, you shall attain perfection.
But if you are unable even to do this, take refuge in my yoga and,
with self-control, renounce the fruits of all actions.
Knowledge is indeed better than practice; meditation is superior to knowledge;
the renunciation of the fruits of action is superior to meditation; and from renunciation follows peace without interruption.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: One should practice that essential knowledge which is the means for accomplishing action;
for this multiplicity of knowledges is indeed an obstacle to yoga.
He who wanders about thirsty, thinking "this is to be known,
this is to be known," will not attain what is to be known even in thousands of eons.
In the Mahābhārata: "O best of the Bharatas, in whatever subject a person reaches a firm conclusion, he recognizes only that [subject] and nothing else."
[211] 20— Now, regarding the signs of the engagement in yoga, they are found therein in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Freedom from greed, health, lack of harshness, a pleasant fragrance, scanty urine and feces,
radiance, clarity, and gentleness of voice.
For this is indeed the first sign of the commencement of yoga.
People feel affection when one's virtues are praised in their absence;
this does not pierce the hearts of beings—this is the supreme sign of success.
For one who experiences no affliction from the most intense extremes such as cold and heat,
and who feels no fear of others, accomplishment has arrived.
The manifestation [of powers] is described as a sign of the yogin’s amazement; through that, consciousness undergoes dissolution. Therefore, these manifestations must be concealed.
In the *Vāyupurāṇa*: "If one sees oneself and the earth as blazing, and if one enters into living beings, one should know that perfection has arrived."
— Now, regarding the obstacles to yoga (yogopasarga), Devala says:

The ten obstacles (*upasarga*) for yogis are: the defeat of one's purpose, the onset of terrifying sleep-deprivation, affliction of knowledge, excessive enjoyment, skill in anger, a particular form of sovereignty, greatness of merit, the fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*), and the radiance of fame.
"Affliction of knowledge" refers to the loss of memory and other such faculties.
[This is stated] in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*.
Even when the Self has been perceived, afflictions still arise for the yogin;
those which occur, I shall explain to you in brief—learn them from me.
Likewise, one desires desirable rites and human pleasures;
women, the fruit of giving, knowledge, magic arts, base metals, wealth, and the day.
Divinity, the status of a lord of the immortals, alchemical elixirs and the rejuvenation of youth,
leaping through the air like the wind, performing sacrifice, and likewise entering into water and fire.
The fruits of faith, non-violence, and generosity, as well as the observances,
penance, fasting, worship of the deities, and wealth.
Touched by those various karmas, he desires them;
thus does the mind proceed in such a way that the yogi must turn it back.
By making the mind attached to Brahman, one is liberated from the *upasargas*;
when these *upasargas* have been conquered, further *upasargas* do not arise thereafter.
Yogins proceed according to their qualities—sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa.
These are the intuitive (prātibha), the auditory (śrāvaṇa), the divine (daiva), as well as the two others: the delusive (bhrama) and the whirlpool-like (āvarta).
These five arise with bitter consequences as obstacles to the yoga of the practitioner:
the Vedānta scriptures, poetry, the science of the self, and various arts and crafts.
That which appears to one is "intuitive" (*prātibha*); it belongs to the yogin, for by means of it he knows all words and their meanings and indeed grasps the word itself.
It is said that he can hear from thousands of *yojanas* when divine beings are visible on all sides at a distance of eight [yojanas].
The wise declare that even this obstacle is a supreme form of destiny,
whereby the mind of the yogin, being without support, is made to wander by its own defect.
That is proclaimed as "confusion" (bhrama) because of the collapse of all supports;
it is like an eddy in water, when the whirlpool of knowledge becomes agitated.
The whirlpool that causes the destruction of the mind is called an obstacle;
by these, all the divine classes whose yoga has been destroyed are [afflicted].
Due to most terrible afflictions, they revolve again and again;
therefore, the yogi [should cultivate] that which consists of mind, which is pure and takes recourse in active engagement.
Having made his mind inclined toward it, the yogi— always engaged in yoga, moderate in diet, and having conquered his senses— should contemplate the Supreme Brahman.
The subtle concentrations are seven; beginning with "Bhūḥ," one should fix them upon the head.
While the yogi maintains the concentration on the Earth element, he attains a state of subtlety.
He considers himself the earth and abandons its odor;
likewise, he [abandons] the subtle taste in water, and similarly the form in fire.
Likewise, for one who maintains that same concentration upon the touch in the air,
he abandons sound there as it proceeds subtly into the ether.
When the mind enters the minds of all beings,
one who maintains mental concentration abandons even the subtlety of the mind.
Having attained this state, the knower of yoga, having reached the unsurpassed subtlety of intellect, relinquishes the intellect of all sentient beings without exception.
The knower of yoga who, having correctly understood reasoning (*tarka*), abandons these seven subtle things, for him there is no further rebirth.
Having repeatedly observed the subtlety of these seven dhāraṇās, the self-possessed one should abandon each attainment as it arises and resort to the next higher one.
Toward whichever being one directs passion, one exalts them;
having become thoroughly attached to that very being, one is destroyed.
Therefore, having understood the subtle elements that are successively attached to one another,
the yogi who abandons them shall attain the supreme state.
O King, these same seven subtle elements lead to bondage; however, for one who knows my true nature, detachment toward the elements beginning with *bhūta* leads to liberation.
O King, this entire world is deeply attached to fragrances and other such objects; it leads to rebirth. That [state] is Brahman; it is not human.
O Lord of Men, having transcended these very seven concentrations, let the yogi enter whichever subtle dissolution he desires among the elements.
It dissolves into the bodies of the gods, asuras, gandharvas, uragas, and rakshasas, and it never incurs attachment anywhere.

‘Human desires’ refers to beings and so forth. ‘The fruit of a wife’ refers to sons and so forth. ‘Knowledge’ refers to that which is beyond the internal (ādhyātmika). ‘Illusion’ refers to sorcery such as the Indra-net (*indrajāla*) and the like. ‘Base metals’ refers to bronze and so forth, other than gold and silver. ‘Falling from the wind’ means traveling by means of the wind. As stated in the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
“Having understood the seven subtle elements and Maheśvara in his six limbs... [215]
One who knows the application of the primary [means] attains the supreme Brahman.
Omniscience, contentment, primordial awakening, sovereignty, and eternally undiminished power;
the All-pervading Lord possesses infinite power and is the knower of all things.
They say there are six limbs of Maheśvara.
One who is constantly devoted to Brahman and disciplined is liberated from the afflictions.
Now, the manifestations of yoga.
Regarding this, Devala says:

There are eight qualities of sovereignty (*aiśvaryaguṇa*): *aṇimā*, *mahimā*, *laghimā*, *prāpti*, *prākāmya*, *īśitva*, *vaśitva*, and *yatra-kāmāvasāyitva*. Among these, the three—*aṇimā*, *mahimā*, and *laghimā*—are bodily; the five beginning with *prāpti* are sensory. In this context, *aṇimā* is the state of having a minute body; by virtue of its atomic nature, one enters even subtle things. *Mahimā* is the greatness of the body; by virtue of its magnitude, one pervades all bodies. *Laghimā* is the rapid movement of the body; by means of it, one reaches even very distant places in an instant. *Prāpti* is the attainment of all objects of experience; through *prāpti*, one becomes a direct perceiver of everything. *Prākāmya* is the power of acting according to one's will; through *prākāmya*, one obtains the best of all enjoyments. *Īśitva* is unimpeded sovereignty; through *īśitva*, one surpasses even the deities. *Vaśitva* is self-mastery; through *vaśitva*, one possesses immeasurable lifespan and has people under one’s control. *Yatra-kāmāvasāyitva* is threefold: *chāyāveśa* (entry into a shadow), *avadhyānāveśa* (entry through meditation), and *aṅgapraveśa* (entry into a limb). *Chāyāveśa* is that by which one subdues the mind of another merely by entering their shadow. *Avadhyānāveśa* is the mastery over the mind of those situated at a distance through meditation. *Aṅgapraveśa* is the entry into the body of a living being or into the life-force itself. Through *yatra-kāmāvasāyitva*, one presides over material objects; this is the station of sovereignty, arising from the excellence of merit, splendor, and knowledge due to the transcendence of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*. Sovereignty arises from that which is accompanied by excellence. Having thus attained these qualities of sovereignty, one whose impurities are shaken off, whose doubts are severed, who perceives directly, and who knows the higher and lower aspects of *dharma*, remains immutable. Knowing that "all this is unreal and impermanent," he attains peace by himself. This is the pervasion of sovereignty.
Just as a small and weak fire, O King,
is extinguished when overwhelmed by thick fuel, even so is yoga, O Lord.
And just as that same man, O King, having gained strength outside and joined with the wind, would quickly burn this entire earth; so too is it with him.
But a yogi who has not yet developed his strength, though possessing radiant splendor and great power,
cannot purify the entire world like the sun at the time of the end.
Just as a weak man, O King, is carried away by a current,
so too is a yogi lacking in strength rendered helpless by the sense objects.
And just as Rāvaṇa obstructs that very stream,
so too, having attained the power of yoga, one arrays oneself against the many objects of the senses.
Likewise: Endowed with the power of both yoga and non-yoga, these lords enter into the Prajāpatis, the ṛṣis, the gods, and the great elements for the sake of piercing the shafts of others.
Neither Yama, nor the Ender, nor Death with his terrifying prowess,
O King, has power over one who possesses yoga and immeasurable splendor.
But having acquired power through yoga, O bull of the Bharatas, one should multiply oneself into many thousands and wander the earth with all of them.
He may enjoy sense-objects by means of some [powers], by others he may undergo suffering, and he may practice austerities;
and he may again withdraw them all, just as the sun withdraws its masses of radiance.
Yājñavalkya says:
invisibility, memory, radiance, as well as knowledge through sight and hearing,
and the power of entering another's body after casting off one's own— these are [the powers].
For the blind, vision is the sign of success in yoga;
indeed, when yoga is perfected, one who casts off the body is fit for immortality.
[219] 23 — Now, regarding the conduct of one whose wisdom is established, it is found therein in the Mahābhārata.
Arjuna said:
What is the description, O Keśava, of one whose wisdom is steady and who is established in samādhi?
How does the one of steady intellect speak, how does he sit, and how does he move?
The Blessed One said: O Pārtha, when one abandons all desires that have entered the mind and is satisfied in the self alone by means of the self, then one is said to be of steady wisdom.
One whose mind is unperturbed amidst sufferings, who is free from longing amidst pleasures,
and from whom passion, fear, and anger have departed— he is called a sage of steady wisdom.
He who is everywhere without attachment, and who neither rejoices nor feels aversion upon encountering various things, whether auspicious or inauspicious— his wisdom is firmly established.
And when he withdraws these senses from the objects of the senses, just as a tortoise draws in its limbs from all sides, his wisdom is firmly established.
That which is night for all beings, therein the self-controlled man keeps watch;
that wherein beings keep watch is night for the sage who sees.
Just as the waters enter the ocean, which is being filled yet remains established in stillness,
even so do all desires enter him.
He attains peace, not the seeker of desires.
The man who, having abandoned all desires, moves about free from longing,
without the sense of "mine," and without egoism— he attains peace.
This is the state of Brahman, O Pārtha; having attained this, one is no longer deluded.
Abiding even at the time of death in this state, one attains the nirvāṇa of Brahman.

Regarding the verse beginning with “That which is night” (*yā niśā*): “night” (*niśā*) refers to the reality of Brahman (*brahmatattva*), for therein all beings lack vision. One who “is awake” (*jāgarti*) in that state is one who experiences the nature of that Brahman; the term “self-controlled” (*saṃyamī*) means one who is established in yoga.

"In that night" means in that night characterized by attachment to sense objects, during which all beings have their eyes open; the meaning is that [the yogin remains awake] due to the cessation of the mental modification consisting in the perception of those [objects]. "With an immovable foundation" (*acalapratiṣṭham*): he whose stability or state is immovable—that is, immovable and without a [sensory] foundation. The meaning is that just as waters enter [a vessel] without causing any transformation, so too sense objects approach the yogin without producing any transformation in his mind.
Likewise: "O Pāṇḍava, both illumination, activity, and even delusion..."
He feels no aversion toward things that have arisen, nor does he long for those that have ceased.
He who sits like one indifferent, not shaken by the qualities (guṇas),
and remains firm in the thought that "it is only the qualities that are acting," does not waver.
Equanimous in pain and pleasure, established in his own nature, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal;
the steadfast one is the same toward the pleasant and the unpleasant, and equal toward blame and praise.
He who is the same in honor and dishonor, the same toward the parties of friend and foe,
and who has renounced all undertakings— he is said to have transcended the qualities.
And he who serves Me with unswerving yoga of devotion,
having transcended these qualities, is fit for becoming Brahman.
For I am the foundation of Brahman, of the immortal and the imperishable,
of the eternal dharma, and of absolute bliss.

Knowledge is the quality of *sattva*; activity is the quality of *rajas*; and delusion is the quality of *tamas*. The word "engaged" (*saṃpravṛttāni*) implies they are directed toward the causes of pleasure; "withdrawn" (*nivṛttāni*) implies they are directed toward the causes of pleasure and pain. "Does not move" (*neṅgate*) means it does not act. Likewise:
when one perceives the distinctness of beings as abiding in the One.
And from that very source, Brahman likewise attains expansion.
Likewise,
those perfected in knowledge and humility see with equanimity a Brahmin, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and even an outcaste.
Even here, rebirth has been conquered by those whose minds are established in equanimity;
for Brahman is faultless and equal, therefore they are established in Brahman.

One who has known Brahman and is established in Brahman— steadfast in intellect and undeluded— should neither rejoice upon obtaining what is pleasant, nor be agitated upon obtaining what is unpleasant.
With his self unattached to external objects of touch, he finds that happiness which is in the Self;
with his self united in yoga with Brahman, he enjoys imperishable bliss.
For those enjoyments born of contact are indeed the source of suffering;
they have a beginning and an end, O son of Kuntī, and the wise man does not delight in them.
He who is able here, even before the dissolution of the body, to endure the impulse arising from desire and anger— he is disciplined, he is a happy man.
He who finds happiness within, who rejoices within, and likewise whose light is solely within—
that yogi, having become Brahman, attains the extinction of Brahman.
The sages, whose taints are exhausted, who have severed all doubts, who are self-controlled, and who delight in the welfare of all beings, attain the Brahman-nirvana.
For those ascetics who are free from desire and anger, whose minds are restrained,
and who have realized the Self, the extinction of Brahman exists on every side.
Likewise,
one who possesses an even mind toward friends, companions, enemies, neutrals, mediators, the hateful, and kinsmen, as well as toward the virtuous and the wicked, is preeminent.
Likewise,
he who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me—
for him I am not lost, and he is not lost to me.
The yogi who, established in unity, worships me as abiding in all beings—
even while engaged in any kind of activity— he dwells in me.
O Arjuna, he who, by comparison with himself, sees equality everywhere—
whether it be happiness or suffering— that yogi is considered supreme.

“When he perceives the distinctness of beings as abiding in one place”—that is, when he perceives the separate existence of all beings as unified within the Supreme Cause during the state of dissolution, and likewise their expansion from that single Supreme Self; the meaning is that by knowing the process of creation and dissolution according to the text, “From this very Self, space was produced,” he attains Brahman. “The wise are equal-seers”: they become equal-seers of Brahman residing within the Brāhmaṇas and others; the meaning is that they perceive the form of Brahman pervading all beings like space.
And so it is said:
At the end of many births, the man of knowledge attains Me, realizing that "Vāsudeva is everything. Such a great-souled person is very rare to find.
The meaning is that for them, everything is Vāsudeva.
Likewise: "A certain Brāhmaṇa, possessing little wealth, walking about in good health..."
The wise King Prahlāda questioned the one who was even wiser than himself.
[Prahlāda said:
Self-composed, capable, gentle, self-controlled, free from desire, and without malice;
eloquent, bold, wise, and discerning—you move about like a child.
You do not long for gain when it is brought to you, nor do you grieve when it is absent;
O Brahmin, as if eternally content, you take no pride in anything at all.
While your subjects are being carried away by the current, you remain as if despondent;
yet in matters of dharma, pleasure, and wealth, you stand as if immovable.
You do not practice virtue or worldly purpose, nor do you pursue sensual pleasure;
disregarding the objects of the senses, you wander like one who is liberated, acting as a witness.
"What indeed is your wisdom, O Sage, or what is your learning, and what is your conduct?
Tell me quickly, O Brahmin, that which you consider to be the highest good in this world."
[Bhīṣma said:
Thus questioned, that wise man, who knew the ordinances of worldly dharma,
spoke in gentle words to Prahlāda with a purpose that was not in vain.
O Prahlāda, seeing the birth of beings without a cause,
as well as their decline, growth, and destruction, I neither rejoice nor am I distressed.
Likewise,
I perceive the celestial bodies moving in the sky— both small and large— falling down at their appointed time.
Thus perceiving all beings to be pursued by death,
and knowing everything in its universal nature, the wise man, having accomplished what was to be done, sleeps in happiness.
I eat even a very large morsel when it is obtained by chance;
yet again, I lie down for many days without eating at all.
They serve me food that is abundant and of many qualities; yet again it is little, then again very scant, and at times it does not even appear.
Sometimes I eat a grain of rice, and at other times I swallow oil-cake;
I eat fine rice and meat, as well as many various kinds of foods.
Sometimes I lie on a couch, and again I lie upon the ground;
sometimes a bed is provided for me even in a palace.
I wear garments of bark, hemp, linen, and deerskins,
and yet I also wear most precious robes.
I do not reject by whim the lawful enjoyment that has come together,
nor do I pursue it when it is very difficult to obtain.
It is immovable, undecaying, auspicious, free from sorrow, pure, incomparable, established in the minds of the wise,
and neither desired nor practiced by the foolish.
I practice this pure vow of the python.
Of unshakable mind and unfallen from his own dharma, he has limited further transmigration and attained supreme liberation;
he is free from fear, passion, greed, and delusion.
I practice this pure vow of the python.
Food, snacks, and drinks whose fruits are not fixed,
prepared according to rule with their place and time duly distinguished—
delightful to the heart, and never consumed by the miserly.
I practice this pure vow of the python.
Having carefully observed with the intellect of reality a person overcome by craving who thinks "this, this," and who is despondent because wealth has not been attained;
I practice this pure vow of the python.
Having observed in many ways how people here, for the sake of wealth, resort to the wretched, the noble, and the ignoble,
the self-possessed one, delighting in tranquility and being peaceful, [proceeded].
I practice this pure vow of the python.
Having observed in reality that pleasure and pain, loss and gain of wealth, joy and sorrow, death and life, are all determined by destiny, I—
I practice this pure vow of the python.
Having observed those who have attained the enjoyment of the fruit— calm, endowed with fortitude, intelligence, and wisdom, and free from fear, passion, delusion, and pride—
I practice this pure vow of the python.
By nature using indeterminate lodgings and seats,
he was endowed with restraint, observances, vows, purity, and truth;
free from the accumulation of fruits, he was joyful.
I observe this pure vow of the python.
Having perceived that which is devoid of the objects of pleasure and free from the aims of exertion, and having directed his intellect toward what resides within himself,
he strives to restrain the thirsty and unsteady mind.
I practice this pure vow of the python.
Neither my heart nor my mind yields to the difficulty of attaining pleasant happiness or to impermanence;
rather, it is as if I am observing both of these things.
I practice this pure vow of the python.
Indeed, this has been said many times by wise poets who spread their own fame far and wide,
crying out "this and that" here and there— alas!
By those who speculate upon the profundity of their own and others' doctrines.
Having reflected upon this, which is like a precipice into which ignorant men here have fallen separately,
one sees it as an unfathomable abyss whose further shore is infinite faults.
I dwell among men, having subdued both faults and craving.
Bhīṣma said:
That high-souled man who, with subdued passion, would here follow the vow of conduct practiced by the ajagara snake—
Free from fear, anger, greed, and delusion,
he indeed shall dwell happily in this state of abiding.
Likewise,
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "Of what character, of what conduct, of what learning, and of what prowess [should he be]?"
One attains the station of Brahman, which is beyond primordial nature and eternal.
Bhīṣma said: One who is disciplined in the duties of liberation, moderate in diet, and has conquered the senses,
attains the station of Brahman, which is supreme and eternal beyond primordial nature.
In this regard, O Bhārata, they cite this ancient history, the dialogue between Jaigīṣavya and Asita.
Asita Devala spoke to the highly wise Jaigīṣavya, who had mastered the traditional teachings on dharma and was neither angry nor elated.
Devala said:
You are not pleased when being praised, nor do you become angry when being reviled.
What is this wisdom of yours, from where does it come, and what is its ultimate foundation?
Bhīṣma said:
Thus questioned by him, that man of great asceticism spoke these great words to him—
words that were free from doubt, full of profound meaning, and pure.
Jaigīṣavya said:
"O twice-born one, I shall fully declare to you that which you ask me concerning the goal, the supreme state, and the power of those who perform meritorious deeds."
O Devala, those who are always impartial toward both those who revile them and those who praise them,
and who conceal their own agreements and their good deeds— [they are the truly wise].
And the wise do not wish to speak ill of one who speaks well,
nor do they desire to strike back at one who strikes them.
They do not grieve for things not yet obtained; they act with the mindset of the present;
they do not grieve for the past, nor do they dwell upon them.
And when those worthy of worship have arrived, O Devala, those who are capable and firm in their vows provide for them according to their desire and means, as the occasion arises.
Those who have matured their knowledge, possessing great wisdom, having conquered anger and subdued their senses,
never commit an offense through thought, deed, or word.
Free from envy, they never harm one another;
these wise ones are never distressed by the prosperity of others.
They do not speak excessively of others' blame or praise,
nor are they ever perturbed by blame or praise.
Those who are entirely tranquil and devoted to the welfare of all beings do not become angry, do not rejoice, and do not offend anyone.
Having untied the knot of the heart, they pass on according to their pleasure—
those who have no kinsmen, nor are they the kinsmen of others.
They have no enemies, nor are they the enemies of anyone;
those mortals who act in this way live happily at all times.
The best of the twice-born, who know the Dharma, follow only the Dharma;
for those who have fallen away from this path both rejoice and tremble with fear.
Having set out upon that path, how could I feel resentment?
Whether I am reviled or praised, for what reason should I rejoice?
Whatever young men desire, they obtain that from him;
yet neither blame nor praise shall cause my decrease or increase.
The knower of reality should be as satisfied with contempt as if it were nectar;
the wise man should always shrink from honor as if it were poison.
He who treats others with contempt sleeps happily both in this world and the next;
for he is liberated from all evils—he who is the scorner awakens [to the truth].
And whatever wise men seek the supreme goal,
those people attain happiness by taking refuge in this Brahman.
Having withdrawn all sacrifices from every quarter and having conquered his senses,
he attains the station of Brahman, which is supreme and eternal beyond primordial nature.
Neither gods, nor gandharvas, nor piśācas, nor rākṣasas can follow upon the track of one who has attained the supreme goal.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa,
Dattātreya said:
"O King, this very day I shall effect the removal of your suffering."
"Speak the truth; O lord of the earth, for what reason do you suffer?"
[Jaḍa said:
Whose are you, or whose is the suffering? Let this very reality be investigated in this way. Reflect upon these limbs of the body and all its parts.
Thus addressed by that wise man, the king reflected upon himself as the locus of all three kinds of suffering.
Having reflected for a long time again and again, that noble-minded hero, the king,
laughed within himself and spoke these words.
I am neither the earth, nor the water, nor the light, nor the wind, nor the ether;
yet, being embodied, I do not find happiness today.
And so, when the sense of "mine" has been abandoned, it is perceived with particular clarity:
that suffering or happiness residing in the mind is supported by the mind.
Therefore, for that reason, I have neither suffering nor happiness, for I am not the mind;
I am not the ego-sense, nor the mind, nor the intellect, because I am not any of these.
"How can that suffering born of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) belong to me as something alien?
For I am not the body, nor am I the mind; since I am distinct from both the body and the mind."
Therefore, whether these pleasures or pains exist in the mind or in the body, what concern is it of mine?
For one who possesses not even his hands and so forth in their entirety— not even flesh, bones, or parts such as veins—
who would need treasuries of elephants, horses, chariots, and the like?
Even a very slight connection exists here for a person.
Therefore, I have no enemy, nor do I have suffering;
I have neither pleasure, nor a city, nor a treasury; nor do I possess the power of horses, elephants, and so forth. Nor does he [possess such things].
Nor does anyone else exist apart from me.
Just as the single space within a collection of jars and pots appears manifold,
so too do Subāhu, that King of Kāśi, and I.
And I consider [them] within bodies through various bodily forms.
[232] In the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*: The King said:
"Are you weary? You have carried my palanquin only a short distance."
"Why do you not look as robust as he did before? You appear emaciated."
The Brahmin said:
"I am not fat, nor am I a carrier of your palanquin;
I am not weary, nor is there any exertion for me to endure, O Lord of the Earth."
The king said:
"You appear visibly fat, yet the palanquin is not [yet] upon you;
for embodied beings certainly experience fatigue from carrying a burden."
The Brāhmaṇa said:
O King, tell me what was seen by you directly;
whether one is strong or weak is a qualifying attribute that should be stated afterwards.
"The palanquin was carried by you, and it remains upon you even now;
this is false, but please listen to my words in this matter."
The pair of thighs rests upon the ground; the two shanks are situated on the two feet;
the two thighs rest upon the two shanks, and the abdomen is likewise supported by them.
The chest, the arms, and the shoulders situated upon the belly—this palanquin rests upon the shoulders; what burden has been placed here upon me?
This body which you have observed standing upon the palanquin—therein you are one person, and I am another; yet this is said otherwise.
I, you, and others—all of us are carried along by the elements;
even this multitude of elements moves, having fallen into the flow of the qualities (guṇas).
O Lord of the Earth, these qualities such as *sattva* and the rest are subject to karma;
that karma, accumulated through ignorance, exists in all living beings without exception.
O King, when there was neither accumulation nor depletion for him,
by what logic did you say, "He was fat"?
When this palanquin was placed upon your shoulder, you were as level with it as if it were situated from your feet up through your calves, hips, thighs, and belly.
Likewise, O King, it is not only by other creatures that a palanquin is raised;
even one dwelling in mountains, trees, or houses, or even one originating from the earth [is supported].
O King, when a man’s state is separate from the causal constituents of nature (prakṛti),
which of those resulting hardships must then be endured by me, O Lord of Men?
Of whatever substance this palanquin is made, of that same substance is the collection of beings;
it has been cultivated by me through the sense of "mine" regarding this entire world, and thus it has been reinforced.
Parāśara said:
Having spoken thus, that twice-born man became silent while continuing to carry the palanquin;
the king, descending to the ground, quickly grasped his feet.
[234] The king said:
"O, O twice-born one, set down the palanquin and show me favor!
Tell me, who are you that stands here assuming the form of a commoner?"
O wise one, let all that you are, the cause for your presence, and the reason for your arrival be told to me, who am eager to hear it.
The Brahmin said:
Listen; it is impossible for anyone to say "Who am I? Furthermore, the act of traveling everywhere is solely for the sake of experience.

The experience of pleasure and pain, which give rise to the body and so forth, originate from merit and demerit; in order to experience these, the living being undergoes birth in a body and other such states.
For indeed, O protector of the earth, dharma and adharma are the cause for every living being in all circumstances; since this is so, why is the cause being questioned?
The King said:
"Neither merit nor demerit is the body; rather, the cause in all actions is [the mind]. And the movement from one place to another in the body is for the sake of experience."
Regarding that which you have said—"Who am I?"—it is impossible to speak of this self; yet, the desire to hear it arises within me.
O Brahmin, how can it be impossible to say, "I am that which exists"?
O twice-born one, this word "I" is not a fault when applied to the Self.
The Brahmin said:
"The notion 'I am sound' leads to error; it is not so with respect to the Self itself. The cognition of the Self in what is not the Self, or the word [expressing it], is characterized by delusion."
The tongue says, "I am," as do the teeth, the lips, and the palate, O King;
for by these, I am produced through the entire apparatus of speech.
Why does she speak by means of reasons, saying "I am speech" herself?
Even so, it is not logical to say "I am speech" in this manner.
Since this body, characterized by the head, hands, and so forth, is distinct from the person, O King, why then do I apply this notion of "I" to it?
O best of kings, if there were anyone else superior to me, such that it might be desired to speak thus of both myself and this other person; [but since there is none, I shall speak].
Since the one Person is established within all bodies, then indeed such words as "Who are you? and "Who am I? are meaningless.
"You are the king, this is the palanquin, and we are the attendants walking before you;
and this world belongs to you"—O King, this which is said is not true.
From the tree comes the wood, and from that, this palanquin occupied by you;
O King, where has the designation "tree" gone, or is it now the designation "wood"?
"This great king is mounted upon a tree," says this person to you;
nor does he say that [the king] standing on the wood is seated in a palanquin.

O best of kings, this palanquin is a construction of wood, existing only through its arrangement and structure; search for it, and you will find that upon its disintegration, the palanquin no longer exists.
In this way, let the separation of the ribs of a parasol be considered:
"Where has the parasol gone? This same principle applies to you and to me.
[236] Man, woman, cow, goat, horse, elephant, bird, and tree— this is to be understood as a conventional designation applied to bodies in the world based on their causes of action (karma).
The self is neither a god, nor a human, nor an animal, nor a plant;
O King, these distinctions of bodily form have their origin in karma.
That which is called "king" in the world, and that which consists of mere right resolve—[all this is the reality].
O King, that which does not even over time assume another designation, despite being produced through transformation and other such processes— what indeed is that entity?
"You are the king of the entire world, the son of your father, the enemy of your foes, the husband of your wife, and the father of your son; O King, whom among these may I call you?"
Are you this head, or is the head yours? Is it the belly, or indeed the feet and so forth? Or are you none of these at all, O lord of the earth?
"You exist as something distinct from all your constituent parts;
who indeed are you? O King, reflect upon this with discernment."
Since reality is thus established, O King, how could it be possible for you to cultivate the notion "I am this" by means of effecting a separation?

“I have been grasped by you as the self characterized by that [body]; therefore, you are there. In this context, “you are there” and “I am here” is said otherwise; the sense is that between us there exists no relationship of signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*). “Flow of qualities” (*guṇapravāha*) means the stream of the transformation of the qualities (*guṇapariṇāma*). “Pure” (*śuddha*) means solitary, devoid of contact with other entities; the meaning is “nameless” (*asaṃjñī*). “Imperishable” (*akṣara*) means indestructible. “Peaceful” (*śānta*) means free from passion and hatred. “Beyond qualities” (*nirguṇa*) means transcending the qualities. “Beyond nature” (*prakṛteḥ paraḥ*) means utterly distinct from the insentient. “O King,” and so forth: the sense is that if a burden were to belong to another even when an entity is being carried by someone else, then you too would have a burden regarding the object to be carried which rests upon the aggregates (*skandha*) characterized by me. Thus, the connection is that the burden is equal to that of other living beings. Not only is the burden arising from the palanquin equal, but even the burden of a mountain is equal. “Foolish” (*jālma*) means one who acts without reflection; the phrase “for the sake of which” refers to the cause of coming. “What is the reason for coming? is a question concerning the intended purpose. “The word ‘I’ leads to error,” and so forth: this word “I,” when applied to the self—that is, to its own user—does not lead to error. Rather, the cognition of the self in what is not the self is an illusion. Likewise, the application of the word “self” to what is not the self is characterized by delusion; such is the meaning. “These, the tongue and so forth,” are the causes for the manifestation of sound; because they are not the agent (*kartṛ*) and because I am bodiless (*aśarīratvāt*), the cognition of the word “I” is something brought about at another time; such is the meaning.
Likewise:
"But as for the ultimate truth, O protector of the earth, hear it from me in brief:
It is one, all-pervading, equal, pure, devoid of qualities, and beyond primordial nature."
The Self is devoid of birth, cognition, and so forth; it is omnipresent, immutable, and composed of supreme knowledge;
the all-pervading Lord is not [defined] by the wicked through names, genus, and other such categories.
O King, he was not a practitioner of yoga, nor was he ever disciplined, nor will he ever be disciplined;
for even though he possesses all three of these causes—himself, others, and both—he lacks even one of them.
For one who does not see reality, this consciousness appears as a supreme object due to duality,
just as the single cavity of a bamboo flute is designated by different names such as "Ṣaḍja" and so forth according to its various divisions.
Just as the wind pervades without distinction, so it is with that Great-Souled One.
Listen, O tiger among kings, to what was sung by Ṛbhu in the past.
By producing awakening in the high-souled Nidāgha.
O King, the son of the supreme Brahmā was named Ṛbhu;
by his very nature, he had realized the true essence of reality.
In former times, his disciple was Nidāgha, the son of Pulastya;
he bestowed upon him complete knowledge with the greatest joy.
For him who had attained the reality of knowledge, there was no longer any latent impression of duality;
that lord of men, Ṛbhu, reflected upon Nidāgha.
O hero, on the bank of the Devikā there is indeed a city named Nagara,
prosperous and exceedingly beautiful, which was established by Pulastya.
O best of kings,
in former times, a knower of yoga named Nidāgha, a disciple of Ṛbhu, lived at the edge of that delightful grove.
When a thousand divine years had passed,
that Ṛbhu went to his city to look for his disciple Nidāgha.
At the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, while he was standing within the range of vision at the doorway,
[the host] offered him the guest-offering (argha) and led him into his own house.
When his lotus-feet had been washed and he had taken his seat,
that best of brahmins respectfully said, "Please eat."
Ṛbhu said: "O best of brahmins, please tell me what may be eaten here in your house;
for my pleasure always lies in even the coarsest food."
Nigādha said: "O best of the twice-born, whatever among the groats, barley-meal, and other foods, as well as the cakes, is pleasing to you in my house, eat that according to your desire."
Ṛbhu said:
"O twice-born one, these foods are poor; give me sweet food, such as saṃyāva, milk-rice (pāyasa), and other delicacies containing grapes and molasses."
Nigādha said:
"O virtuous lady, whatever is most excellent in my house—
whether it be food or condiments, sweet or otherwise— with that prepare her meal."
Thus addressed by him, that wife prepared sweet food for the twice-born man out of respect for her husband's words.
O protector of the earth, once that great sage had finished eating the sweet food he desired,
Nidāgha, standing bowed with humility, spoke to him.
Has supreme satisfaction arisen in you, as well as contentment? O twice-born one, has your mind been made healthy by this food?
"O Brahmin, where is your residence, or where are you prepared to go? Or from where have you come—let that be told by you, O twice-born one."
Ṛbhu said:
"O Brāhmaṇa, satisfaction arises from food for one who is hungry;
I have neither hunger nor satisfaction. Why, O twice-born one, do you question me?"
[240] When the earth element is consumed by fire, hunger arises;
and when water is exhausted, satiety does not occur for human beings.
O twice-born one, since hunger and thirst are known as attributes of the body and do not belong to me,
I am indeed always satisfied due to the absence of the occurrence of hunger.
O twice-born one, well-established contentment is a property of the mind, not of "me";
for a person is not joined with those [qualities] of the consciousness that you have asked about.
When asked, "Where is your residence? and "Where are you going?
and "From where have you come here?"—understand my reply to these three questions as follows.
Since this person is all-pervading and omnipresent like space, from where, to where, or whither would you go? How, then, could even that [concept of going] be meaningful for you?
I am neither a goer nor a comer, nor do I have a dwelling in any single place;
you and others are not you, and that [Self] is not you, nor are others, nor even am I myself.
"Sweet food is what is desired"—this inquiry of yours has been made by me.
O best of the twice-born, listen now to what you will say regarding that as well.
O best of the twice-born, what is unpalatable and what is sweet for one eating food?
That which is sweet is indeed the cause of agitation when it becomes unpalatable.
What is unrefined becomes refined, yet people shrink from what is refined;
what, then, is the cause of pleasure at the beginning, middle, and end?
For just as a house made of clay becomes stable when plastered with clay,
so too this body, which is composed of earth, [is sustained] by earthly atoms.
Barley, wheat, mung beans, and so forth; ghee, oil, milk, and curd; molasses, fruits, and the like, as well as the atoms of earth, O kings.
Having understood this, you should—discerning between the pleasant and the unpleasant—make that mind your support through equanimity; for indeed, equanimity leads to liberation.
Having heard those words of his, which were endowed with the ultimate truth, O King,
the illustrious Nidāgha prostrated himself and spoke these words:
Be gracious for my benefit; tell me, who are you that have come here? O twice-born one, my delusion has indeed vanished upon hearing these words.
Ṛbhu said:
"I am Ṛbhu, your teacher; O twice-born one, I have come here for the sake of bestowing wisdom upon you. I shall now depart; the ultimate truth has been declared to you."
O Brahmin, this entire world was originally one;
it is the very nature of the Supreme Self known as Vāsudeva.
Having been told "So be it" by Nidāgha,
and having been honored with prostrations and supreme devotion, Ṛbhu departed according to his own will.
Furthermore, O lord of men, when another thousand years had passed,
he went to that very same city in order to bestow the knowledge of the summer season.
Then, outside the city, while the king was entering the town with a vast retinue of great power, he saw the sage Nidāgha.
He saw the illustrious one standing at a distance, avoiding the crush of people,
his throat parched with hunger, returning from the forest with sacrificial fuel and *kuśa* grass.
Having seen Nidāgha, that Ṛbhu approached him, saluted him, and said:
"O twice-born one, why are you standing in this secluded place?"
Nidāgha said:
"O Brahmin, this great crowd of people is gathered because the lord of men is about to enter the beautiful city; therefore, I am staying here."
Ṛbhu said:
"O best of the twice-born, who here is the lord of men and who is the other person? Tell me, for you are considered by me to be one who knows."
Nidāgha said:
This lord of men, who has mounted this intoxicated king of elephants as lofty as a mountain peak— he is both the world beyond and this one.
R̥bhu said:
"Indeed, these two kings of elephants were shown to me simultaneously; you did not distinguish them specifically, nor were they marked by separate characteristics."
Therefore, O illustrious one, let the distinction between these two be told by you;
I wish to know which here is the elephant and which is the lord of men.
Nidāgha said:
"O Brahmin, this elephant that is here—this king is its rider;
O twice-born one, who indeed does not know the relationship between the vehicle and the rider?"
Ṛbhu said: "O Brahmin, I know this; nevertheless, instruct me as to how it is.
What is designated by the word 'below,' and what is called 'above'?"
The Brāhmaṇa said:
Having been addressed thus, Nidāgha immediately ascended and spoke to that Ṛbhu:
"Listen, I shall tell you that which you ask of me."
"Just as I am the king above, so you are the elephant below;
O Brahmin, this illustration has been shown by me for your understanding."
[243] Ṛbhu said:
"O best of the twice-born, you stand like a king, while I, an ascetic, stand like an elephant.
Therefore, explain this very point: which of us two am I, and which are you?"
The Brāhmaṇa said:
Thus addressed, Nidāgha quickly grasped both of his feet and said,
"O Blessed One, you are certainly the preceptor Ṛbhu."
No one else’s mind has been so refined by the impressions of non-duality as that of the Teacher; therefore, I consider you to have attained the status of a Guru.
Ṛbhu said:
"O Nidāgha, honored by your previous service, I, the teacher named Ṛbhu, have come here to impart instruction to you."
O Mahāmati, they summarize this as follows:
that which is the very essence of the ultimate truth is non-duality in its entirety.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
Having spoken thus, the learned teacher Ṛbhu departed from Nidāgha;
and Nidāgha, too, through that instruction, became devoted to non-duality.
He beheld all beings as non-different from his own self.
In that way, the twice-born man, intent upon the Supreme Brahman, attained supreme liberation;
so too may you, O knower of dharma, who regard yourself, enemies, and friends as equal.
One who knows the self as all-pervading is liberated,
just as the single sky appears divided by distinctions such as white and blue.
By those of deluded vision, even the Self is perceived individually and separately within that One;
yet that which exists here as a whole is Acyuta alone, and there is nothing else apart from Him.
Therefore, both I and you, and all this— abandon the delusion of duality regarding the nature of the Self.
Likewise, there is the account of Prahlāda.
Prahlāda said:
"Everything has been taught to me by my preceptor; there is no doubt in this matter."
And it has been accepted by me, yet this is not my own considered view.
Conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and likewise punishment—
these are indeed said to be the means for winning over friends and others.
Therefore, O dear one, I do not see friends and the like; do not be angry.
O mighty-armed one, when there is no goal to be accomplished, what is the use of the means?
O dear one, when Govinda— the Supreme Self, the soul of all beings, the Lord of the world, and composed of the world— is present, where is the talk of friend or foe?
The Blessed Lord Viṣṇu resides in you, in me, and elsewhere as well; since He is everywhere, how can there be any distinction such as "this one is my friend" or "that one is my enemy"?
Therefore, enough with this excessively difficult and prolix discourse;
O dear one, effort should be directed toward that which is auspicious and lies within the sphere of ignorance.
O dear one, knowledge arises from ignorance due to lack of understanding;
does a child not mistake a firefly for fire, O Lord of Asuras?
That action which does not lead to bondage is knowledge, while that which leads to liberation is true learning; other action leads to exhaustion, whereas other knowledge is merely skill in the arts.
Having understood this, O illustrious one, I prostrate myself before you and speak to you: please listen to me regarding the supreme essence within that which is essence-less.
No one thinks, "Who will have the kingdom? or "Who desires wealth? Nevertheless, both of these are obtained by men simply as they must be.
O highly fortunate one, everyone indeed exerts effort toward greatness;
nevertheless, for men, it is their fortunes, not their efforts, that are the cause of prosperity.
O Lord, even for people who lack discernment, who do not listen to advice, and who possess no wisdom,
there exist kingdoms that are the enjoyment of their fortune.
Therefore, one should strive for dharma if one desires great prosperity;
one should also strive with a sense of self-reliance if one desires even nirvana.
Gods, humans, animals, birds, trees, and reptiles—
this form of the infinite Viṣṇu stands as if it were divided.
One who understands this should regard the entire world, both stationary and moving,
as being like the Self, because this Viṣṇu assumes the form of the universe.
When he is known thus, that Blessed One, the beginningless Supreme Lord, becomes gracious;
when he is gracious, there is the destruction of the afflictions.
Now, regarding the destiny of one who has fallen from yoga,
it is stated therein in the Mahābhārata:
Arjuna said:
O Kṛṣṇa, what goal does one who is endowed with faith but lacks self-restraint, whose mind has strayed from yoga, reach when failing to attain perfection in yoga?
O mighty-armed one, does he not perish like a scattered cloud, fallen from both paths,
without support, bewildered on the way of Brahman?
O Kṛṣṇa, you ought to sever this doubt of mine completely;
for indeed, no one other than you is capable of being the dispeller of this doubt.
The Blessed One said: O Pārtha, neither in this world nor in the next does destruction exist for him;
for no one who performs good deeds, my dear, ever goes to a miserable state.
Having reached the worlds of those who perform meritorious deeds and having dwelt there for countless years,
one who has fallen from yoga is reborn in the home of the pure and the prosperous.
Or else, one is born into a family of illustrious yogis;
for such a birth as this is indeed more difficult to obtain in the world.
[247] There he regains that same connection with wisdom acquired in his previous body;
and from that point, O joy of the Kurus, he strives even more for perfection.
For by that very same prior practice, he is carried along even against his will;
even one who merely desires to know yoga transcends the Brahman of sound.
But the yogi who strives with a serene mind, having purified all taints and perfected himself through many births, then attains the supreme goal.
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"The yogi first becomes one joined in yoga while practicing;
but when his samādhi is perfected, he attains the realization of the supreme Brahman."
If the human mind is released from the fault of obstacles,
liberation arises exactly as before for one who practices through successive births.
But the yogin who has perfected samādhi, having burned away the accumulation of karma by the fire of yoga, attains liberation in that very birth before long.
Then Devala [spoke] regarding the omens of death there.
Now I shall duly declare the signs of death (ariṣṭa) regarding the practice of yoga,
as previously taught by the sages for the purpose of understanding the lifespan from the very beginning.
O twice-born one, he who does not see Arundhatī, Dhruva, the shadow of the moon (Soma-chāyā), and the Great Path (Mahāpatha) shall not live beyond a year.
Having seen trees with golden branches and cities of the Gandharvas,
if he should see ghosts and Piśācas, he lives for ten months.
If one's urine or feces always appear with the luster of gold or silver,
whether perceived directly or in a dream, he shall live for nine months.
He who suddenly becomes stout or suddenly becomes emaciated,
and who is indeed altered from his natural state, lives for only eight months.
If one's footprint appears in dust or even in mud,
whether in front or behind, such a person lives for seven months.
He upon whose head a crow, a pigeon, or a vulture settles,
as do carnivorous birds, shall live for six months.
If, moreover, his shadow is seen to be crushed by a shower of wind or a shower of dust,
or if he perceives it to be deformed, he shall live for five months.
If one sees an indivisible lightning flash situated in the southern direction, that yogin shall live for four months; of this there is no doubt.
Clad in red garments and perfumes, wearing garlands, he may go facing south;
or he may mount a donkey or a camel—if so, he does not live beyond three months.
If a man should see a rainbow over water during the day, he will die within two months; there is no doubt about this.
Indeed, for one who has just bathed, if the thighs and feet dry up,
or if he does not see his own reflection in water or in a mirror;
Or if one sees a deformed shadow, he lives for one month;
or if there should be smoke on his head, he lives for half a month.
He whose body emits the odor of a corpse and who suffers from loose teeth,
and who sees himself dead in a dream, lives for twelve days.
He whose hands are black, whose tongue has the luster of a lotus, whose face is indeed like a lotus,
and who has red pustules on his cheeks, shall live for four days.
If the wind cuts through the vital points in one's limbs,
that man, though he be a Brahmin, may live for three days, but after that there will be doubt.
If one touched by water does not shiver, and lives for two days;
if he hears no sound in his ear nor sees light with his eyes—
he is indeed a Brahmin who is still alive, and one should have him perform auspicious rites.
In the *Vāyupurāṇa*: "If one should go toward the southern direction on a chariot yoked with bears and monkeys while singing in a dream, one should know that death has arrived."
If a woman wearing black garments, dark-complexioned, or singing,
leads one toward the southern direction in a dream, even he does not live.
A man who in a dream sees a torn garment, a black garment,
or a naked ascetic, should know that death has arrived.
A "śramaṇa" is a Kṣapaṇaka.
But one who is submerged up to the surface of his head in an ocean of mud—
having seen such a thing in a dream, he does not live even for an instant.
He who for ten nights sees ashes, charcoal, hair, a dried-up river, or serpents, does not live.
He who, in a dream, is struck with stones by hideous, dark-complexioned men with uplifted weapons, does not live long.
If jackals howl facing him at daybreak, at the rising of the sun, that man shall indeed have his life departed.
If, immediately after eating, one's heart is oppressed by hunger and the teeth begin to chatter, one should declare that person's life-span to be exhausted.
But he who trembles again and again, whether by night or by day,
and does not perceive the scent of lamps, should know that death has arrived.
If one should see variegated garments at night and the circle of stars during the day,
or if one does not see oneself in the eyes of others, that person does not live.
He whose single eye flows, whose ears and nose are whirling,
and whose nose becomes crooked, should be known as one whose life has departed.
He whose tongue is black and rough, whose mouth has the luster of a lotus,
and who has red swellings on his cheeks— death has approached him.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: "If one who has fallen into a pit dies in his sleep and does not rise from that abyss, his life comes to an end."
The gaze is upward and unsteady,
the face is flushed and repeatedly turning,
there is heat in the mouth, and the navel is sunken.
They declare it to be another body for men.
He who enters fire in a dream and does not emerge again,
or likewise from entering water— for him, life ends there.
If a man sees his own garment as stainless white, red, or likewise black,
one should indeed predict that death is near for him.
When there is a reversal of one's own nature and a deviation from one's innate character,
men say that Yama and Antaka have drawn near to them.
Those whom he has constantly disciplined and who are considered his most venerable, he treats with contempt and reviles.
He does not worship the deities, he reviles his elders, teachers, and Brahmins,
and he shows disrespect toward his parents and his sons-in-law.
When the time has arrived for yogis, those possessed of knowledge, and other great-souled ones, that [state] should be recognized by the discerning as the Supreme Person (puruṣa).
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"And when one perceives a lizard at the aperture of Brahmā, which has black garments and a yellow color..."
Then he abandons that body, O protectorless one, like a fool in a fearful forest.
At sunrise and sunset, or at midnight,
one should cast the shadow of the moon upon one's head; likewise,
having extended the two staff-like arms, one should [cast] one's own shadow.
Having seen the headless trunk (kabandha), he abandons the body.
Seeing her deprived of her right arm, he would have abandoned his elder brother;
yet seeing her deprived of her left arm, he did not.
Then one should abandon one's two sons and one's wife.
They do not see Arundhatī, though she has been seen before in any way;
likewise, they say that Dhruva, the full moon, and even the lamp [are no longer seen].
O King, those who have a missing foot on the right side have but a year to live; likewise, those who do not see their own reflection in the eyes of others.
They too have a lifespan of one year; their form is like the shadow of a self, and they possess excessive luster, excessive wisdom, or lack of wisdom, as well as radiance.
The transformation of one's natural constitution over six months is a sign of death;
he disregards the deities and comes into conflict with Brahmins.
A complexion that has become dark or blackish for six months is a sign of death;
one whose navel is decayed like a wheel perceives a hole in the moon.
Likewise, one who beholds the thousand-rayed sun [at night] is subject to death within seven nights;
there is also the twitching of the ears and nose, the clashing of teeth, and loss of passion.
O Lord of Men, he whose perception is lost, who possesses a disfigured appearance, in whom sudden death is foreseen,
and whose left eye twitches without cause— [such a person is doomed].
And smoke arises from the crown of the head as a sign of imminent death;
having recognized these signs of his own end, a self-possessed man [should act accordingly].
At night, one should unite the self within oneself with the Supreme Self;
awaiting that time, whatever is to come shall happen for its sake.
If he should desire not to die but wish to remain, he should perform this rite;
being composed, he should maintain all fragrances and flavors.
Likewise, O bull among men, having understood this and having fixed his concentration with a focused inner self directed toward death;
The yogin should mutter [the mantra] through the yoga of death by means of the supreme self;
having reached dissolution into Kṛṣṇa, he shall go to the unborn, auspicious, and imperishable state—
the eternal, immovable abode that is difficult to attain for those who have not disciplined themselves.
Likewise,
O King, he who meets his end when the sun has reached its northern course,
and under an auspicious constellation and at a holy moment, is a doer of meritorious deeds.
Now follows the departure of the soul; on this point, Devala says:
Having abandoned fear and despondency, becoming pure and composed,
the twice-born man should indeed go forth toward either the eastern or the northern direction.

On a site sloping toward the east or north, level, free of stationary obstacles, and pure, the twice-born man, having shaken off his impurities, should perform [the rite] according to that very procedure with its instructions.
One should maintain the concentration (*dhāraṇā*) upon the crown of the head for one hundred or even eight hundred [breaths].
In a place "devoid of stationary objects" (*niḥsthāvare*), meaning free from trees and the like,
the wind of one who is exhausted by these concentrations shall then ascend upward.
The yogin who consists of the syllable *Oṃ* becomes imperishable while remaining within the imperishable;
thus the yogin devoted to yoga attains nirvāṇa.
Having perceived the signs of death, the best of ascetics, a yogi devoted to meditation, should remain intent on dhyāna;
abandoning the body while meditating, he goes to the Supreme Maheśvara.
The Sāṃkhya is solitary, ultimate, the supreme Brahman, eternal,
and free from birth, death, old age, disease, fear, and attachment.
The knower of reality, whose mind is absorbed in that, approaches that which is difficult for even the gods or hosts of sages to reach and hard to transcend.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
Having seen an ill omen, the yogi then abandons the fear of death;
having perceived its true nature, he remains until the appointed time arrives.
During that period, the knower of yoga should likewise practice yoga every day,
whether in the forenoon, the afternoon, or at midday.
Or rather, during whichever part of the night that ill omen was observed,
one should remain engaged in yoga practice right there until that very day has arrived.
Then, having abandoned all fear and conquered that time,
the self-possessed man should remain in that very dwelling— or wherever his own steadfastness lies.
Having conquered the three qualities, the wise yogi should unite with the Supreme Self;
becoming one with the Self through the mind, he should abandon the fluctuations of the consciousness.
Beyond that, he attains the supreme nirvāṇa, which is beyond the senses, not within the range of the intellect,
and which cannot be described.
In the Mahābhārata,
the Blessed One said:
"And at the time of death, remembering Me alone while casting off the body,"
He who proceeds in this manner attains true being; there is no doubt about this.
Whatever state of being one remembers when one finally leaves the body at the end,
to that very state one goes, O son of Kuntī, for one is constantly permeated by that state of being.
Therefore, at all times remember me and be enlightened by me;
with your mind and intellect dedicated to me, you shall come to me alone, without doubt.
With a mind disciplined by the yoga of practice and not wandering elsewhere,
O Pārtha, one goes to the supreme, divine Person by constantly meditating upon Him.
Whoever should meditate upon the ancient Seer, the ruler, subtler than the subtle,
the sustainer of all, whose form is inconceivable—
Of solar hue, beyond the darkness.
At the time of departure, with a steady mind, endowed with devotion and the power of yoga,
one should properly fix the vital breath between the eyebrows.
He attains that supreme, divine Person.
That which those who know the Vedas call the Imperishable,
into which the ascetics free from passion enter,
and desiring which they lead the life of celibacy—
I shall declare that state to you in brief.
Having restrained all the gates of the senses and fixed the mind within the heart,
placing the vital breath of the self in the head, he remains established in the practice of yoga-concentration.
Uttering the single-syllable Brahman "Om" and remembering Me,
he who departs, casting off the body, attains the supreme goal.
For that yogi who, with a mind focused on no other, remembers me constantly and perpetually,
I am easily attained, O Pārtha, for him who is ever-disciplined.
Having come to Me, these great-souled ones do not attain rebirth— which is transient and an abode of suffering— for they have reached the supreme perfection.
[258] Manu says: Just as a tree leaves the riverbank, or as a bird leaves a tree,
so one who abandons this body is liberated from the crocodile of distress.
Having cast off both good deeds toward those dear to him and evil deeds toward those unpleasant,
he attains the eternal Brahman through the yoga of meditation.
In the Mahābhārata:
Being liberated from evils like the moon from the clouds,
free from passion and awaiting his time, the steadfast man attains perfection through fortitude.
Now, regarding the path beginning with light, Yājñavalkya says:
"Infinite are its rays, which reside in the heart like a lamp."
White, black, tawny, blue, brownish-red, yellow, and crimson.
One among them stands above; having pierced the solar orb and transcended the world of Brahmā, by that [path] one goes to the supreme goal.
That other hundred rays of his which are positioned directly upwards—
by means of them, he attains the bodies and abodes of the gods.
Because his rays below are of a single form and of dull luster,
he wanders here helplessly through them for the sake of experiencing karma.
In the Mahābhārata it is said: "For one who ascends by means of the feet, the station of Viṣṇu is declared;
but by means of the shanks, one shall attain the Vasu gods—so have we heard."
By kneeling on both knees, one shall obtain all the great-souled beings who are to be accomplished;
by the hips, the earth; and by the thighs, Prajāpati.
They say that from his two sides he goes to the Maruts and the gods, from the nāgas to the moon itself,
from his two arms to Indra, and from his chest to Rudra.
By constantly upholding this seer (ṛṣi) as a deity, one attains the unsurpassed;
furthermore, one shall obtain all the gods through the mouth and all [objects] through the ear.
With the nose he [beheld] all of them, with the two eyes the Sun himself,
with the eyebrows the two divine Aśvins, and then with the forehead the ancestors.
He likewise attains the all-pervading Brahmā, the first-born of the gods, through his head.
Yājñavalkya says: Indeed, he [the Self] is to be sought after by all the stages of life (āśramas) in this very manner;
furthermore, He is to be seen, reflected upon, and heard by the twice-born.
Those twice-born ones who thus find this [truth], and those who have retired to the forest and worship it with supreme faith, attain the Truth.
In due order, they pass through the flame, the day, the bright fortnight, and likewise the northern solstice,
the world of the gods, the sun, and that which possesses lightning.
A person born of the mind (mānasa-puruṣa) approaches those staying there in the world of Brahmā and makes them [fit for it];
for them, there is no returning again to this world.
For those men who have conquered heaven by means of sacrifice, austerity, and gifts,
[they go] by way of smoke, night, the dark fortnight, and the southern solstice.
To the world of the ancestors, to the moon, to the wind, to rain, to water, and to the earth—
they arise here in this sequence and return there once again.
He who does not understand these two paths of his own self shall become either a venomous snake,
a moth, an insect, or a worm.

This Supreme Self is to be sought after in various ways by those belonging to all stages of life (*āśrama*). He states that very method: “It is to be seen,” meaning it is to be made directly perceived (*aparokṣīkartavya*). He states the means for that: “It is to be heard and reflected upon. “To be heard” means it is to be determined through the study of Vedānta; “to be reflected upon” means it is to be investigated through logical reasoning. Thereafter, it becomes directly perceived through meditation. Those twice-born ones who, endowed with great faith, have resorted to the forest (*āraṇyaka*), a secluded place, and worship this True Brahman in the manner described, they “find” it—they obtain and attain it. He describes the path of the gods (*devayāna*) leading to the attainment of Brahman: “In due order, they come into being. Those who have known the Self, “in due order,” reach the stations of the presiding deities of fire and so forth, which constitute the path to liberation. These wise ones attain the supreme state. “*Arcis*” is fire. “*Ahar*” is the day. “*Śuklaḥ*” is the bright fortnight. “*Uttaram*” is the northern solstice. “*Devalokam*” is the abode of the gods. “*Savitā*” is the sun. “*Tejaḥ*” is light. For those who have thus reached the stations beginning with *arcis* in this sequence, a “mental person” (*mānasaḥ puruṣaḥ*) makes them inhabitants of the world of Brahmā. The world of Brahmā is the world that is Brahman itself; he leads them there. They become one with the Supreme Self. He describes the path of the ancestors (*pitṛyāna*) with the words beginning with “by sacrifice,” etc. “But those who”—meaning those who, through sacrifices, gifts, and austerities, are enjoyers of the fruits of all worlds—they, having reached in due order the deities presiding over the entities beginning with smoke, and having again reached air, rain, water, and earth, and having attained the state of rice and other grains, enter the womb of transmigratory beings. “*Daṃdaśūkaḥ*” refers to venomous serpents and the like.
In the Mahābhārata:
"O bull among the best of men, I shall declare that time at which departing yogins go either to non-return or to return."
Fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, and the six months of the northern solstice—
departing there, people who know Brahman go to Brahman.
Smoke, night, as well as the dark fortnight, and the six months of the sun’s southern course—
having attained the lunar light during that time, the yogin returns.
These two paths, the bright and the dark, are considered to be eternal for the world;
by one a person goes to non-return, by the other he returns again.
Knowing these two paths, O Pārtha, no yogin whatsoever is deluded.
Therefore, at all times, be disciplined in yoga, O Arjuna.
Whatever meritorious fruit is prescribed for the Vedas, sacrifices, austerities, and gifts—
all that he transcends by knowing this.
The yogi attains the supreme, primordial state.
By the words “Agni is light,” the deity of the flame (arcis) is indicated;
and thus says the Śruti: “From the flame to the day, from the day to the waxing fortnight.”
By the words "day" and so forth, the deities presiding over them are indicated.
Likewise:
"Even the gods are bewildered on the path of one who has become the self of all beings, who perceives all beings correctly, and who seeks the state of his own true nature."
Just as his coming was not seen, even so was the departure of this Great-souled One.

Thus ends the Mokṣakāṇḍa (the Section on Liberation) in the Kṛtyakalpataru composed by Śrī Lakṣmīdhara, the son of Śrī Hṛdayadhara, who served as the Great Minister for Peace and War to the illustrious Govindacandra, the Emperor of Emperors.
